tip: Creeping fescue of lawns and verges with reddish-tinged panicle; leaf sheaths of non-flowering shoots split, distinguishing it from Sheep's-fescue.

name: Festuca vivipara
tip: Upland tufted fescue whose spikelets turn into small leafy plantlets rather than flowers; tussocky on mountain grassland and rocks.

name: Glyceria declinata
tip: Low, creeping, often muddy-margin grass with a slender raceme and spikelets on short stalks; leaves are bluish-green and the ligule is long.

name: Glyceria fluitans
tip: Wet-ground grass floating in ponds and ditches with a long, narrow, one-sided raceme of nearly stalkless spikelets; ligule long and pointed.

name: Glyceria maxima
tip: Very tall water-edge grass making dense stands, with a big pyramidal panicle of small spikelets and broad leaves; shorter ligule than Floating Sweet-grass.

name: Glyceria notata
tip: Wet-ground sweet-grass with an open panicle of lined spikelets, branches spreading; leaves medium broad and shorter than Reed Sweet-grass.

name: Helictochloa pratensis
tip: Oat-grass of chalk grassland with stiff, blue-green leaves and few large spikelets with a bent awn; leaves are folded and hairless.

name: Holcus lanatus
tip: Softly downy, grey-green grass with velvety leaves and sheaths; pinkish-white panicle with spikelets bearing a short hooked awn; ligule short.

name: Holcus mollis
tip: Similar to Yorkshire-fog but leaves hairless with hairy nodes and creeping rhizomes; spikelet awns stick out clearly beyond the glumes.

name: Hordeum distichon
tip: Cultivated cereal with a stiff nodding head of long-awned spikelets, only the central one of each three fertile; leaves broad.

name: Hordeum murinum
tip: Annual of walls and waysides with a bristly, yellowish-green spike that breaks up; central spikelet of each three is stalkless, laterals stalked.

name: Hordeum secalinum
tip: Perennial barley of old damp meadows with a narrower, shorter-awned spike than Wall Barley, blue-green leaves and a bristly feel.

name: Koeleria macrantha
tip: Dense, shiny, pale spike-like panicle on dry calcareous grassland; leaves bluish with soft hairs at the base and no awns.

name: Lolium multiflorum
tip: Rye-grass with awns on the spikelets and rolled young leaves, broader and glossier than Perennial Rye-grass; short-lived, sown in leys.

name: Lolium perenne
tip: Common sown grass with a flat two-rowed spike, spikelets facing the stem edge-on and awnless; young leaves folded, shiny underneath.

name: Melica uniflora
tip: Woodland grass with delicate loose raceme of few brownish-purple spikelets; no awns, sheaths slightly hairy and ligule short with a lobe.

name: Milium effusum
tip: Tall, graceful woodland grass with a large open panicle of drooping branches, small unawned spikelets, broad flat soft leaves and a long ligule.

name: Molinia caerulea
tip: Large tussocks on wet heath with a narrow purplish panicle; ligule is a fringe of hairs and the stem has only one node near the base.

name: Nardus stricta
tip: Wiry, bristly-leaved tussock of acid upland grass with a slim one-sided spike of purplish spikelets; leaves stiff and harsh, bleached in winter.

name: Phalaris arundinacea
tip: Tall riverside grass making stands, with a lobed greenish-purple panicle becoming buff; flat, broad, rough-edged leaves and long ligule.

name: Phalaris canariensis
tip: Birdseed casual with a short, egg-shaped, dense head of pale striped spikelets with winged keels; stem leaves broad and unawned.

name: Phleum bertolonii
tip: Short cylindrical head with short awns and a wedge-shaped, shorter spikelet than Timothy; smaller grass of dry grassland, tapered cylinder.

name: Phleum pratense
tip: Long, narrow, evenly cylindrical head, soft and pale green; spikelets with short awns, and the stem base is swollen into a bulb.

name: Phragmites australis
tip: Very tall, reedy grass of fens and margins forming vast stands with purplish silky plumes; ligule is a fringe of hairs and leaves are broad.

name: Poa angustifolia
tip: Meadow-grass with narrow, stiff, rolled blue-green leaves and creeping rhizomes; panicle open and slightly smaller than Smooth Meadow-grass.

name: Poa annua
tip: Small, pale-green, tufted grass flowering all year; crinkled leaf blades with a boat-shaped tip and a spreading panicle; very common on paths.

name: Poa compressa
tip: Distinctive for its flat, wiry stems and blue-green leaves; narrow dense panicle, creeping rhizomes, grows on walls and dry ground.

name: Poa humilis
tip: Meadow-grass similar to Smooth Meadow-grass, with blue-green leaves and slender creeping rhizomes; panicle more open with spreading branches.

name: Poa nemoralis
tip: Slender woodland meadow-grass with wiry, thin stems and a thin open panicle; leaves narrow and tufted with a very short ligule.

name: Poa pratensis
tip: Common meadow-grass spreading by rhizomes with smooth sheaths and a short ligule; leaf tips boat-shaped, with twin lines along the leaf blade.

name: Poa trivialis
tip: Meadow-grass of damp shaded ground with a long pointed ligule and rough sheaths; stoloniferous and light green, with panicle open.

name: Polypogon viridis
tip: Introduced grass of damp places with a dense, green, lobed cylindrical panicle that has no awns; stems often creeping and ligule long.

name: Puccinellia distans
tip: Grass of saltmarsh and salted road verges with branches bent downwards once flowering has finished; small spikelets and no awns.

name: Puccinellia maritima
tip: Creeping grass of salt marshes with bluish-green flat or folded leaves and a stiff panicle with spreading branches; no awns.

name: Schedonorus arundinaceus
tip: Coarse, tall tufted grass with broad rough leaves, auricles with hairs on the edge, and a large panicle; spikelets awnless or shortly awned.

name: Schedonorus giganteus
tip: Woodland grass with a large nodding panicle of long-awned spikelets and broad shiny leaves with small auricles; shade-loving.

name: Schedonorus pratensis
tip: Meadow grass with a narrow panicle with shiny, unawned spikelets, hairless auricles and glossy leaves, shorter than Tall Fescue and finer.

name: Trisetum flavescens
tip: Shining golden-yellow panicle on hay meadows; spikelets have a fine bent awn and sheaths and leaves are softly hairy; ligule short.

name: Triticum aestivum
tip: Cultivated cereal with a stiff, thick, two-rowed ear; either awnless or awned varieties, with broader leaves and short ligule.

name: Vulpia bromoides
tip: Small annual with a short, stiff, curved spike-like raceme, spikelets with a long awn; upper sheath not enclosing the panicle base.

name: Vulpia myuros
tip: Annual of dry waste ground with a long, thin, curved head whose lower part is often hidden in the upper leaf sheath; spikelets long-awned.

name: Agrimonia eupatoria
tip: Tall spike of small yellow flowers with hooked burrs; fruit grooved to the base, leaves lacking lemon scent; dry grassland and verges. Compare Fragrant Agrimony

name: Agrimonia procera
tip: Taller and coarser than Agrimony, scented when crushed; fruit bell-shaped with spreading lower bristles, grooves only part way; favours shady hedge banks and woodland edges.

name: Alchemilla filicaulis
tip: One of the lady's-mantle microspecies, a specialist group; leaves hairy, stems with downward-pressed hairs; yellow-green flowers without petals; grassland and verges, mainly north and west.

name: Alchemilla glabra
tip: Lady's-mantle with leaves and stems hairless, rounded lobes with teeth; upland grassland, rock ledges and roadsides in the north and west. Specialist group; check with a specialist.

name: Alchemilla mollis
tip: Large garden plant with soft velvety hairy leaves and big frothy yellow-green flower sprays; escapes onto roadsides and waste ground. Native lady's-mantles are smaller and less downy.

name: Alchemilla xanthochlora
tip: Lady's-mantle with leaves mostly hairless above but hairy beneath on veins, stems hairy low down; damp grassland, verges and woods. Part of a specialist microspecies group.

name: Aphanes arvensis
tip: Tiny low, greyish, hairy annual with fan-shaped three-lobed leaves and minute greenish flowers hidden in leaf axils; arable and dry bare ground. Separate from Slender Parsley-piert by larger fruit.

name: Aphanes australis
tip: Tiny annual like Parsley-piert but fruit smaller, sepal tube narrower and more cylindrical; acid sandy soils, arable and bare ground. Needs a lens to separate.

name: Comarum palustre
tip: Wetland plant with dark purplish-red star-like flowers, sepals longer than petals; leaves with five or seven toothed leaflets; bogs, fens and wet margins.

name: Cotoneaster horizontalis
tip: Low shrub with fishbone-pattern branches, tiny glossy rounded leaves and pinkish-white flowers; red berries persist; escapes onto walls, rocks and dunes. Flat habit separates it from other cotoneasters.

name: Cotoneaster integrifolius
tip: Small evergreen shrub with leaves white-felted beneath, pink-tinged flowers and red fruits; spreads on limestone cliffs and rocks. Leaves smaller than Himalayan Cotoneaster.

name: Cotoneaster simonsii
tip: Upright semi-evergreen shrub with orange-red fruits and flowers pink outside; leaves hairy beneath. Common bird-sown escape on hedges and waste ground; taller than Wall Cotoneaster.

name: Crataegus laevigata
tip: Hawthorn with shallow three-lobed leaves and flowers with two or three styles and fruits with two stones; ancient woodland and old hedges, mainly lowland England.

name: Crataegus monogyna
tip: Common hedge thorn with deeply cut lobed leaves and one style per flower, one stone per haw; flowers May, white; compare shallow-lobed Midland Hawthorn.

name: Filipendula ulmaria
tip: Tall plant of damp places with frothy creamy flower heads, almond scent and divided leaves white-downy beneath; compare Dropwort of dry chalk.

name: Filipendula vulgaris
tip: Low plant of dry chalk and limestone grassland with fern-like, finely cut leaves and flat heads of creamy flowers, buds tinged pink; much smaller than Meadowsweet.

name: Fragaria ananassa
tip: Larger than Wild Strawberry in flower, fruit and leaves; white flowers often with more than five petals; escapes from gardens onto verges and waste ground.

name: Fragaria vesca
tip: Small creeping plant with three-leaflet leaves, white flowers and tiny red fruit with seeds on the surface; woods, banks. Barren Strawberry has dry fruit and notched petals.

name: Geum rivale
tip: Nodding bell-like flowers dull orange-pink with purple-brown sepals; damp woods, meadows, streamsides. Hybridises with Wood Avens, giving intermediate flowers.

name: Geum urbanum
tip: Upright yellow five-petalled flowers and hooked fruit burrs; lower leaves pinnate with big terminal lobe; shady hedgerows and woods. Flowers face up, unlike Water Avens.

name: Malus domestica
tip: Cultivated apple escaping from gardens: leaves downy beneath, white flowers flushed pink, large sweet fruit. Wild Crab Apple has hairless leaves and small sour fruit.

name: Malus sylvestris
tip: Native tree of woods and hedges with blossom white flushed pink; leaves hairless when mature, small sour yellow-green fruit; twigs sometimes spiny. Cultivated Apple has downy leaves.

name: Potentilla anglica
tip: Creeping yellow cinquefoil with stalked leaves of three or five leaflets, flowers with four or five petals, rooting at nodes later; heaths, woods. Compare Tormentil and Creeping Cinquefoil.

name: Potentilla anserina
tip: Creeping plant with silvery feathery leaves and solitary yellow flowers on long stalks, rooting stolons; trampled grassland, tracks, damp ground.

name: Potentilla erecta
tip: Slender yellow flower with four petals, unlike other cinquefoils; leaves stalkless with three or five leaflets; heaths, moors, acid grassland.

name: Potentilla reptans
tip: Long creeping rooting stems; leaves with five stalked leaflets, yellow flowers with five petals; hedgebanks, roadsides, grassland. Compare Trailing Tormentil with fewer leaflets.

name: Potentilla sterilis
tip: Looks like Wild Strawberry but petals are white with gaps between, the end leaflet tooth shorter, and no fleshy fruit; very early flowers on dry banks and woodland edges.

name: Poterium sanguisorba
tip: Chalk grassland plant with rounded green-purple flower heads, red stigmas at top and stamens below; leaves of many toothed leaflets, cucumber-scented. Compare Great Burnet, taller with dark red heads.

name: Prunus avium
tip: Tall tree with white flowers in clusters, glossy red-brown peeling bark with horizontal lines, drooping leaves; fruit red to black. Flowers April, with the new leaves.

name: Prunus cerasifera
tip: Early white flowers, often before leaves, from February; twigs green and hairless, often thornless; bears round red or yellow plums. Hedges and bushes. Blackthorn flowers later and is thorny.

name: Prunus domestica
tip: Includes Bullace and Damson; larger oval leaves, downy twigs, flowers white in pairs; fruit bigger than Blackthorn sloes. Hedgerow tree from gardens; sometimes slightly spiny.

name: Prunus laurocerasus
tip: Large evergreen shrub with big glossy leathery leaves, almond smell when crushed, and upright spikes of small white flowers; black cherry-like fruit. Compare Portugal Laurel with red leaf stalks.

name: Prunus lusitanica
tip: Evergreen shrub with dark glossy leaves on red stalks, long spikes of fragrant white flowers appearing in summer, later than Cherry Laurel; fruit dark purple.

name: Prunus padus
tip: Drooping spikes of white almond-scented flowers; leaves oval, finely toothed; black bitter fruit; damp woods, northern England and Scotland. Compare Wild Cherry with clusters not spikes.

name: Prunus spinosa
tip: Spiny black-barked thicket shrub with white flowers on bare twigs in early spring; fruit are blue-black sloes. Hawthorn flowers later and has lobed leaves.

name: Pyracantha coccinea
tip: Thorny evergreen with clusters of small white flowers and bright orange or red berries in autumn; walls, hedges and waste ground. Cotoneasters lack thorns.

name: Pyrus communis
tip: Tree with glossy oval leaves, white flowers with purple anthers, branches sometimes spiny; gritty pear fruit. Apple has hairier leaves and pink-tinged flowers.

name: Rosa arvensis
tip: Trailing white-flowered rose with green purple-tinged stems, hooked prickles; styles joined into a column; woods and hedges, mainly southern England. Flowers later than Dog-rose.

name: Rosa caesia
tip: Dog-rose group with hairy leaves and leaflets that are double-toothed, bluish-green; usually sepals persistent on hip; northern and western hedges. Needs careful checking against Dog-rose.

name: Rosa canina
tip: Commonest wild rose, arching stems with hooked prickles, pale pink or white flowers, hairless leaflets; sepals soon reflexed and drop. Compare Sweet-briar scented and Field-rose with joined styles.

name: Rosa rubiginosa
tip: Rose with apple-scented sticky glands under leaflets, strong hooked and straight prickles, bright pink flowers; calcareous scrub and grassland. Smell crushed leaves.

name: Rosa rugosa
tip: Dense bushy garden rose with wrinkled leaves, very bristly stems, large magenta or white flowers and big tomato-like hips; common on dunes and verges.

name: Rosa sherardii
tip: Dog-rose relative with soft hairy leaves, glandular, bluish; pink flowers; hip bristly, sepals persistent; northern and western hedges and rocky places. Needs careful checking.

name: Rosa spinosissima
tip: Low suckering rose of dunes and heaths with dense straight prickles, small ferny leaves and creamy white flowers; hips round and black-purple.

name: Rubus caesius
tip: Trailing slender bramble with bluish waxy bloom on stems and few big drupelets; leaves of three leaflets; flowers white; calcareous grassland and damp sites. Fewer prickles than Bramble.

name: Rubus fruticosus
tip: Hundreds of microspecies needing a specialist; arching prickly stems, white or pink flowers, black fruit in summer and autumn. Raspberry has white-felted leaves; Dewberry has bloom.

name: Rubus idaeus
tip: Upright stems with weak prickles, leaves white-felted beneath, small white flowers with narrow petals; red fruit that parts from the core; heaths, woods and clearings.

name: Rubus saxatilis
tip: Low unarmed herb of rocky northern slopes with three-leaflet leaves, small white narrow-petalled flowers and few red berries; no strong prickles. Spreads by runners.

name: Sanguisorba officinalis
tip: Tall plant of damp meadows with oval dark crimson heads and divided leaves with toothed leaflets; flowers lack petals. Salad Burnet is shorter, dry and green-purple.

name: Sorbus aria
tip: Tree with oval toothed leaves strongly white-felted beneath; white flowers, red fruits. Rowan has pinnate leaves; Sorbus has specialist microspecies groups. Chalk and limestone woodland.

name: Sorbus aucuparia
tip: Tree with pinnate leaves of toothed leaflets, flat clusters of creamy flowers and orange-red berries; heaths, woods and hills. Sorbus has specialist microspecies groups, mainly whitebeams.

name: Sorbus intermedia
tip: Planted tree with lobed leaves grey-felted beneath, shallowly cut, between Whitebeam and Rowan; flowers white, fruit orange-red; street and park tree that self-sows.

name: Sorbus torminalis
tip: Woodland tree with maple-like lobed leaves, hairless, turning red in autumn; clusters of white flowers; small brown speckled fruit. Ancient woods, mainly southern England.

name: Bolboschoenus maritimus
tip: Tall triangular-stemmed plant of brackish marshes and estuaries with a tight clump of chestnut-brown spikelets and long leafy bracts overtopping the head; leaves flat, keeled and rough-edged.

name: Carex acutiformis
tip: Blue-green broad leaves with a ligule that is long and pointed; two or three thick male spikes above, stout upright females below with pointed utricles; wet ground and ditches.

name: Carex arenaria
tip: Found on coastal dunes, with long creeping runners that send up stems in a straight line; spikes in a loose brownish cluster, each with male flowers on top and female below.

name: Carex binervis
tip: Moorland and heath sedge with a single male spike above and spaced, stalked, upright to slightly nodding female spikes; leaves greyish-green and utricles with two clear green ribs.

name: Carex canescens
tip: Small grey-green tufts in wet acid places, with several rounded, pale spikes spaced along the stem, each with female flowers above male; utricles pale and small.

name: Carex caryophyllea
tip: Low early-flowering sedge of dry grassland and limestone with one male spike and short downy-fruited female spikes; base of stems has reddish-purple sheaths; leaves short and soft.

name: Carex dioica
tip: Tiny single-spiked sedge of base-rich flushes and fens, with male and female spikes on separate plants; stems slender, leaves narrow, spreading by short runners.

name: Carex distans
tip: Coastal and brackish sedge with bluish-green leaves and a short ligule; female spikes widely spaced, small, held close to the stem, with a long-beaked yellowish-green utricle.

name: Carex disticha
tip: Wet meadow and fen sedge with long creeping runners; the spike is a dense brown cylinder of stacked small spikelets, male flowers in the middle and female at both ends.

name: Carex divulsa
tip: Greyish-green sedge of hedgebanks, with a long interrupted head of small spikes, lower ones well spaced, each with male above female; utricles brownish-green with a long beak.

name: Carex echinata
tip: Small yellowish-green sedge of wet acid ground whose few spikes cluster together and fruits spread out starlike when ripe; spikes show male above female within each.

name: Carex flacca
tip: Leaves distinctly blue-grey beneath, and stiff on chalk and limestone; blackish-purple male spikes with a short nodding female spike lower down; runs by rhizomes.

name: Carex hirta
tip: Leaves, sheaths and fruits all bear obvious hairs; creeping plant of rough grassland and ditches with widely spaced female spikes below two or three male spikes.

name: Carex hostiana
tip: Yellowish-tawny sedge of fens and flushes; compact female spikes are clustered near the male spike, each fruit with a bent-back short beak; leaves flat and rather pale.

name: Carex laevigata
tip: Broad, shiny, bright green leaves with smooth edges in damp woods; slender female spikes slightly nodding, widely spaced, on smooth stems, with a pale winged utricle.

name: Carex leporina
tip: A tight oval cluster of pale straw-coloured spikes at stem top, each with male flowers above female; damp grassland and rushy pastures; the fruit is flat and winged.

name: Carex muricata
tip: Green spikes on short compact stalks, with spreading fruit giving a prickly look; lowest spikes spaced, flowers male above female; includes similar close relatives, so check details.

name: Carex nigra
tip: Smooth blue-green leaves; one or two slender male spikes, and black-scaled narrow female spikes with short stalks in boggy and grassy places; fruit small and rounded.

name: Carex otrubae
tip: Dense, green, clustered head of spikes, often over 5 cm, with a long pointed ligule and a lower sheath that stays pale; damp grassland, ditches, often brackish.

name: Carex pallescens
tip: Pale green sedge with hairy leaves and sheaths; short egg-shaped female spikes hang on thin stalks below a single male spike; woods and grassland.

name: Carex panicea
tip: Waxy blue-green leaves like carnation foliage; one male spike and widely spaced female spikes with plump, rounded fruits bearing a short beak; damp meadows and fens.

name: Carex paniculata
tip: Forms large tussocks in fens and carr; branched, plume-like head of many small spikes, male and female mingled; stem sharply triangular and rough; leaves stiff.

name: Carex pendula
tip: Big tufted sedge with long, thick, drooping female spikes up to 16 cm hanging on slender stalks; leaves broad and shiny; woods and damp shady banks.

name: Carex pilulifera
tip: Small tufted heath sedge with round, hairy-fruited female spikes clustered tight at the base of the male spike, like little pills; leaves are soft and slender.

name: Carex pseudocyperus
tip: Yellow-green leaves and long hanging female spikes with fruits bearing long, spreading awns; edge of ponds and slow water; looks like Pendulous Sedge but spikes thinner.

name: Carex pulicaris
tip: Small wiry tufted sedge of damp base-rich ground with one small spike, male flowers above and shiny dark brown fruits below that curve down like fleas.

name: Carex remota
tip: Soft, thin, pale green leaves in shady damp woods and ditches; small green spikes well separated up the stem, with long leafy bracts below them; fruit tiny.

name: Carex riparia
tip: Big grey-green creeping sedge of pond edges with three to five thick male spikes and long upright females; leaves broad, rough-edged; the ligule is blunt.

name: Carex rostrata
tip: Bluish-green sedge of bogs and lake margins; yellowish female spikes with spreading bottle-shaped fruits having a long beak; leaves narrow and rolled.

name: Carex spicata
tip: Dense compact cluster of male and female spikes at the top of a sharply triangular stem; grassy verges and rough ground; fruits small, pointed and ribbed.

name: Carex sylvatica
tip: Bright green leaves and thin, long-stalked, drooping female spikes spaced up the stem; woodland sedge with fruit that is slender and beaked.

name: Carex vesicaria
tip: Swollen, inflated yellowish-green fruits spreading from stout female spikes; wet places, pond margins; leaves yellow-green with blunt ligule; paler than Bottle Sedge.

name: Cyperus longus
tip: Rare tall plant of wet places with a spreading umbel of reddish-brown flat spikelets and long leafy bracts; stem triangular; unlike a sedge, no sac-like fruits.

name: Eleocharis multicaulis
tip: Slender spike-rush of wet heaths and bogs, one brown spikelet per stem; stems many, thin and round; the sheath mouth is oblique and reddish.

name: Eleocharis palustris
tip: Leafless round green stems, each with a single large oval brown spikelet; creeping in shallow water and wet ground; the stem is smooth and ridged when dry.

name: Eleocharis quinqueflora
tip: Short stiff stems with a single small dark brown spikelet of few flowers on damp base-rich ground; lowest scale clasps the spikelet's base completely.

name: Eleogiton fluitans
tip: Aquatic plant with thin, soft floating leaves in pools and ditches; tiny single spikelet at stem tips; stems trail and root; looks like a slender mat of green threads.

name: Eriophorum angustifolium
tip: Several nodding white cottony heads per stem in acid bogs and wet moors; leaves keeled and triangular at tip; spreads by runners, not in tussocks.

name: Eriophorum vaginatum
tip: Single large white cottony head on each stem, forming dense tussocks on wet moorland and bogs; leaves thin and bristle-like; blooms early.

name: Isolepis setacea
tip: Tiny tufted plant with thread-like stems, a few small brown spikelets clustered at the side, and one longer bract; damp bare ground and paths.

name: Schoenoplectus lacustris
tip: Tall leafless round green stems with a drooping cluster of brown spikelets near the tip, in lakes and rivers; stem is dark green, not glaucous like Grey Club-rush.

name: Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani
tip: Very similar to Common Club-rush but stems greyish-blue and glaucous, spikelets paler with rough hairy scales; brackish and freshwater edges.

name: Schoenus nigricans
tip: Stiff dark tufts of narrow rush-like leaves in fens and wet heath; shiny blackish-brown, small spikelet head at stem tip with a long leafy bract.

name: Scirpus sylvaticus
tip: Tall plant of damp woods with broad leaves, a large branched head of many tiny clustered green spikelets, and a triangular stem; resembles a rush but is a sedge relative.

name: Trichophorum germanicum
tip: Dense tufts in moorland and bog, wiry round stems each with a small single brown spikelet; leaves reduced to sheaths with only tiny blades.

name: Taraxacum officinale agg.
tip: The familiar dandelion: a single yellow head on a hollow leafless stalk above a rosette of toothed leaves, milky sap, then a round seed clock. Hundreds of microspecies, which need a specialist.

name: Achillea distans
tip: Rare naturalised yarrow with finely divided hairy leaves and flat clusters of white to pinkish heads; a specialist should confirm it against garden yarrows.

name: Achillea filipendulina
tip: Garden escape with dense flat-topped clusters of bright golden yellow heads above grey-green, feathery, finely cut leaves; far more yellow than native yarrow.

name: Achillea maritima
tip: Coastal shingle and dune plant, densely white-woolly all over, with yellow button heads lacking rays; rare, found on southern and south-western coasts and eastern Ireland.

name: Achillea nobilis
tip: Yarrow-like plant with creamy white to pale yellow heads and finely cut greyish hairy leaves; rare casual, told from common yarrow by its cream colour.

name: Anaphalis margaritacea
tip: Garden escape on waste ground with white-woolly stems and narrow leaves; papery pearly white bracts surround small yellow discs, unlike any native cudweed.

name: Anthemis arvensis
tip: Arable weed with white-rayed daisy heads and finely divided leaves, but scentless, unlike stinking chamomile; stems are hairy and the receptacle bears scales.

name: Anthemis cotula
tip: Daisy-like weed of disturbed ground with white rays and a yellow cone; foul smell when crushed, and finely cut leaves, separate it from mayweeds.

name: Anthemis punctata
tip: Silvery silky-haired garden plant with white-rayed daisy heads and feathery leaves; occasional escape, mostly on walls and waste ground.

name: Arctotis aspera
tip: Rare casual from South Africa with large daisy heads, pale or yellowish rays, and woolly lobed leaves; mostly a bird-seed or garden escape.

name: Arnoseris minima
tip: Small annual with dandelion-like yellow heads on stalks that swell and club-shaped below the head; leafless stems, toothed rosette leaves; extinct in the wild, formerly eastern England.

name: Artemisia absinthium
tip: Aromatic, silvery silky-hairy plant with finely divided leaves and many small yellow-green nodding button heads; very bitter, found on rough ground and roadsides.

name: Artemisia campestris
tip: Rare plant of sandy Breckland heaths with slender, almost hairless, feathery-leaved stems and tiny yellowish-red nodding heads; East Anglia only.

name: Artemisia maritima
tip: Aromatic grey-white salt-marsh and sea-wall plant, cut leaves covered with fine felt, with small drooping greenish yellow heads in leafy spikes.

name: Artemisia norvegica
tip: Tiny alpine mugwort with silky silvery leaves and few drooping yellowish heads; extremely rare, known only from Scottish Highlands mountain sites.

name: Artemisia stelleriana
tip: Dune and sand plant, whitish felted all over with rounded lobed leaves; yellow button heads in spikes; naturalised on a few coasts.

name: Artemisia verlotiorum
tip: Tall spreading mugwort of waste ground, leaves dark green above and aromatic, with narrow segments; flowers late, in autumn, unlike common mugwort.

name: Bidens connata
tip: Rare plant of wet ground with leafy yellow discoid heads lacking rays, narrow toothed leaves, and barbed seeds that stick; mostly near the Thames.

name: Bidens frondosa
tip: North American bur-marigold of damp banks and ponds; leaves of three to five toothed leaflets, orange-yellow heads with few or no rays, and barbed seeds.

name: Buphthalmum salicifolium
tip: Garden escape with large yellow daisy heads on stems with narrow willow-like toothed leaves; occasional on grassy banks.

name: Buphthalmum speciosum
tip: Tall garden perennial with big yellow daisies with narrow rays and large heart-shaped toothed leaves; naturalised on streamsides and damp woods.

name: Calendula arvensis
tip: Rare casual with small yellow-orange daisy heads and narrow smooth to slightly toothed leaves; sticky-hairy, with curved seeds, distinct from garden pot marigold.

name: Carduus pycnocephalus
tip: Spiny thistle with spiny-winged, cottony stems and small purple heads in clusters; very localised near Plymouth and other south-western coast sites.

name: Carduus tenuiflorus
tip: Spiny-winged thistle with small, narrow pink-purple heads in tight clusters; stems cottony, mainly coastal, and heads are smaller than welted thistle.

name: Centaurea aspera
tip: Rare casual with purple heads whose bracts bear a stout spine and smaller spines at base; rough branched stems; formerly in dunes of south-west England.

name: Centaurea calcitrapa
tip: Spreading spiny plant with pink-purple heads, each bract bearing a long yellowish spine; found on waste ground and roadsides, mostly southern England.

name: Centaurea jacea
tip: Knapweed with dry papery brown bracts and pink-purple heads, often with enlarged rays; leaves narrow; casual in Britain, scattered on grassland.

name: Chamaemelum nobile
tip: Low, sweet-scented, mat-forming daisy with feathery leaves and white-rayed heads, found on sandy commons, grazed lawns and heaths; apple-like smell when crushed.

name: Cicerbita alpina
tip: Mountain plant of Scottish Highlands with tall leafy stems, pale blue-violet heads, and glandular-hairy bristles; shaded cliff ledges, unusual in a thistle-like plant.

name: Cicerbita bourgaei
tip: Tall garden escape with blue-violet heads and large lobed leaves with a big end lobe; rarely naturalised, hairy stem.

name: Cicerbita plumieri
tip: Tall naturalised plant of shady banks, with blue-lilac heads in loose clusters and large lobed leaves; stems lack glandular hairs, unlike common blue-sow-thistle.

name: Cirsium dissectum
tip: Slender thistle of damp meadows with unlobed, hardly spiny leaves white-felted beneath, and a single dull purple head; no winged stems.

name: Cirsium eriophorum
tip: Large thistle of chalk grassland with a big globe head covered with cobweb-like white wool, and fiercely spiny deeply cut leaves.

name: Cirsium oleraceum
tip: Unusual thistle with pale creamy yellow heads surrounded by big leaf-like bracts and only soft bristly leaves; rare casual of damp places.

name: Cirsium tuberosum
tip: Rare thistle with a single large purple head on a nearly leafless stem and deeply cut leaves; only on Wiltshire chalk grassland.

name: Coreopsis grandiflora
tip: Garden escape with big golden daisy heads with notched rays, and narrow or lobed leaves; hairless, found on banks and waste ground.

name: Cota tinctoria
tip: Escape with golden yellow daisy heads and finely cut, whitish hairy leaves; unlike chamomiles with white rays, it is wholly yellow.

name: Cotula alpina
tip: Tiny creeping rock-garden plant with small yellowish button heads and finely divided hairy leaves; casual in a few spots only.

name: Cotula australis
tip: Small branched annual weed of bare ground with feathery leaves and tiny yellowish button heads lacking rays; scarce casual.

name: Cotula coronopifolia
tip: Fleshy hairless plant of brackish mud and saltmarsh, with narrow leaves and yellow button heads without rays; naturalised in places.

name: Cotula squalida
tip: Creeping mat-forming lawn weed from New Zealand with feathery, finely divided leaves and tiny yellowish-brown button heads; spreading in lawns, mostly Scotland and Ireland.

name: Crepis foetida
tip: Annual hawk's-beard smelling unpleasantly, with nodding flower buds, pale yellow heads and downy lobed leaves; extremely rare, formerly Kent coast.

name: Crepis mollis
tip: Tall hawk's-beard of upland meadows and streamsides, with soft hairy, toothed clasping leaves and yellow heads; northern England and Scotland.

name: Crepis praemorsa
tip: Hawk's-beard with a basal rosette and almost leafless stem bearing pale yellow heads; in Britain recorded long ago in the north, perhaps extinct.

name: Delairea odorata
tip: Climber with glossy, fleshy, ivy-like lobed leaves and clusters of small yellow button heads; rare, in sheltered gardens and walls in the south-west.

name: Dittrichia graveolens
tip: Sticky, strong-smelling plant with narrow leaves and small yellow heads with short rays, flowering late; casual on salted roadsides and waste ground.

name: Dittrichia viscosa
tip: Tall sticky, aromatic fleabane with leafy stems and many yellow daisy heads in autumn; rare casual from the Mediterranean, mostly roadsides in southern England.

name: Doronicum columnae
tip: Garden escape with large yellow daisies on stems with heart-shaped basal leaves and smaller clasping stem leaves; naturalised on shady banks.

name: Doronicum plantagineum
tip: Garden escape with yellow daisy heads on stems with broad plantain-like basal leaves, finely hairy; occasionally naturalised in woods and verges.

name: Echinops bannaticus
tip: Spiny garden plant with ball-shaped blue heads and deeply cut leaves woolly beneath; rare escape, told from thistles by globe-shaped flower heads.

name: Echinops exaltatus
tip: Very tall spiny garden escape with ball-shaped whitish blue heads and deeply cut leaves white-felted beneath; uncommon on waste ground.

name: Echinops sphaerocephalus
tip: Tall spiny plant with big spherical grey-white to blue heads and deeply cut leaves, cobwebby underneath, with sticky glands; scattered garden escape.

name: Erigeron annuus
tip: Slender daisy with many small white heads with very narrow rays, toothed hairy leaves; spreading on walls and verges, mainly England; taller than common daisy.

name: Erigeron bonariensis
tip: Tall weed of urban pavements and waste ground with small whitish heads in leafy clusters, rays barely longer than the bracts; stems grey-hairy.

name: Erigeron borealis
tip: Small mountain plant of Scottish high-level rock ledges, with few mauve to purple rayed heads with yellow centre; leaves basal and hairy, scarce.

name: Erigeron floribundus
tip: Urban weed of walls and pavements with small whitish heads of tiny rays, narrow hairy toothed leaves; common in southern England, often mistaken for Canadian fleabane.

name: Erigeron glaucus
tip: Garden plant naturalised on coastal cliffs and walls with fleshy spoon-shaped leaves and big lilac to pink daisy heads with yellow centres.

name: Erigeron philadelphicus
tip: Garden escape with pink or white daisy-like heads with numerous very slender rays, soft hairy stem and clasping leaves; walls and pavements.

name: Erigeron sumatrensis
tip: Tall hairy weed of urban waste ground, heads cream with tiny rays hidden in cluster; resembles Canadian fleabane but greyer and taller.

name: Euthamia graminifolia
tip: Tall North American goldenrod with narrow grass-like leaves bearing translucent dots, flat-topped clusters of tiny golden yellow heads; naturalised on damp waste ground.

name: Felicia bergeriana
tip: Tender blue daisy from South Africa with narrow bristly leaves and sky-blue yellow-centred heads; occasional garden escape.

name: Filago germanica
tip: Small grey woolly annual of dry sandy ground, with clustered rounded heads on spiky pointed bracts; leaves narrow and erect, cudweed-like.

name: Filago lutescens
tip: Rare cudweed of sandy ground in eastern England, with woolly stems and heads in tight rounded clusters whose bract tips are reddish; specialist confirmation advised.

name: Filago pyramidata
tip: Rare cudweed of chalky arable edges, with broad white-woolly leaves and pointed five-angled heads that overtop the leaves; southern England only.

name: Galatella linosyris
tip: Rare limestone cliff plant with narrow stalkless leaves and clusters of yellow heads, usually lacking rays; sea cliffs in south-west England and Wales.

name: Galinsoga parviflora
tip: Small hairy annual of gardens and waste ground with tiny white three-rayed heads around yellow discs, oval toothed leaves; Shaggy-soldier is hairier.

name: Gamochaeta purpurea
tip: Low woolly annual of bare ground and paths, narrow grey-green leaves, small brownish heads clustered into a spike; scarce but spreading.

name: Gazania rigens
tip: Garden plant with big orange or yellow daisy heads and dark lobed leaves white-felted beneath; casual escape, especially on southern coasts.

name: Grindelia stricta
tip: Sticky North American coastal plant with large yellow daisies, sticky white gum on bracts, and toothed clasping leaves; casual on saltmarsh edges.

name: Helianthus tuberosus
tip: Tall sunflower relative with many yellow daisy heads in autumn, rough stems and broad toothed leaves; found on waste ground and river banks.

name: Helichrysum bellidioides
tip: Creeping mat-forming plant with small white-woolly rounded leaves and papery whitish button heads; rare garden escape, mostly in the south and west.

name: Helichrysum italicum
tip: Silver-leaved aromatic shrubby plant smelling of curry, with narrow leaves and flat clusters of small golden yellow button heads; garden escape on walls.

name: Helichrysum petiolare
tip: Sprawling garden plant with felted grey-white rounded leaves and small creamy button heads in clusters; rare casual on waste ground.

name: Hieracium alpinum
tip: Short mountain hawkweed of Scottish hills, with a single large yellow head, leaves mostly in a basal rosette, shaggy bristly stem; specialist needed to confirm.

name: Hieracium amplexicaule
tip: Hawkweed with glandular sticky hairs and stem leaves clasping the stem, yellow heads; grows on rocks and walls; specialist needed to confirm microspecies.

name: Hieracium anglicum
tip: Hawkweed microspecies with yellow dandelion-like heads and toothed leaves rosette-forming; widespread on rocks and walls in northern Britain; specialist needed to confirm.

name: Hieracium hethlandiae
tip: Hawkweed microspecies endemic to Shetland, found on cliffs and rocky ledges, with yellow dandelion-like heads; specialist needed to confirm identification.

name: Hieracium holosericeum
tip: Hawkweed microspecies of mountain cliffs with silky white hairs on leaves and yellow heads; specialist needed to confirm identification from others.

name: Hieracium lanatum
tip: Hawkweed microspecies with grey woolly leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; a specialist is needed to confirm it among similar hawkweeds.

name: Hieracium lanceolatum
tip: Hawkweed microspecies with narrow lance-shaped leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; a specialist is needed to confirm identification.

name: Hieracium latobrigorum
tip: One of many similar hawkweeds with leafy stems, toothed leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; only a specialist can confirm the species. Mainly upland Britain.

name: Hieracium leyi
tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow dandelion-like heads and toothed leaves on a branched stem; needs a specialist to confirm. Very local, chiefly in Wales and the Welsh borders.

name: Hieracium lingulatum
tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow heads and tongue-shaped leaves; separating it from other hawkweeds needs a specialist. Mainly rocky upland sites.

name: Hieracium prenanthoides
tip: Tall hawkweed with many stem leaves that clasp the stem, upper leaves heart-based, pale green; heads yellow with dark hairy bracts. Rocky ground and walls, mainly upland.

name: Hieracium proximum
tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow dandelion-like heads and toothed leaves; specialist needed to confirm. Rare and local, mostly northern Britain.

name: Hieracium speluncarum
tip: A critical hawkweed of rocky crags with yellow heads and toothed leaves; specialist needed to confirm. Very local, mainly Scotland and northern England.

name: Hieracium subcrocatum
tip: A critical hawkweed with orange-yellow dandelion-like heads and leafy stems; specialist needed to confirm. Rare, mainly Scotland.

name: Hieracium trichocaulon
tip: A critical hawkweed with a hairy stem, toothed leaves and yellow dandelion-like heads; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Hieracium vagum
tip: A critical hawkweed with yellow dandelion-like heads, leafy stems and toothed leaves; a specialist is needed to confirm it. Local in upland Britain.

name: Hieracium villosum
tip: Densely shaggy with long white hairs on stem and leaves, which clasp the stem; large yellow heads. Rock ledges on limestone and mountain crags in northern Britain.

name: Homogyne alpina
tip: Small mountain plant with round toothed glossy leaves and a leafless stem topped by a pinkish-purple tuft of tubular florets. Rare, Scottish mountains only.

name: Hypochaeris glabra
tip: Small hairless cat's-ear with shiny, lobed leaves and small yellow heads that barely open. Rare, on sandy or gravelly ground, mostly in south and east England.

name: Hypochaeris maculata
tip: Large yellow heads on a stem with a few scales, rough leaves usually blotched with purple spots; unlike common cat's-ear. Very rare on sea cliffs and limestone in Devon and Wales.

name: Inula helenium
tip: Very tall plant with huge, rough, softly downy leaves and big yellow shaggy-rayed heads; leaves white-felted beneath. Old medicinal plant, naturalised on roadsides and hedgerows.

name: Inula hookeri
tip: Garden plant with solitary large yellow heads with very narrow, spreading rays, and sticky-hairy stems; occasional garden escape on rough ground.

name: Inula orientalis
tip: Garden perennial with large solitary yellow heads on woolly stems, rays narrow and ragged; rare escape on tips and waste ground.

name: Inula salicina
tip: Stiff plant with hairless, shiny, stalkless leaves clasping the stem by heart-shaped bases, and yellow heads. Lake shores in Ireland and a few sites in Britain.

name: Jacobaea maritima
tip: Silvery-white woolly plant with deeply lobed leaves and yellow daisy-like heads; looks unlike common ragworts. Planted, naturalised on south and west coasts.

name: Jacobaea paludosa
tip: Tall ragwort with narrow, toothed, stalkless leaves woolly beneath and many yellow heads. Very rare, fens of East Anglia, reintroduced at Wicken Fen.

name: Lactuca saligna
tip: Slender lettuce with very narrow, often lobed leaves held upright against the stem, and small pale yellow heads. Rare, dry grassland and sea walls, south-east England.

name: Lactuca sativa
tip: Cultivated lettuce, bolting to a tall stem with small pale yellow heads; leaves oval, clasping the stem and not prickly. Occasional escape on tips and waste ground.

name: Lactuca tatarica
tip: Tall hairless lettuce with deeply cut leaves and pale blue-lilac heads. Rare casual of waste ground and shingle, chiefly coastal.

name: Laphangium luteoalbum
tip: Grey woolly cudweed with small clusters of yellowish-brown heads at the stem tips and leaves wrapping around the stem. Damp sandy ground, local in southern England.

name: Leucanthemella serotina
tip: Tall late-flowering plant with white daisy-like heads and narrow toothed leaves; looks like a big oxeye daisy but flowers in autumn. Garden escape on waste ground and roadsides.

name: Limbarda crithmoides
tip: Fleshy, hairless coastal plant with narrow, succulent leaves and golden-yellow daisy heads; unlike rock samphire its heads are not umbels. Salt marshes and sea cliffs.

name: Logfia gallica
tip: Tiny grey woolly annual which forks repeatedly, with clusters of small heads set in the forks and pointed leaves. Rare on sandy fields in south and east England.

name: Logfia minima
tip: Tiny, upright grey woolly annual with small clustered heads at stem tips and tiny narrow leaves. Dry sandy heaths and grassland, scattered.

name: Olearia macrodonta
tip: Evergreen shrub with holly-like leaves, wavy and spiny-toothed, white felted beneath, and clusters of white daisies. Planted in gardens, rarely persisting near the south-west coast.

name: Omalotheca norvegica
tip: Upright mountain cudweed with several brown-bracted heads in a spike along the stem, leaves green above and woolly beneath. Rare, Scottish mountains.

name: Omalotheca supina
tip: Tiny tufted mountain cudweed with one to few brown-bracted heads close to the ground and grey woolly leaves. Mountain tops in Scotland, northern England and Wales.

name: Osteospermum jucundum
tip: Mat-forming garden daisy with pink-purple rays, dark centre and toothed leaves; the garden escape is found in warm sheltered spots near the south-west coast.

name: Pericallis hybrida
tip: Pot plant with heart-shaped toothed leaves and clusters of showy daisies in many colours; occasional on tips and waste ground, rarely persisting.

name: Petasites albus
tip: Spreading plant with round, heart-shaped, toothed leaves, white felted beneath, appearing after small whitish heads. Naturalised near streams and in woods, mainly Scotland and northern England.

name: Petasites japonicus
tip: Huge, rounded leaves up to a metre across on stout stalks, with pale greenish-yellow heads in early spring; much larger than butterbur. Naturalised by streams and in wet woods.

name: Petasites pyrenaicus
tip: Winter-flowering plant with vanilla-scented pale lilac-white heads and rounded kidney-shaped leaves forming dense patches. Common on roadsides and banks.

name: Pilosella caespitosa
tip: Mouse-ear-hawkweed relative with pale yellow heads in tight clusters and bristly stem; lacks the orange-red of fox-and-cubs. Garden escape on banks and walls.

name: Pilosella flagellaris
tip: Mouse-ear hawkweed with leafy runners rooting at the tips and a solitary yellow head; leaves bristly and star-haired. A specialist may be needed to confirm it.

name: Pilosella peleteriana
tip: Mat-forming plant covered in long shaggy white hairs, with solitary pale yellow heads on short stems. Local on sandy ground and dunes, mostly coastal.

name: Pilosella praealta
tip: Tall hawkweed relative with compact clusters of small yellow heads and narrow bristly leaves; usually without runners. Rare, naturalised on banks and waste ground.

name: Pseudognaphalium undulatum
tip: Grey woolly cudweed with wavy-edged leaves clasping the stem and clusters of whitish heads. Casual from gardens or ports, occasional in the south.

name: Pulicaria vulgaris
tip: Small, branching, grey-hairy annual with little yellow daisies with short rays and wavy-edged leaves. Wet sandy hollows, very local, mainly the New Forest.

name: Rhaponticum repens
tip: Creeping knapweed with narrow grey-green leaves, the lower ones lobed, and pinkish-purple thistle-like heads without spines. Rare casual on waste ground.

name: Rudbeckia laciniata
tip: Tall plant with deeply lobed leaves and drooping yellow rays around a greenish-yellow conical centre. Garden escape on riverbanks and waste ground.

name: Saussurea alpina
tip: Mountain thistle relative without spines, leaves narrow and toothed, white woolly beneath, with dense clusters of purple heads. Rare, mountain ledges in Scotland, northern England, Wales.

name: Scorzonera humilis
tip: Plant with narrow grass-like leaves and solitary pale yellow dandelion-like heads on a tall stem. Very rare, on damp grassland in Dorset.

name: Senecio cambrensis
tip: Fertile hybrid ragwort with small yellow heads, short rays and lobed leaves; looks like a mix of groundsel and Oxford ragwort. Local on waste ground in Wales and England.

name: Senecio doria
tip: Tall garden ragwort with big oval toothed leaves and loose clusters of yellow daisy-like heads. Rare escape in gardens.

name: Senecio doronicum
tip: Low plant with large solitary orange-yellow heads on woolly stems and oval, softly woolly leaves. Garden escape on rocky or waste ground.

name: Senecio glastifolius
tip: Shrubby South African plant with spiny-edged, holly-like leaves and lilac daisies with yellow centres. Casual or planted, mainly near the coast.

name: Senecio grandiflorus
tip: Tall garden species with purplish daisy-like heads; rarely escapes into waste ground. Not well known in the wild.

name: Senecio minimus
tip: Tall, upright annual with toothed or lobed leaves and untidy greenish-white heads without rays. Casual on cleared woodland and burnt ground.

name: Senecio ovatus
tip: Tall woodland ragwort with oval, toothed, short-stalked leaves and open clusters of yellow heads; leaves less lobed than common ragwort. Rare naturalised plant.

name: Senecio sarracenicus
tip: Tall riverside ragwort with undivided, broad, finely toothed leaves and many yellow heads. Uncommon, river banks and damp woods in northern Britain.

name: Senecio smithii
tip: Large white-rayed ragwort with big yellow centre, broad leaves and woolly stalks. Naturalised on wet ground in Scotland, Ireland and western Britain.

name: Sigesbeckia serrata
tip: Annual with sticky glandular hairs, oval toothed leaves and small yellow daisies backed by sticky green bracts. Rare casual on waste ground.

name: Silybum marianum
tip: Thistle with large glossy leaves marbled with white veins, spiny edges, and big purple spiny heads with curved spiny bracts. Roadsides and waste ground.

name: Sinacalia tangutica
tip: Tall leafy perennial with large lobed, hairless leaves and spires of small yellow ragwort-like heads. Occasional garden escape.

name: Solidago rugosa
tip: Tall goldenrod with hairy stems and wrinkled, oval, sharply toothed leaves; plume of small yellow heads. Naturalised on waste ground.

name: Solidago sempervirens
tip: Fleshy-leaved goldenrod of the coast with smooth, untoothed leaves and plumes of yellow heads. Rare garden escape on sea walls and sand.

name: Sonchus palustris
tip: Very tall sow-thistle with narrow, deeply cut leaves and blue-green stems with dark glandular hairs; pale yellow heads. Very rare, fens and marshes in East Anglia and Kent.

name: Symphyotrichum laeve
tip: Michaelmas-daisy with bluish-grey, hairless stems and thick leaves clasping the stem, with lilac-blue rays. Garden escape on waste ground.

name: Symphyotrichum novae-angliae
tip: Tall, hairy, sticky plant with leaves clasping the stem and deep violet-purple rays; heads larger than other Michaelmas-daisies. Garden escape on waste ground.

name: Symphyotrichum pilosum
tip: Bushy plant with hairy stems, narrow leaves and many small white or pale-lilac daisies. Waste ground and railway land, uncommon.

name: Symphyotrichum puniceum
tip: Tall with rough, hairy stems, and leaves with a clasping base; large lilac-purple daisies. Garden escape on roadsides and waste ground.

name: Symphyotrichum squamatum
tip: Branched annual with small, pale lilac-white daisies with short rays and narrow, hairless leaves. Casual on waste ground, mostly southern England.

name: Tanacetum balsamita
tip: Aromatic plant with oval, toothed grey-green leaves smelling of mint and clusters of button-like yellow heads, rays often absent. Old herb persisting on banks.

name: Tanacetum macrophyllum
tip: Tall tansy with large, finely divided leaves and flat clusters of small white-rayed daisies. Occasional garden escape.

name: Taraxacum croceiflorum
tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Distinguished only by detailed leaf, bract and pollen features; yellow-orange heads.

name: Taraxacum duplidentifrons
tip: A dandelion microspecies in the large group of common weedy dandelions; specialist needed to confirm. Distinguished by fine leaf and bract details.

name: Taraxacum euryphyllum
tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Leaf shape and bract details separate it from other dandelions.

name: Taraxacum faeroense
tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Mainly northern, Atlantic localities; leaf shape and bracts are the key.

name: Taraxacum hamatum
tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Identified by leaf lobes and bract features, not visible to a beginner.

name: Taraxacum lacistophyllum
tip: A small dandelion microspecies of dry grassland, with small heads and narrow, deeply cut leaves; specialist needed to confirm it.

name: Taraxacum obliquum
tip: A small dandelion microspecies of dry sandy or calcareous ground, with narrow, deeply cut leaves; specialist needed to confirm it.

name: Taraxacum palustre
tip: A dandelion group of wet meadows and fens, with narrow, nearly untoothed leaves and small pale heads; specialist needed to confirm. Local.

name: Taraxacum platyglossum
tip: A dandelion microspecies; specialist needed to confirm. Wide ray florets and leaf details separate it from other dandelions.

name: Tephroseris integrifolia
tip: Low, woolly plant with a rosette of oval leaves and yellow daisy-like heads in a flat cluster. Dry chalk grassland, southern and eastern England.

name: Tragopogon porrifolius
tip: Tall plant with grass-like leaves and large purple dandelion-like heads, closing by midday, with bracts longer than the florets. Stalks swell below the head. Roadsides and grassland.

name: Blysmus compressus
tip: A single flattened spike of two neat ranks of chestnut-brown florets on a creeping plant of damp, base-rich turf and flushes; the spike is larger and paler than Saltmarsh Flat-sedge.

name: Blysmus rufus
tip: A small, dark reddish-brown two-ranked spike on short stems in upper saltmarsh turf, mostly Scotland and northern coasts; much smaller and darker than Flat-sedge, with a short lowest bract.

name: Bolboschoenus laticarpus
tip: A tall, triangular-stemmed club-rush of brackish ditches and estuaries, bearing clustered brown spikelets with leafy bracts; very close to Sea Club-rush and needing a specialist to separate it by its fruit shape.

name: Carex acuta
tip: A creeping, stoloniferous sedge of wet meadows and river margins with sharply three-angled rough stems and flat leaves; unlike Tufted-sedge it does not form big tussocks and has narrower, pointed glumes.

name: Carex appropinquata
tip: A tussocky sedge of calcareous fens with tangled fibrous old leaf bases and short, pale brown spikes; separate from Greater Tussock-sedge by its shorter, compact spikes and the fibrous tufts rather than tall tussocks.

name: Carex aquatilis
tip: A tall, creeping sedge of wet peaty margins and fens with long grey-green leaves and dark spikes; the spikes are dark with blunt black-tipped glumes, and it forms extensive patches unlike tussocky relatives.

name: Carex atrata
tip: A mountain sedge of Scottish rocky ledges with a few dark, almost black, nodding spikes with the top spike mostly male; look for broad, bluish leaves and egg-shaped blackish spikes on drooping stalks.

name: Carex atrofusca
tip: A very rare, tiny, sooty-black sedge of high, wet, base-rich mountain flushes in Scotland, with one drooping dark spike on a slender stem and short, dark female glumes.

name: Carex bigelowii
tip: A creeping sedge of mountain tops and exposed heaths with stiff, upright stems and a bluish-green look; has one male spike and one to three short, dark, oval female spikes held upright.

name: Carex buchananii
tip: A coppery, bronze, tufted garden sedge from New Zealand that occasionally escapes; the very narrow curly leaves are the key feature, with slim brown spikes on thin stems.

name: Carex buxbaumii
tip: A rare, creeping sedge of coastal marshes with a club-shaped terminal spike that is male at the top and female below, plus blackish short spikes; blue-green leaves are an aid, and it occurs in a few eastern and Irish sites.

name: Carex capillaris
tip: A small mountain sedge of base-rich flushes with extremely slender stems carrying one tiny male spike and a few small female spikes hanging on hair-fine stalks, the fruit having a long beak.

name: Carex cespitosa
tip: A very rare tufted sedge of damp grassland, resembling Tufted-sedge but with a larger dense tuft and blunt dark glumes; a specialist should confirm any record as this species is extremely scarce or lost in Britain.

name: Carex chordorrhiza
tip: A very rare creeping sedge of wet peat bogs in the Scottish Highlands, with long string-like underground runners and short, compact heads of small brown spikes.

name: Carex comans
tip: A pale olive to bronze tufted garden sedge from New Zealand that sometimes escapes, with fine arching leaves and drooping slender female spikes; looks like a thin mop-headed tuft of hair.

name: Carex depauperata
tip: A very rare woodland sedge confined to a few sites in the south of England, with a few widely spaced, fat spikes on slender stalks and large, plump, beaked fruits.

name: Carex diandra
tip: A tufted sedge of fens and wet meadows with compact heads of small brown spikes and shiny, rounded fruits; stems are rough, and it is lesser and neater than Greater Tussock-sedge.

name: Carex digitata
tip: A woodland sedge of limestone with spikes spread like fingers, the lowest sheaths purplish red and a pale, short male spike above a few female ones; leaves are short and narrow.

name: Carex divisa
tip: A creeping sedge of brackish grassland and dune slacks with a dense, compact head of many small spikes that look like a bunch; found mostly in the south and east near the coast.

name: Carex elata
tip: A big tussock-forming sedge of fens and lake edges with stiff yellowish-green leaves and dark spikes; the tussocks are the clue, as the similar Slender Tufted-sedge forms creeping patches.

name: Carex elongata
tip: A tufted sedge of wet woods and fen margins with a narrow, slender row of many small greenish spikes, a bit like an elongated bottle brush and quite distinct from other brown-headed ones.

name: Carex ericetorum
tip: A very rare, low creeping sedge of calcareous grassland in East Anglia and Scotland, flowering early with hairy fruits and small spikes tucked among the leaves.

name: Carex extensa
tip: A tufted sedge of saltmarsh and coastal rocks with stiff greyish-green, curled leaves and one or two stalkless female spikes with very long, leaf-like bracts that stick out.

name: Carex flava
tip: A yellowish-green sedge of marshes and fens with a cluster of pale female spikes near the male spike, their long, down-curved beaks giving a spiky look; much larger than Common Yellow-sedge.

name: Carex humilis
tip: A very rare tiny sedge of southern chalk grassland in Dorset, Wiltshire and Hampshire, flowering early with short spikes hidden among curly, grass-like leaves.

name: Carex lachenalii
tip: A mountain sedge of late snow patches in Scotland with a tight cluster of two to four small, brown, egg-shaped spikes that look like a hare's foot.

name: Carex lasiocarpa
tip: A creeping sedge of wet fens and bog pools with very narrow, rolled grey-green leaves and large, hairy fruits on thick female spikes that stand erect.

name: Carex limosa
tip: A creeping sedge of wet peat bog pools with greyish, narrow leaves and short, plump, oval female spikes hanging on thread-like stalks.

name: Carex magellanica
tip: A rare northern sedge of acid bog and wet moorland with a few pale, drooping female spikes on slender stalks, and a male spike above; shorter stalks and paler greenish leaves tell it from Bog-sedge.

name: Carex maritima
tip: A tiny Scottish dune and sandy shore sedge with one little, rounded, rust-brown head sitting on curved stems and short, curved leaves, so it looks a bit like a bent shoot.

name: Carex microglochin
tip: A very rare tiny Scottish mountain sedge of base-rich flushes, with a single slender spike bearing a bristle-like extension of the fruit stalk beyond the sacs.

name: Carex montana
tip: A small sedge of dry, grassy limestone and heath with soft hairy fruits, early-flowering short spikes and leaves that look limp and soft; creeps slowly to form loose patches.

name: Carex norvegica
tip: A rare Scottish mountain sedge with a tight head of two to four dark spikes crowded together, stalks drooping a bit; the dense head and blackish glumes are the clues.

name: Carex ornithopoda
tip: A rare, small, tufted sedge of limestone pastures in northern England with a group of spikes spreading like a bird foot and short, fine hairs on the fruits.

name: Carex pauciflora
tip: A creeping sedge of wet acid bogs with a single slim spike holding only two or three pale yellowish-green fruits that bend downward, giving a sparse look.

name: Carex punctata
tip: A coastal sedge of rocky cliffs and damp seepage in south-west England, Wales and Ireland, with dotted, yellowish-green fruits, a male spike above and short stalked females beneath.

name: Carex rariflora
tip: A scarce creeping sedge of wet Scottish mountain bogs with greyish, narrow leaves and a few drooping dark, pale-glumed female spikes on thread-like stalks.

name: Carex recta
tip: A rare creeping sedge of upper saltmarsh and estuary banks in Scotland, with tall stems, stiff grey-green leaves and a few narrow dark spikes; a specialist should check hybrids with Water Sedge.

name: Carex rupestris
tip: A small mountain sedge of calcareous rocky ledges, with a single small spike at the top of a curved, wiry stem and narrow, curly leaves; local in the Scottish Highlands.

name: Carex salina
tip: A rare saltmarsh and coastal sedge of northern coasts needing a specialist to identify; it is a smaller relative of Lyngbye's and Estuarine Sedge, with dark spikes and creeping runners.

name: Carex saxatilis
tip: A creeping sedge of wet peaty mountain flushes in Scotland with one male spike and a single stout, dark purplish-brown female spike that droops or stands up on short stalks.

name: Carex simpliciuscula
tip: A small, tufted mountain plant of limestone ground in northern England and Scotland with a single narrow spike and bristle-like leaves, looks like a small rush; stems are wiry.

name: Carex strigosa
tip: A woodland sedge of damp clay with wide, bright green leaves and thin, long, spaced, drooping female spikes with few fruits, all on arching stalks; the shape is fine and sparse.

name: Carex vaginata
tip: A rare Scottish mountain sedge, creeping, with a single male spike and one nodding female spike on a thin stalk, and conspicuous pale sheaths on the stem.

name: Carex vulpina
tip: A tufted sedge of wet grassland and ditches with dense fox-brown spike heads that are bright green or brown and a sharply winged, rough three-angled stem; inner leaf sheaths are green not red.

name: Carex vulpinoidea
tip: A tufted sedge, introduced and naturalised in a few wet places, resembling True Fox-sedge but with finer, greener spike heads and narrow, long bracts reaching beyond the head.

name: Cladium mariscus
tip: A tall, robust fen plant forming dense stands, with sharply saw-edged, keeled leaves that cut, topped by branched clusters of small brown spikelets; the cutting leaf is the giveaway.

name: Cyperus eragrostis
tip: A yellowish-green tufted plant of damp waste ground with flat, umbrella-like heads of pale flat spikelets from a leafy whorl, introduced from South America and spreading in the south.

name: Cyperus fuscus
tip: A small, very rare annual of bare, damp pond mud, with small clusters of dark red-brown flattened spikelets on short stems; looks like a tiny version of other galingales.

name: Eleocharis acicularis
tip: A tiny, creeping plant with hair-thin stems forming a green mat at the edges of ponds, with a small, pale spikelet at each stem tip and no leaf blades.

name: Eleocharis mamillata
tip: A northern spike-rush of lake and pond margins with a blunt single spikelet and a wide, prominent bump on top of the fruit; stems are stout and grooved, and a specialist may need to confirm.

name: Eleocharis parvula
tip: A tiny, rare spike-rush of coastal muddy brackish margins in southern and eastern England, forming short, bright green turf with narrow stems and tiny single spikelets.

name: Eleocharis uniglumis
tip: A spike-rush of damp grassland, dune slacks and brackish marsh with a single pointed spikelet, the lowest glume completely encircling the base; the spikelet is slimmer than Common Spike-rush.

name: Eriophorum gracile
tip: A rare cottongrass of wet bogs with usually one to three small drooping white cotton heads on thin stems and very narrow, triangular leaves; heads are less fluffy than in other species.

name: Eriophorum latifolium
tip: A cottongrass of calcareous fens with several nodding white heads and flat, broad leaves, rough edges and a stem that is three-sided above; the heads cluster, unlike Common Cottongrass.

name: Isolepis cernua
tip: A tiny, tufted rush-like plant of damp seepage and dune slacks with a single small, pale brown, nodding spikelet and hair-like leaves, narrow and grass-like; fine and pale.

name: Rhynchospora alba
tip: A tufted bog plant with clusters of white or cream spikelets at stem ends and grass-like leaves; the fruits are beaked, and the white heads set it apart from Brown Beak-sedge.

name: Rhynchospora fusca
tip: A very local creeping plant of damp heath hollows in the New Forest and Surrey, with rich brown spikelets in small clusters on slim stems; browner and rarer than White Beak-sedge.

name: Schoenoplectus pungens
tip: A rare tall brackish-water club-rush of south-west coasts with sharply three-angled, pointed stems and clustered brown spikelets, with a short sharp bract continuing the stem; rare in Britain.

name: Schoenoplectus triqueter
tip: A very rare, tall club-rush of tidal river mud in the Thames, Tamar and few estuaries, with sharply three-sided green stems and a small cluster of brown spikelets close below the tip.

name: Schoenus ferrugineus
tip: A very rare, tufted, dark-headed plant of lime-rich wet flushes in Scotland, with stiff wiry stems and a small cluster of dark chestnut brown spikelets above a long bract.

name: Scirpoides holoschoenus
tip: A tall, tufted plant with rounded heads of reddish-brown spikelets on rigid stems, found in a tiny number of southern coastal sites; one of few sedges with globular heads.

name: Trichophorum cespitosum
tip: A densely tufted bog plant with wiry round stems, each carrying one small, pale brown spikelet and with leaves reduced to sheaths; very common on upland blanket bog and wet heath.

name: Ajuga chamaepitys
tip: Low, sticky, pine-scented plant with leaves cut into three narrow lobes and small yellow flowers sitting singly or in pairs in the axils, on bare chalky arable soil.

name: Ajuga pyramidalis
tip: Bugle with a neat square-sided pyramid of leafy bracts and pale blue flowers, with no creeping runners. Rocky ground in western Scotland and western Ireland.

name: Clinopodium acinos
tip: Small annual with violet flowers marked white on the lower lip, in whorls on slender branched stems. Bare chalky arable ground and disturbed turf, mostly in southern England.

name: Clinopodium ascendens
tip: Hairy mint-scented perennial with loose branched clusters of lilac flowers in the leaf axils, on roadsides and dry banks. Told from Lesser Calamint by larger leaves and flowers.

name: Clinopodium menthifolium
tip: Tall, mint-scented hairy perennial with dense, many-flowered axillary clusters of pale pink flowers, with large leaves. Very rare, confined to the Isle of Wight woodland edges.

name: Clinopodium nepeta
tip: Smaller than Common Calamint, with small leaves and many tiny lilac flowers in stalked clusters. Dry chalk and limestone grassland, mainly in East Anglia and the south.

name: Galeopsis angustifolia
tip: Annual hemp-nettle with narrow, almost entire leaves and bright pinkish-red flowers in whorls. Rare on arable fields and bare ground in southern England.

name: Galeopsis bifida
tip: Bristly annual hemp-nettle with small flowers whose lower lip has a pale blotch and two small teeth, and with oval toothed leaves. Common in arable fields and waste ground.

name: Galeopsis speciosa
tip: Stout annual hemp-nettle with big pale yellow flowers with a violet lower lip and a stem swollen below each node. Arable fields, mainly in Scotland and northern England.

name: Hyssopus officinalis
tip: Aromatic evergreen shrubby plant with narrow leaves and dense one-sided spikes of deep blue flowers, grown in gardens and occasionally escaping onto old walls and dry banks.

name: Lamium confertum
tip: Small annual dead-nettle with pink flowers whose corolla tube is longer than the calyx, and with blunt, rounded, shallowly toothed leaves. Arable land mainly in northern Scotland.

name: Lamium hybridum
tip: Annual dead-nettle with leaves deeply and sharply toothed or cut, and purplish-pink flowers. Told from Red Dead-nettle by its cut leaf bases and sharper teeth. Common on arable land.

name: Lamium maculatum
tip: Garden dead-nettle with a white stripe down the middle of each leaf and large pinkish-purple flowers. Established on hedgebanks and roadsides near gardens.

name: Lavandula angustifolia
tip: Familiar grey-green shrub with narrow leaves and spikes of fragrant violet-blue flowers. A garden plant that is only occasionally found on walls or dry banks.

name: Leonurus cardiaca
tip: Tall plant with deeply palmately lobed leaves and spiny-calyxed pink flowers in dense whorls up the stem. A scarce relic of cultivation on waste ground and hedgerows.

name: Marrubium vulgare
tip: Woolly white-grey plant with wrinkled rounded leaves and dense whorls of small white flowers with spiny-hooked calyx teeth. Dry grassland near the coast and chalk.

name: Melissa officinalis
tip: Lemon-scented perennial with oval toothed leaves and small whitish flowers in leafy whorls. Established garden escape on hedgebanks and waste ground.

name: Melittis melissophyllum
tip: Distinctive woodland labiate with large flowers, white with a pink or purple blotch on the lip, in pairs in the leaf axils. Rare in south-west England and Wales.

name: Mentha pulegium
tip: Low, creeping, strong-smelling mint with tiny rounded whorls of lilac flowers along the stem. Found on seasonally flooded grassy ground and pond edges, mostly in southern England.

name: Mentha requienii
tip: Tiny, mat-forming mint with leaves just a few millimetres across and pale lilac flowers in the axils. Strong peppermint smell. Naturalised on damp paths and shaded ground.

name: Mentha spicata
tip: Garden mint with smooth, pointed, almost stalkless leaves and slender spikes of pale pink-lilac flowers. Common naturalised on damp waste ground and roadsides.

name: Mentha suaveolens
tip: Hairy, grey-green mint with rounded, wrinkled leaves, and spikes of white or pale pink flowers. Frequent in damp places and gardens, especially in the south-west.

name: Nepeta cataria
tip: Grey, downy, minty plant with heart-shaped toothed leaves and whorled spikes of white flowers spotted with purple. Rare on dry hedgebanks and chalk in England.

name: Phlomis russeliana
tip: Large garden perennial with big heart-shaped, felty leaves and tiered whorls of hooded yellow flowers. Occasionally escapes onto roadsides and waste ground.

name: Prunella grandiflora
tip: Selfheal with larger violet flowers and mostly unstalked upper leaves, held in a neat terminal head. Scarce on chalk and limestone grassland, often as an escape.

name: Prunella laciniata
tip: Selfheal with creamy-white flowers and variably lobed or cut leaves, forming a terminal head. Rare on dry chalk grassland in southern and eastern England.

name: Rosmarinus officinalis
tip: Evergreen shrub with narrow, leathery, aromatic leaves and small pale blue flowers in the upper axils. Cultivated and occasionally persisting on old walls and dry banks.

name: Salvia glutinosa
tip: Tall sage with sticky hairs and large pale yellow hooded flowers marked brownish, and arrow-shaped leaves. Rare naturalised plant in woods and hedges.

name: Salvia pratensis
tip: Showy sage with whorled spikes of bright violet-blue flowers and wrinkled, mostly basal leaves. Local on dry chalk and limestone grassland, mainly in the south and Cotswolds.

name: Salvia verbenaca
tip: Sage-like plant with wrinkled, lobed leaves and small lilac-blue flowers in whorls on a slender spike. Dry grassland, roadsides and banks, mostly in the south and near coasts.

name: Salvia verticillata
tip: Hairy clary with heart-shaped basal leaves and dense whorls of small lilac-purple flowers, with a foetid scent. Naturalised in rough grassland and waste ground.

name: Satureja montana
tip: Small, woody, aromatic plant with narrow pointed leaves and pale pink-white flowers in whorls. Grown in gardens and occasionally found on dry walls and chalk banks.

name: Scutellaria altissima
tip: Tall skullcap with long one-sided spikes of blue-violet flowers and oval toothed leaves. Naturalised in hedges and rough ground, notably in Somerset and the south-west.

name: Scutellaria minor
tip: Small creeping skullcap with pale pink flowers in the leaf axils and narrow, nearly stalkless leaves. Wet heaths and boggy ground, mainly in the west.

name: Stachys alpina
tip: Stinking, hairy woundwort with dull pink-purple flowers in spaced whorls and heart-shaped leaves. Very rare, in a few old limestone woods in Wales and western England.

name: Stachys arvensis
tip: Small, sprawling, hairy annual with tiny pale pink flowers in few-flowered whorls and blunt, heart-shaped leaves. Weed of acid arable fields, often near the coast.

name: Stachys germanica
tip: Tall woundwort densely covered in white woolly hairs, with pink-purple flowers in compact whorls. Very rare, now confined to Oxfordshire on field edges and chalky ground.

name: Stachys recta
tip: Woundwort with pale yellow flowers in whorls and narrow, toothed, stalkless upper leaves. Naturalised on dry walls, banks and waste ground.

name: Teucrium botrys
tip: Small annual with deeply cut, oak-like leaves, and pink flowers in whorls that have no upper lip. Scarce on bare chalk and limestone in southern England.

name: Teucrium chamaedrys
tip: Low evergreen with shiny small toothed leaves and pink-purple flowers lacking an upper lip, in whorls forming one-sided spikes. Rare escape on walls, banks and rough ground.

name: Teucrium scordium
tip: Hairy plant smelling of garlic when crushed, with pink flowers lacking an upper lip in axillary pairs. Rare in damp dune slacks and fen edges in England and Ireland.

name: Thymus pulegioides
tip: Thyme with erect flowering stems that are square and hairy only on the angles, and small oval leaves. Grassy chalk banks and dry slopes.

name: Thymus serpyllum
tip: Mat-forming thyme with stems hairy all round and leaves with hairy margins at the base. Found only on sandy Breckland heath and grassland in East Anglia.

name: Thymus vulgaris
tip: Small bushy shrub with narrow, strongly aromatic leaves curled under at the edges, and pale pink or white flowers. Garden herb, occasionally escaping to dry banks and walls.

name: Agrostis castellana
tip: Bent with an open purplish panicle, creeping by stolons and rhizomes, often awned and with a short blunt ligule; the awn and fine leaves separate it from Common Bent. Rare introduction.

name: Agrostis curtisii
tip: Densely tufted heathland bent with very fine bristle-like leaves, a long pointed ligule and awned spikelets; only in southern English and Welsh heaths, never in Common Bent habitats.

name: Agrostis lachnantha
tip: Rare alien bent with an open panicle and hairy-based florets; unlikely to be met, so a specialist should confirm any record against other bents with awns.

name: Agrostis scabra
tip: North American bent with a very diffuse, hair-fine panicle that breaks off in autumn; rare casual, told from Common Bent by rough branches and often a short awn.

name: Alopecurus aequalis
tip: Short, slender foxtail with orange anthers and a curved awn barely sticking out; much smaller than Meadow Foxtail, found on bare muddy pond margins.

name: Alopecurus bulbosus
tip: Foxtail with a swollen bulb-like stem base and a slender spike; grows in grazed brackish coastal grassland in southern and eastern Britain, unlike inland Meadow Foxtail.

name: Alopecurus magellanicus
tip: Small mountain foxtail of wet Scottish ground with a short, woolly, purplish spike and inflated upper leaf sheath; the only foxtail in high, damp, rocky sites.

name: Ammophila arenaria
tip: Stiff blue-green dune grass with rolled sharp leaves and a dense pale spike-like panicle; the main sand-binder of coastal dunes, spreading widely by underground stems.

name: Anemanthele lessoniana
tip: Garden escape forming arching tufts of fine bronze-green leaves, with a loose nodding panicle of purplish awned spikelets; occasionally self-sown on walls and paving.

name: Anisantha madritensis
tip: Annual brome with a dense, erect, compact panicle on stiff branches and long awns; shorter and more upright than Barren Brome. Local on sandy waste ground in the south.

name: Anisantha rigida
tip: Very large annual brome with big drooping panicle and spikelets bearing very long awns up to 5 cm; casual on waste ground and in the south.

name: Anisantha tectorum
tip: Annual brome with a one-sided drooping panicle of fine branches and long awns; spreading on dry waste ground and railway land in the south and east.

name: Apera interrupta
tip: Annual with a tight, narrow, lobed panicle and fine long awns; rare in East Anglian fields and casual elsewhere, far denser than Loose Silky-bent.

name: Apera spica-venti
tip: Annual of arable fields with a large airy panicle on hair-fine branches and long wavy awns; the loose, feathery look separates it from Dense Silky-bent.

name: Aristavena setacea
tip: Very fine, stiff tussocks with wiry leaves and a small purplish awned panicle; confined to wet heaths and bogs in the far south-west England and a few other places.

name: Avena barbata
tip: Oat with a nodding panicle and spikelets bearing long bent awns, and florets with dense stiff hairs at the base; scarce casual, unlike the common Wild Oat.

name: Avena strigosa
tip: Cultivated oat relic with spikelets ending in two bristle points and a bent awn; florets lack the dense hairs of Wild Oat. Mostly on arable ground in the north and west.

name: Brachypodium pinnatum
tip: Tough tufted grass with stiff yellowish-green leaves and a spike of short-stalked spikelets in two rows; dominates chalk and limestone turf in the south, with rolled leaf tips.

name: Briza maxima
