tip: Annual quaking-grass with large, drooping, inflated spikelets over 1 cm long, bigger than those of Lesser Quaking-grass; garden escape and casual in the south.

name: Briza minor
tip: Delicate annual with tiny heart-shaped, trembling spikelets in a spreading panicle; much smaller spikelets than Greater, found on arable and waste ground in the south.

name: Bromopsis benekenii
tip: Brome of calcareous woodland with a nodding panicle and hairy leaf sheaths; the stem nodes are hairy, helping tell it from Hairy-brome. Local in the south and east.

name: Bromopsis inermis
tip: Rhizomatous perennial brome with an erect panicle and awnless or very short-awned spikelets; the creeping habit separates it from other bromes. Naturalised on roadsides.

name: Bromus interruptus
tip: Brome with dense short-stalked clusters of velvety spikelets down a stout panicle; extinct as a wild plant, known from Cambridgeshire, now only in cultivation.

name: Bromus lepidus
tip: Annual brome with a compact panicle of small hairless-to-silky spikelets with short awns; scarce in grassland and waste ground. Told from Soft-brome by narrower, flatter spikelets.

name: Bromus pseudosecalinus
tip: Rare brome with a hairy sheath and a loose panicle bearing awned spikelets; a specialist should confirm it among the annual bromes, which are hard to separate.

name: Calamagrostis canescens
tip: Tall reed of fens and wet woods with a drooping, purplish panicle and short awns well inside the glumes; creeping and rare, mainly in eastern England.

name: Calamagrostis purpurea
tip: Rare small-reed of a few Scottish and northern damp sites, with a lax panicle and awn attached midway; a specialist should confirm it against Purple Small-reed.

name: Calamagrostis scotica
tip: Very rare small-reed of Caithness damp ground, with a narrow panicle and hairs shorter than the glume; only a specialist can separate it from related small-reeds.

name: Calamagrostis stricta
tip: Slender creeping small-reed of wet northern meadows, with a narrow, erect panicle and a short awn; much slimmer than Wood Small-reed, local in Scotland, northern England and Ireland.

name: Catabrosa aquatica
tip: Soft, creeping grass of streams and ditches with a pyramidal panicle in whorls and blunt, notched tips to the glumes; the broad pale leaves float or sprawl in shallow water.

name: Ceratochloa carinata
tip: Large annual or perennial brome with a flattened, compressed spikelets and short awns; a casual of waste ground, told from Rescue Brome by shorter awns.

name: Ceratochloa cathartica
tip: Big brome with a drooping panicle of flattened, keeled spikelets and short awns; common casual on waste ground. Leaf sheaths are downy, unlike hairless Prairie Brome.

name: Ceratochloa marginata
tip: North American brome with big flattened spikelets and hairs at the stem nodes; occasional casual. A specialist should check it against similar Ceratochloa species.

name: Chimonobambusa quadrangularis
tip: Bamboo with distinctly four-angled stems and tiny spines at the nodes, spreading by rhizomes in gardens; flowers almost never seen in Britain.

name: Cortaderia richardii
tip: Big tussock with feathery silver plumes and razor-edged leaves; flowers earlier than Pampas-grass, with plumes held well above the foliage. Escape on cliffs and waste ground.

name: Corynephorus canescens
tip: Small bluish-grey tufts of bristle-fine leaves, with a narrow panicle of club-shaped awned spikelets; confined to dry sandy heaths and coastal dunes, mainly in East Anglia.

name: Cynodon dactylon
tip: Creeping mat-former with three to five finger-like spikes radiating from the stem top; rare on southern sandy coasts and the Channel Islands, with a fringe of hairs as ligule.

name: Cynosurus echinatus
tip: Annual with one-sided lobed clusters of spikelets bearing long awns, unlike Crested Dog's-tail; scarce on dry open ground and waste, mainly in southern England.

name: Dactylis polygama
tip: Slender woodland form of cock's-foot with slimmer clumps and fewer tufts; a specialist should confirm it against ordinary Cock's-foot, which has stout dense heads.

name: Digitaria ischaemum
tip: Small annual with two to six finger-like spikes joined at the top and hairless spikelets; rare casual, separated from Hairy Finger-grass by the lack of hairs.

name: Digitaria sanguinalis
tip: Sprawling annual with finger-like spikes and bristly hairy leaf sheaths, purplish when ripe; occasional casual on arable and waste land in the south.

name: Drymochloa sylvatica
tip: Tall shade-loving fescue with broad flat leaves and a loose nodding panicle; found in ancient woods in the south and north, unlike tough Giant Fescue.

name: Eragrostis curvula
tip: Tufted South African grass with very fine curled leaves and a drooping lead-grey panicle; escapes from planting in towns and roadsides. Leaves are extremely thin and wiry.

name: Eragrostis pilosa
tip: Delicate annual with a very fine airy panicle of greyish spikelets and hairs at the throat; rare casual, mostly seen in towns and waste ground.

name: Festuca armoricana
tip: Rare fine-leaved fescue of Brittany type with a small panicle; a specialist should confirm it among the fine-leaved fescues, which are very difficult to separate.

name: Festuca gautieri
tip: Garden fescue forming dense cushions of bristly, rolled green leaves; occasionally escapes onto walls. Short panicle, otherwise like other fine fescues, so check carefully.

name: Festuca glauca
tip: Garden fescue with neat tufts of bright blue-grey bristle leaves and a short panicle; seen on walls and pavements. Colour distinguishes it from Sheep's-fescue.

name: Festuca heterophylla
tip: Tufted fescue with fine, bristly basal leaves and flat, broader stem leaves, giving two leaf types; mostly naturalised in woods and parks in the south.

name: Festuca huonii
tip: Small tufted fescue from Australasia, rarely grown in gardens; the very fine leaves look like other fine fescues, so a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Festuca lemanii
tip: One of the fine-leaved Sheep's-fescue group, with narrow tufted leaves and a dense little panicle; a specialist needs to examine the leaf anatomy to confirm it.

name: Festuca longifolia
tip: Blue-grey fine-leaved fescue forming tufts, close to Hard and Blue Fescues; a specialist is needed to confirm it, and it is rare outside gardens.

name: Festuca trachyphylla
tip: Stiff, bluish-green tufted fescue with rolled hard leaves that are rough to the touch; common on dry banks and verges. A specialist should confirm it among the fine-leaved fescues.

name: Gastridium ventricosum
tip: Slender annual with a shining, narrow, spike-like panicle of glossy spikelets bearing a bent awn; rare, on arable field edges and tracks in the south of England.

name: Gaudinia fragilis
tip: Slender grass with an unbranched spike, spikelets in two rows with a bent awn from the back, and hairy sheaths; local on damp meadows in the south and Channel Islands.

name: Glyceria canadensis
tip: North American manna-grass with a broad, spreading, nodding panicle of oval spikelets that look like a rattlesnake tail; rare naturalised plant of wet ground.

name: Hierochloe odorata
tip: Sweet-scented rhizomatous grass with a loose bronze panicle of shining spikelets, flowering early; very rare in northern Scotland and Ireland on damp stream banks.

name: Hordelymus europaeus
tip: Woodland grass with a nodding barley-like spike, spikelets in threes, awned; leaves are broad and hairy at the sheath. Local on shady calcareous ground in the south.

name: Hordeum jubatum
tip: Barley with soft, silky, nodding spike of long, spreading awns, often tinged purple; a casual on roadsides, widely seen on salted verges.

name: Hordeum marinum
tip: Short barley of saltmarshes and sea walls, with a narrow spike where the central spikelet is stalkless and the others outward-awned; Sea Barley has short stiff leaves.

name: Hordeum vulgare
tip: Cultivated cereal with a large spike of long awns, either two- or six-rowed; relict on field margins and tips, with broad leaves and clasping auricles.

name: Koeleria vallesiana
tip: Tufted grass with a dense shining cylindrical panicle and tough rolled leaves with fibrous old sheaths; extremely rare, on limestone in the Avon Gorge, Somerset.

name: Lagurus ovatus
tip: Annual with a soft woolly ovoid head and long bent awns, easily recognised; Mediterranean plant naturalised on dunes in the Channel Islands, casual elsewhere.

name: Leersia oryzoides
tip: Rhizomatous grass of ditches and pond edges with a wide airy panicle and flat leaves with razor-sharp edges that cut skin; local in southern England.

name: Leymus arenarius
tip: Stout blue-grey coastal grass forming broad clumps, with a thick spike of paired spikelets in two rows; widely spreading rhizomes make it a dune builder.

name: Lolium temulentum
tip: Annual rye-grass with a long spike and spikelets bearing a long awn, much longer glumes than Perennial Rye-grass; very rare as a relict weed of cereals.

name: Melica nutans
tip: Woodland grass with a one-sided raceme of purple-brown nodding spikelets, leaves rough, and bases swollen; scarce in limestone woods and often in the north and west.

name: Mibora minima
tip: Tiny annual with a minute purplish flat spike, flowering very early on bare sandy ground; rare, from Cornwall, Anglesey, Gower and the Channel Islands.

name: Milium vernale
tip: Small annual of dry sandy ground and open sites with a loose, small panicle; very rare, found in Channel Islands, with flowering in early spring.

name: Nassella tenuissima
tip: Fine hair-leaved tufted garden grass with a silky, feathery pale panicle that soon becomes airy; an escape from gardens now self-sown on paths and walls.

name: Oloptum miliaceum
tip: Mediterranean grass with a large open panicle of tiny glossy spikelets bearing a short awn; casual near ports and on waste ground in the south.

name: Parapholis incurva
tip: Tiny annual with a curved, stiff, narrow spike that is partly hidden in the sheath; lower than Hard-grass and restricted to coastal mud and shingle in the south.

name: Parapholis strigosa
tip: Annual of saltmarsh edges with a stiff, nearly straight spike that breaks up in pieces; longer and straighter than Curved Hard-grass, on southern and eastern coasts.

name: Paspalum distichum
tip: Creeping sprawler with paired, thin spikes joined at the tip in a V-shape and short ligules; rare naturalised on wet ground and pond margins in the south.

name: Phalaris aquatica
tip: Tufted canary-grass with a dense oblong head and swollen stem base; uncommon casual on waste ground, with shorter heads than Reed Canary-grass.

name: Phalaris minor
tip: Annual with a dense egg-shaped head of white and green striped spikelets that do not shatter whole; casual weed of arable and waste ground in the south.

name: Phalaris paradoxa
tip: Annual canary-grass with a dense head of spikelets in clusters, sterile ones with short awns; a casual on waste ground and docks in the south.

name: Phleum alpinum
tip: Mountain cat's-tail with a short, fat, dark purplish head and awned spikelets; the head is stubbier than Timothy. Found on high damp rocky ground in Scotland.

name: Phleum arenarium
tip: Small annual of dune sand with a short ovoid head and distinctive hair-fringed keel; coastal, mainly in southern and eastern England.

name: Phleum phleoides
tip: Slim tufted cat's-tail with a long thin spike and truncate glumes with short awns; very rare in the Breckland of East Anglia, on dry sandy soil.

name: Pleioblastus chino
tip: Spreading garden bamboo with slender stems and narrow leaves; naturalised in a few places, rarely flowers in Britain. A specialist may be needed to confirm among dwarf bamboos.

name: Pleioblastus pygmaeus
tip: Low, dense, spreading bamboo only about knee-high, used as ground cover; flowers essentially never seen in Britain. Told from taller bamboos by size.

name: Pleioblastus simonii
tip: Tall clump-forming garden bamboo with solid green canes and long narrow leaves; escapes from plantings occasionally. Rarely flowers here.

name: Poa alpina
tip: Small tufted meadow-grass of high mountain ledges with short, broad, blunt leaves and compact purplish panicles often with bulbils; only in Scottish and northern uplands.

name: Poa bulbosa
tip: Small meadow-grass with a swollen bulb-like stem base and spikelets that sprout into tiny leafy bulbils; found on dry coastal grass and sandy ground in the south and east.

name: Poa chaixii
tip: Large meadow-grass with flattened stems and broad leaves in dense tufts, and a big open panicle; naturalised in woods and verges, especially in Scotland.

name: Poa flexuosa
tip: Delicate mountain meadow-grass with wavy, fine stems and a small panicle; very local on high Scottish summits. A specialist may be needed to confirm it.

name: Poa glauca
tip: Blue-grey meadow-grass of mountain cliffs and ledges with a stiff, open panicle; limited to a few base-rich uplands in Scotland, Wales and England.

name: Poa infirma
tip: Little annual meadow-grass that flowers in winter and early spring, with a small compact panicle; confined to warm coasts of the south-west and Channel Islands.

name: Poa palustris
tip: Tall, loose meadow-grass of wet ground with a nodding yellowish-brown panicle and slightly rhizomatous base; naturalised from North America and rare.

name: Polypogon monspeliensis
tip: Annual with a dense, soft, bristly cylindrical head of long-awned spikelets, resembling a foxtail; rare casual of wet places and coasts in the south.

name: Pseudosasa japonica
tip: Common tall garden bamboo with stout canes and large glossy leaves, often naturalised; flowers extremely seldom in Britain.

name: Puccinellia fasciculata
tip: Small tufted annual of bare saltmarsh edges and sea walls with a stiff, short, one-sided panicle; branches stay erect in fruit, unlike the spreading Common Saltmarsh-grass. Mainly southern and eastern coasts.

name: Puccinellia rupestris
tip: Rigid saltmarsh grass with a stiff, spreading panicle on wiry, one-sided branches; grows on drier coastal sites, unlike Common Saltmarsh-grass with its flexible branches.

name: Sasa palmata
tip: Garden bamboo with big broad hand-like leaves at the stem tips, spreading by rhizomes; the largest-leaved bamboo you may meet. Flowering unknown here.

name: Sasa veitchii
tip: Low garden bamboo with big broad leaves that bleach at the margins in winter, forming dense patches; escapes occasionally. Flowers practically never seen.

name: Sasaella ramosa
tip: Hybrid bamboo with many fine branches and slightly hairy leaves, forming spreading thickets; occasional escape. Flowering is very rare in Britain.

name: Secale cereale
tip: Tall cereal with a long dense spike and long awns, hairs just beneath the spike; occasional relic on field edges and tips, taller than wheat or barley.

name: Sesleria caerulea
tip: Tufted grass of limestone with a blue-purple dense ovoid head, flowering very early in spring; abundant in northern England and Scotland on calcareous turf.

name: Setaria viridis
tip: Annual with a bristly cylindrical head, each spikelet backed by green bristles with forward-pointing barbs; casual on arable land and waste, mostly in the south.

name: Spartina alterniflora
tip: American cord-grass of saltmarsh mud with thick stems, many spikes and long smooth leaves; rare, in a few southern estuaries where it forms patches.

name: Spartina anglica
tip: Dense stout grass of muddy estuaries with several erect spikes pressed together; the commonest cord-grass, with stems up to a metre or more and a fringe of hairs.

name: Spartina maritima
tip: Native cord-grass of upper saltmarsh with one to three short spikes and fine inrolled leaves; very rare in Dorset, Hampshire and Essex, thinner than Common Cord-grass.

name: Spartina patens
tip: Fine, wiry mat-former of salt marsh with curly inrolled leaves and spreading spikes; rare introduction from North America on a few southern sites.

name: Spartina pectinata
tip: Tall stout cord-grass with long, arching leaves that cut the hands; planted on estuaries and banks, with many spikes in rows along the stem.

name: Sporobolus indicus
tip: Tufted tropical grass with a long narrow spike-like panicle of tiny spikelets; an uncommon casual near ports and on roadsides, often with leaf rust.

name: Triticum spelta
tip: Ancient wheat with a lax, brittle ear of awnless to short-awned spikelets in two rows; occasional relic of cultivation on arable edges and tips.

name: Vulpia ciliata
tip: Annual fescue with very long awns and a stiff curved panicle held in one side; rare on sandy ground near the coast in southern England.

name: Vulpia fasciculata
tip: Annual fescue with a dense, one-sided spike-like panicle and long awns, with the upper sheath enclosing the base; local on sand dunes around the coasts.

name: Vulpia unilateralis
tip: Tiny annual fescue with an unbranched, one-sided stiff spike, resembling Mat-grass; very rare on chalk and coastal turf in southern England.

name: Yushania anceps
tip: Tall clump-forming bamboo with thin canes arching out into a fountain shape; planted in gardens, but flowering is not recorded in the wild.

name: Zizania latifolia
tip: Tall aquatic grass with large drooping panicle, male spikelets awnless and female ones awned; a rare plant of pond edges and rivers, mostly in cultivation.

name: Aconitum lycoctonum
tip: Tall plant with spikes of pale yellow flowers, each with a long helmet-like hood; leaves deeply palmately lobed. Rare garden escape in woods and shady grassy places, mainly northern Britain.

name: Anemone ranunculoides
tip: Low woodland plant with a single glossy yellow flower above a ruff of three stalkless lobed leaves; looks like a buttercup but has no true sepals. Naturalised, rare.

name: Aquilegia pyrenaica
tip: Small tufted columbine with nodding violet-blue flowers with hooked spurs and divided bluish leaves. Very rare garden escape, usually on rocky or wall sites.

name: Clematis flammula
tip: Slender climber with sweetly scented small white four-sepalled flowers in loose clusters and compound leaves; fruits are feathery heads. Rare escape from gardens, hedges and walls, mostly in the south.

name: Hepatica nobilis
tip: Early spring woodland plant with violet-blue, sometimes pink or white, star-like flowers and distinctive leathery three-lobed leaves; flowers appear before the new leaves. Rare garden escape.

name: Ranunculus aconitifolius
tip: Tall branched plant with palmately divided leaves like monkshood and white buttercup-like flowers; double form is Bachelor's-buttons. Garden escape in damp grassland, mainly northern Britain.

name: Ranunculus marginatus
tip: Small annual buttercup with pale yellow flowers, reflexed sepals and flattened achenes with a distinct rim; lower leaves are kidney-shaped. Rare casual of waste and arable ground. Specialist should confirm.

name: Ranunculus muricatus
tip: Annual buttercup with shiny, rounded, lobed leaves and spiny fruits in a spreading head; petals pale and small. Local, in damp arable ground and ditch edges, mostly in the south.

name: Ranunculus paludosus
tip: Hairy perennial with tuberous, swollen root fibres, lobed basal leaves and narrow upper leaves, plus bright yellow flowers; found in Channel Islands, not mainland Britain. Specialist should confirm.

name: Thalictrum speciosissimum
tip: Very tall meadow-rue with large airy plumes of fluffy pale yellow flowers and finely divided leaves; much taller than native meadow-rues. Rare garden escape on damp verges and rough ground.

name: Acaena anserinifolia
tip: Mat-forming garden escape with neat pinnate leaves and round heads of tiny flowers turning into burrs with barbed spines; the spines are slender and usually reddish.

name: Acaena caesiiglauca
tip: Mat-forming escape with blue-grey pinnate leaves with many small leaflets and round heads that become barbed burrs; the blue-grey foliage separates it from the green New Zealand species.

name: Acaena inermis
tip: Creeping carpet with bronze-tinged small pinnate leaves; the round fruiting heads lack the long barbed spines of other pirri-pirri-burs, hence the name. Rare naturalised escape.

name: Acaena novae-zelandiae
tip: Creeping mat with pinnate leaves and round heads of tiny flowers; fruiting heads bristle with red-tipped barbed spines that cling to clothing, common on dunes and heaths.

name: Acaena ovalifolia
tip: Creeping escape with pinnate leaves of few broad leaflets, silky beneath; burrs carry just two or four barbed spines, fewer than in the commoner pirri-pirri-bur. Rare.

name: Alchemilla acutidens
tip: Lady's-mantle with rounded shallowly lobed leaves and pointed teeth, hairy stalks pressed down; greenish-yellow flower clusters. A specialist is needed to confirm this microspecies.

name: Alchemilla acutiloba
tip: Large lady's-mantle with deeply cut leaf lobes and sharp teeth, hairy stalks. Microspecies of northern grassy places; a specialist must confirm it.

name: Alchemilla alpina
tip: Small mountain plant whose leaves are cut to the base into separate narrow lobes, silvery with silky hairs beneath and edged with silver; unlike any other lady's-mantle.

name: Alchemilla conjuncta
tip: Lady's-mantle with deeply cut leaf lobes joined at the base, silky-silver beneath and with silvery margins; garden escape, naturalised on northern roadsides and banks.

name: Alchemilla glaucescens
tip: Small lady's-mantle, leaves greyish and densely hairy on both sides, with shallow rounded lobes; limestone grassland. A specialist is needed to confirm this microspecies.

name: Alchemilla glomerulans
tip: Lady's-mantle of damp northern hill rocks and streamsides; flowers form dense clusters, leaves hairy on both sides. A specialist is needed to confirm this microspecies.

name: Alchemilla micans
tip: Lady's-mantle with softly hairy leaves and stalks, hairs spreading and shiny; nine lobes. Local on grassy banks in the north. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Alchemilla monticola
tip: Lady's-mantle with spreading hairs on leaf stalks and both leaf sides, shallow lobes; northern grassland and verges. A specialist is needed to confirm this microspecies.

name: Alchemilla subcrenata
tip: Large lady's-mantle with big leaves having broad blunt teeth and spreading hairs on stalks; scattered in northern meadows. A specialist is needed to confirm this microspecies.

name: Alchemilla tytthantha
tip: Lady's-mantle with tiny flowers and mostly hairless stalks, leaves lightly hairy; mostly Northern England and Scotland roadside verges. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Alchemilla venosa
tip: Lady's-mantle with prominent leaf veins and short hairs, of Scottish and northern grassland. A specialist is needed to confirm this microspecies.

name: Alchemilla wichurae
tip: Compact lady's-mantle of mountain limestone ledges with hairless, shiny, leathery leaves cut into shallow lobes; Scottish Highlands and northern England. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Amelanchier lamarckii
tip: Large shrub with copper-tinged young leaves and showy white spring flowers in loose clusters, then purple-black berry-like fruits; naturalised on sandy heaths and woods.

name: Aremonia agrimonioides
tip: Low hairy herb with agrimony-like pinnate leaves with a large end leaflet, and small yellow five-petalled flowers in clusters; naturalised in a few scattered places.

name: Aronia arbutifolia
tip: Suckering shrub with oval finely toothed leaves, white to pink flowers in clusters and red berry-like fruits; leaves hairy beneath, unlike black chokeberry. Rare escape.

name: Aronia melanocarpa
tip: Suckering shrub with glossy oval finely toothed leaves turning red in autumn, white flowers and shiny black berry-like fruits; leaves hairless beneath. Rare escape.

name: Aruncus dioicus
tip: Tall leafy herb with big feathery plumes of tiny creamy flowers and large pinnate leaves; not to be confused with the yellow-flowered goat's-beard of grassland. Garden escape.

name: Cotoneaster apiculatus
tip: Spreading deciduous shrub with rounded leaves ending in a small point, solitary pinkish flowers and large bright red berries; often branches in a herringbone pattern.

name: Cotoneaster bullatus
tip: Large deciduous shrub with big puckered leaves with sunken veins, pink flowers in clusters and large red berries; common escape in scrub.

name: Cotoneaster cambricus
tip: Rare, small, evergreen shrub confined to limestone cliffs on the Great Orme in Wales; leaves are small, dark and rounded, with white-pink flowers and red fruit. Specialist confirmation advised.

name: Cotoneaster dielsianus
tip: Arching deciduous shrub with small oval leaves, woolly beneath, pink flowers in small clusters and orange-red berries; escape in scrub. Distinguishing Cotoneaster species needs a specialist.

name: Cotoneaster divaricatus
tip: Deciduous shrub with stiffly spreading branches, glossy small leaves and pink flowers in pairs or threes, then red egg-shaped berries; leaves turn red in autumn.

name: Cotoneaster franchetii
tip: Evergreen to semi-evergreen shrub with grey-green leaves, white downy beneath, pinkish-white flowers and orange-red berries; frequent garden escape on waste ground and scrub.

name: Cotoneaster frigidus
tip: Large semi-evergreen shrub or small tree with big oval leaves and flat clusters of white flowers followed by many red berries; Cotoneaster species are tricky, so confirm with a specialist.

name: Cotoneaster induratus
tip: Evergreen, arching shrub with leathery dark leaves, felty white beneath, white flowers and red fruit. A rare escape; a specialist is needed to identify it.

name: Cotoneaster lacteus
tip: Evergreen shrub with leathery leaves that are densely felted beneath, dense heads of creamy white flowers and long-lasting red berries; frequent in hedges and scrub.

name: Cotoneaster microphyllus
tip: Evergreen low spreading shrub with tiny, dark, glossy leaves, solitary white flowers and crimson fruits; very common escape from gardens on walls and rough ground.

name: Cotoneaster nitens
tip: Deciduous shrub with small glossy leaves, pink flowers and dark purple-black berries; black fruit separates it from most escapes. A specialist should confirm.

name: Cotoneaster obtusus
tip: Low, deciduous or semi-evergreen shrub with blunt, rounded leaves, small pink flowers and red fruit; rare escape and tricky from other Cotoneaster species, so confirm with a specialist.

name: Cotoneaster salicifolius
tip: Evergreen shrub with long, narrow, wrinkled leaves like willow, creamy flowers in flat clusters and bright red berries; widespread escape.

name: Cotoneaster zabelii
tip: Deciduous arching shrub with oval leaves, woolly beneath, pink flowers in drooping clusters and red pear-shaped berries; rare escape. Specialist confirmation advised.

name: Crataegus orientalis
tip: Thorny small tree with grey, deeply lobed woolly leaves, white flowers and large orange-red fruits; rare planting differing from our native hawthorns in its grey, felted leaves.

name: Dasiphora fruticosa
tip: Small shrub with silky grey-green five-parted leaves and bright yellow flowers; wild only on a few rocky river banks in Upper Teesdale, Cumbria and western Ireland, but often planted.

name: Dryas octopetala
tip: Mat-forming mountain plant with small oak-like glossy leaves, white beneath, and large white flowers with eight petals and a yellow centre, then fluffy seed heads; on limestone upland.

name: Filipendula camtschatica
tip: Very tall hairy herb with large palmate lobed leaves and frothy heads of creamy-white to pinkish flowers; a rare garden escape of streamsides and damp ground.

name: Fragaria moschata
tip: Taller than wild strawberry, with large flowers and trifoliate leaves with spreading hairs on stalks; fruit pale red musky strawberries. Rare naturalised in woods and hedges.

name: Geum macrophyllum
tip: Hairy herb with a huge, rounded end lobe on its lower leaves and yellow five-petalled flowers; fruit heads are burrs with hooked spines. Rare naturalised in northern Britain.

name: Kerria japonica
tip: Arching green-stemmed shrub with pointed double-toothed leaves and bright golden-yellow flowers, often double in the common form; naturalised on hedges and banks.

name: Mespilus germanica
tip: Small crooked tree with large oval leaves and single big white flowers, then brown apple-like fruits with a wide open top; local in hedges and old woods in southern England.

name: Oemleria cerasiformis
tip: Early-leafing suckering shrub with oval leaves smelling of cucumber and drooping clusters of small white flowers in spring; fruits are plum-like. Rare escape.

name: Potentilla argentea
tip: Cinquefoil with five-fingered leaves that are white-felted beneath with rolled edges, and small yellow flowers; found on dry sandy and gravelly ground, mainly in eastern England.

name: Potentilla crantzii
tip: Tufted mountain cinquefoil with five-fingered leaves, basal leaflets toothed at the tips only, and golden flowers often with an orange spot; Scottish, Welsh and northern upland rocks.

name: Potentilla indica
tip: Creeping strawberry-like plant with trifoliate leaves, yellow flowers and bright red strawberry-like fruits that are dry and tasteless, with leafy bracts beneath; garden escape.

name: Potentilla montana
tip: Mat-forming cinquefoil with trifoliate or fingered leaves, silky beneath, and white flowers; a rare garden escape, in contrast to the native white-flowered barren strawberry.

name: Potentilla norvegica
tip: Upright, hairy annual or short-lived cinquefoil with three-parted leaves and small yellow flowers with petals shorter than the sepals; casual of waste ground and disturbed soil.

name: Potentilla recta
tip: Tall hairy cinquefoil with five to seven narrow toothed leaflets and large pale lemon-yellow flowers in flat clusters; naturalised on roadsides, banks and waste ground.

name: Potentilla rupestris
tip: Rare upright plant with pinnate leaves and white flowers about 2 cm across; known only from a few rocky outcrops in Wales, Herefordshire and Sutherland.

name: Potentilla verna
tip: Low, mat-forming, golden-yellow cinquefoil of dry limestone grassland, with five-fingered leaves and flowers in spring; in Britain mostly Upper Teesdale. Close to creeping cinquefoil but with upright stems.

name: Prunus cerasus
tip: Smaller than wild cherry, often suckering, with glossy leaves and white flowers in short-stalked clusters; the sour red fruits are borne on long stalks. Often found in hedges.

name: Prunus incisa
tip: Small tree or shrub with deeply double-toothed, sharply pointed leaves and early pink-white blossom; planted in parks and gardens and not often naturalised.

name: Prunus mahaleb
tip: Small tree with round, glossy, finely toothed leaves and short upright spikes of fragrant white flowers; fruit black and bitter. Rare in hedges and scrub, mostly in the south.

name: Prunus pensylvanica
tip: Tree with narrow glossy red-brown leaves, flowers in small stalked umbels of white blossom, and small red cherries; rarely planted in Britain.

name: Prunus serotina
tip: Tree with long glossy leaves and long hanging spikes of small white flowers, then black fruits; naturalised in sandy woods and heaths, with red-brown hairs under the midrib.

name: Pyrus cordata
tip: Very rare small thorny pear with small oval leaves, white flowers and tiny brown pears; known wild from hedges around Plymouth, Devon, and in Cornwall.

name: Rosa agrestis
tip: Sweet-briar rose with leaves bearing a smell of apples (less strong), white or pale pink flowers, hairless sepals and stalks; mostly southern limestone hedges. Roses of this group need a specialist.

name: Rosa corymbifera
tip: Dog-rose group member with downy leaves, hairy beneath, and hooked prickles; widespread in hedgerows. Told from true dog-rose by the hairy leaves, and distinct from sweet-briars by lack of apple scent.

name: Rosa gallica
tip: Low suckering rose with rough, stiff leaves, deep pink to crimson large fragrant flowers and many stiff prickles and bristles; rare escape of grassy banks and hedges.

name: Rosa glauca
tip: Rose with distinctive purple-grey, hairless leaves and stems, rich pink flowers with white centres, and few straight prickles; widely planted and often naturalised on verges.

name: Rosa luciae
tip: Trailing, ground-hugging rose with glossy small leaves and clusters of fragrant white flowers in late summer; often used on banks and sometimes escaped. Small hooked prickles.

name: Rosa micrantha
tip: Sweet-briar with smaller pink flowers, scented apple-like glands on leaves underneath, and hairless sepals; mainly in southern English scrub and hedges. A specialist is needed to confirm this group.

name: Rosa mollis
tip: Rose with soft, bluish-grey downy leaves, bristly stalks, deep pink flowers and nearly straight prickles; found in northern and western hills of Britain and Ireland.

name: Rosa multiflora
tip: Vigorous arching rose bearing large panicles of small white fragrant flowers and fringed leaf stipules; fruit tiny red hips. Naturalised from gardens, scrambling over hedges and scrub.

name: Rosa setigera
tip: Climbing rose with three-leaflet leaves, long arching stems, rose-pink flowers in clusters that fade to white, flowering late in summer; rare escape in hedges.

name: Rosa squarrosa
tip: Dog-rose relative with leaning, spreading sepals and bristly-free stems; needs a rose specialist to separate from other dog-rose group members by leaf toothing and hairs.

name: Rosa stylosa
tip: Climbing white field-rose with styles joined into a short column, unlike the loose styles of dog-roses; mostly southern England, Wales and Ireland.

name: Rosa tomentella
tip: Dog-rose group member with rounded, hairy, glandular-toothed leaflets and stout hooked prickles; a specialist is needed to confirm it among similar hairy-leaved roses.

name: Rosa tomentosa
tip: Densely downy leaflets with gland-tipped double teeth and a sticky resin smell; pink flowers and bristly hips separate it from the glabrous dog-rose.

name: Rosa villosa
tip: Large bristly hips and softly hairy, gland-scented leaves with few prickles; deep pink flowers. Mainly northern Britain and Wales, often by streams and hedges.

name: Rosa virginiana
tip: Garden escape with glossy, hairless leaflets, bright pink flowers and near-straight paired prickles; leaves turn red in autumn. Hips are small and round.

name: Rosa vosagiaca
tip: Greyish-purple tinged leaflets with simple teeth, hairless, and pink flowers; a specialist is needed to separate it from the red-leaved rose and other forms. Rare, mostly northern Britain.

name: Rubus chamaemorus
tip: Low upland herb with single white flowers and lobed, crinkled leaves, no prickles; fruit ripens from red to amber. Northern moors and bogs.

name: Rubus cockburnianus
tip: Arching stems coated in chalky white bloom, small purplish flowers and black fruit; a garden shrub sometimes naturalised near habitation.

name: Rubus fissus
tip: Bramble microspecies of the southern and eastern heaths and woods; a batologist is needed to confirm it from other brambles by stem, leaf and prickle details.

name: Rubus nessensis
tip: Low arching bramble with weak slender prickles and hairy, rather few leaflets; a bramble specialist must confirm it. Scattered in Scotland and northern England on acid soils.

name: Rubus odoratus
tip: Unarmed garden shrub with large maple-like lobed leaves, bristly glandular stems and showy magenta-pink flowers; sometimes naturalised in hedges.

name: Rubus parviflorus
tip: Unarmed shrub with large soft maple-like leaves and white flowers; fruit is a flat red thimble. Naturalised in a few places from gardens.

name: Rubus phoenicolasius
tip: Stems and flower buds covered with dense red glandular bristles; leaves white-felted beneath with three leaflets; orange-red raspberry-like fruit in a hairy calyx.

name: Rubus scissus
tip: Bramble microspecies with deeply toothed leaflets; local, mainly in southern England, and needing a specialist to confirm among the many similar brambles.

name: Rubus spectabilis
tip: Naturalised garden shrub with three-leaflet leaves, magenta flowers in spring, weak prickles and orange to red raspberry-like fruit; found in a few scattered woods.

name: Rubus tricolor
tip: Evergreen ground cover with undivided, heart-shaped leaves dark above and white beneath, and bristly red stems; a garden escape on banks.

name: Sanguisorba canadensis
tip: Tall perennial with long white bottle-brush spikes and pinnate leaves; no petals. Garden plant, rarely escaping to damp ground, flowering late summer.

name: Sibbaldia procumbens
tip: Tiny mountain plant with greyish three-toothed trefoil leaves and clustered, very small yellowish flowers; Scottish high mountains, snow patches and ledges.

name: Sorbaria sorbifolia
tip: Unarmed suckering shrub with long pinnate leaves and big plumes of small white flowers; garden escape on banks and waste ground.

name: Sorbaria tomentosa
tip: Similar to False Spiraea but pinnate leaves woolly beneath and large plumes of white flowers; rare garden relict. Do not confuse with meadowsweet.

name: Sorbus admonitor
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain; leaves oval, white-felted beneath. A specialist is needed to confirm it among the whitebeam group.

name: Sorbus anglica
tip: Whitebeam with shallowly lobed leaves, grey-felted beneath, and red fruit; local in SW England, Wales and Ireland, on limestone. A specialist confirms the species.

name: Sorbus arranensis
tip: Endemic to Arran: deeply lobed to pinnate leaves with grey felt beneath, red fruit; confirmed only by specialists against the Arran Whitebeam.

name: Sorbus arvonicola
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of north-west Wales; oval grey-felted leaves, a specialist is needed to confirm identification.

name: Sorbus bristoliensis
tip: Whitebeam confined to the Avon Gorge with broad oval leaves, grey-white beneath, and orange-red fruit with pale spots; specialist confirmation advised.

name: Sorbus cambrensis
tip: Rare Welsh whitebeam microspecies on cliffs, with oval leaves white-felted beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Sorbus cheddarensis
tip: Very rare whitebeam restricted to Cheddar Gorge, Somerset; oval leaves white-felted beneath. Only a specialist can confirm it.

name: Sorbus croceocarpa
tip: Obscure whitebeam-group taxon with orange fruit; leaves lobed or oval and felted beneath. A specialist is essential to identify it.

name: Sorbus cuneifolia
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies with wedge-shaped leaves, white beneath; localised in western Britain and requires specialist confirmation.

name: Sorbus devoniensis
tip: Large tree whitebeam of Devon and Somerset with broad oval leaves and big, sparsely dotted, yellowish-red fruit; specialist confirmation advised.

name: Sorbus domestica
tip: Pinnate-leaved tree like rowan but with sticky buds, bark scaly and fruit large and pear- or apple-shaped; very rare native on Glamorgan cliffs, sometimes planted.

name: Sorbus eminens
tip: Whitebeam with rounded oval leaves, white beneath, and red fruit; local on limestone in Wye Valley, Avon Gorge, Wales and Ireland. Specialist advised.

name: Sorbus eminentiformis
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies resembling Round-leaved Whitebeam; a specialist must confirm it. Occurs very locally in western Britain.

name: Sorbus eminentoides
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies near Round-leaved Whitebeam; occurs very locally in western Britain and a specialist is needed.

name: Sorbus evansii
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval felted leaves; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Sorbus glabriuscula
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies, leaves oval with only thin felt beneath; localised, and confirmation needs a specialist.

name: Sorbus greenii
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval leaves grey-felted beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Sorbus herefordensis
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of the Welsh borders and Wye Valley; oval felted leaves, needs specialist confirmation.

name: Sorbus hibernica
tip: Irish endemic hybrid-origin whitebeam with leaves pinnately lobed at the base and grey beneath; red fruit. Specialist confirmation is advised.

name: Sorbus lancastriensis
tip: Whitebeam of limestone in Lancashire, Cumbria and north Wales, with lobed leaves grey-felted beneath and red fruit; a specialist should confirm it.

name: Sorbus latifolia
tip: Large whitebeam with broad, shallowly lobed leaves, grey beneath, and brownish-red fruit; local in Devon and Somerset. Specialist confirmation advised.

name: Sorbus leighensis
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies restricted to the Avon Gorge area; oval leaves felted beneath. A specialist is needed.

name: Sorbus leptophylla
tip: Rare whitebeam with thin oval leaves, whitish beneath, found on limestone cliffs in the Wye Valley; specialist confirmation needed.

name: Sorbus leyana
tip: Extremely rare small whitebeam of cliffs in the Brecon Beacons, with deeply lobed leaves grey-felted beneath; only a specialist can confirm it.

name: Sorbus margaretae
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of the Mendip area; oval leaves white-felted beneath and a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Sorbus minima
tip: Small shrubby whitebeam of Brecon limestone cliffs and Cumbria, with oval leaves grey beneath and red fruit; very rare, specialist confirmation advised.

name: Sorbus parviloba
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain; leaves oval to shallowly lobed, felted beneath. A specialist is needed.

name: Sorbus porrigentiformis
tip: Whitebeam of limestone in SW England, Wales and Ireland with oval, grey-green leaves, lightly felted beneath; red fruit. A specialist should confirm it.

name: Sorbus pseudofennica
tip: Endemic to Arran: leaves lobed at the tip but pinnate at the base, grey beneath, with red fruit. Specialists separate it from Arran Service-tree.

name: Sorbus pseudomeinichii
tip: Rare whitebeam-group microspecies with lobed leaves felted beneath; localised in western Britain and needs specialist confirmation.

name: Sorbus richii
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval felted leaves; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Sorbus rupicola
tip: Native whitebeam of limestone cliffs in western Britain and Ireland, with leaves narrowing to the base, grey beneath, and scarlet fruit; specialists confirm it.

name: Sorbus rupicoloides
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies similar to Rock Whitebeam, with oval leaves felted beneath; only a specialist can confirm it.

name: Sorbus saxicola
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of rocky limestone sites in the west; oval leaves white beneath. A specialist is needed for identification.

name: Sorbus scannelliana
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies with oval leaves felted beneath; localised in the west, and requires specialist confirmation.

name: Sorbus spectans
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval felted leaves; identification must be confirmed by a specialist.

name: Sorbus stenophylla
tip: Rare whitebeam microspecies of south Wales, with narrower oval leaves grey beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Sorbus stirtoniana
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies of western Britain with oval leaves felted beneath; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Sorbus subcuneata
tip: Whitebeam of the Somerset and Devon coast and gorges, with oval, white-felted leaves and red fruit; specialist confirmation advised.

name: Sorbus vexans
tip: Whitebeam of Somerset and Devon with oval leaves grey-felted beneath and deep red fruit; specialist confirmation advised.

name: Sorbus whiteana
tip: Very rare whitebeam microspecies in the Wye Valley and Avon Gorge area; oval leaves felted beneath. A specialist is needed.

name: Sorbus wilmottiana
tip: Rare whitebeam of the Avon Gorge with oval leaves white-felted beneath and orange-red fruit; confirmation needs a specialist.

name: Spiraea alba
tip: American shrub with narrow oval leaves, hairless, and slender white flower spikes; rare garden escape, unlike pink steeple-bush flowers.

name: Spiraea chamaedryfolia
tip: Garden shrub with elm-like oval double-toothed leaves and rounded clusters of white flowers; rare escape in hedges and waste ground.

name: Spiraea douglasii
tip: Common suckering escape with spires of deep pink flowers and oval leaves, white-woolly beneath; forms thickets in damp ground, unlike Bridewort.

name: Spiraea salicifolia
tip: Suckering shrub with narrow willow-like leaves and dense spikes of pale pink flowers; naturalised in damp places, unlike hairy steeple-bush.

name: Spiraea tomentosa
tip: American relative of steeple-bush with dense pink spires and rounded leaves woolly-white beneath; rare garden relict.

name: Acanthus mollis
tip: Garden escape with big glossy, deeply lobed, mostly spineless leaves and tall spikes of white flowers hooded by purplish spiny bracts; softer than Spiny Bear's-breeches.

name: Acanthus spinosus
tip: Like Bear's-breeches but leaves are cut into narrow lobes ending in sharp spines, so it is far more prickly; rare garden outcast near gardens.

name: Strobilanthes pentastemonoides
tip: Rare garden plant with toothed, pointed oval leaves and nodding tubular purple-blue flowers in late season; unlikely in the wild and seldom flowering outdoors in Britain.

name: Acorus calamus
tip: Tall iris-like waterside plant with a crinkled leaf edge, aromatic when crushed, and a green finger-like spike sticking out sideways from a leaf-like stem.

name: Acorus gramineus
tip: Small tufted waterside plant with leaves in a flat fan, like a miniature sweet-flag; spike short and greenish. Only occasionally escapes from gardens and ponds.

name: Aptenia cordifolia
tip: Fleshy mat-forming garden escape with heart-shaped shiny leaves and small bright pink-purple daisy-like flowers; found on warm walls and coastal spots in the south.

name: Carpobrotus acinaciformis
tip: Mat-forming succulent with three-angled curved leaves and large magenta-pink flowers; often grown on sea cliffs, and hybridises with Hottentot-fig, so check intermediates.

name: Carpobrotus edulis
tip: Sprawling succulent carpeting coastal cliffs in the south-west, with thick three-sided leaves and big flowers that are yellow in the centre and pale pink toward the edge.

name: Carpobrotus glaucescens
tip: Coastal succulent close to Hottentot-fig with fleshy three-angled leaves and pink or purplish flowers; separating the two is hard, so confirmation by a specialist is wise.

name: Disphyma crassifolium
tip: Low creeping succulent with thick, bluish-green fleshy leaves and pale pink flowers; naturalised mainly on southern and south-western coasts, easily confused with other iceplants.

name: Drosanthemum floribundum
tip: Straggling shrubby succulent with narrow sausage-like leaves covered in glistening bumps and many small pink-purple daisy-like flowers; a coastal garden escape in the south-west.

name: Erepsia heteropetala
tip: South African succulent rarely met as a coastal garden escape; fleshy three-sided leaves and magenta daisy-like flowers make it look like other iceplants, so confirm with a specialist.

name: Lampranthus aureus
tip: Sprawling shrubby succulent with narrow fleshy leaves and bright orange-yellow daisy-like flowers; a rare escape on warm south-western coasts, easily mistaken for related iceplants.

name: Lampranthus falciformis
tip: Low succulent with curved, sickle-shaped fleshy leaves and pink-purple daisy-like flowers; rare garden relic on southern coasts and not easy to separate from relatives.

name: Lampranthus roseus
tip: Small shrubby succulent with narrow fleshy leaves and rose-pink daisy-like flowers; occasional on southern coasts as an escape, with many similar relatives needing an expert.

name: Oscularia deltoides
tip: Shrubby succulent with small, flat triangular blue-green leaves that are finely toothed near the tip and pink flowers; naturalised on Channel Islands and Scilly coasts.

name: Ruschia caroli
tip: Rare South African succulent seen only as a garden throw-out, with small fleshy leaves and pink or white daisy-like flowers; hard to place without a specialist.

name: Alisma gramineum
tip: Rare aquatic with long ribbon-like submerged leaves and tiny white flowers on a small, much-branched stem; very local, mainly in East Anglia and the Midlands.

name: Alisma lanceolatum
tip: Water-plantain with narrow pointed leaves tapering gradually to the stalk and small flowers, usually pinker than Common Water-plantain; mostly southern and eastern England in shallow water.

name: Baldellia ranunculoides
tip: Small plant of wet peaty edges with narrow leaves and an umbel of pale pink, three-petalled flowers with a yellow spot at the base of each.

name: Damasonium alisma
tip: Very rare plant of drying pond mud in the south-east, small white flowers followed by spreading, star-shaped fruits of six spiky arms; leaves oval.

name: Luronium natans
tip: Aquatic with narrow ribbon submerged leaves and small oval floating leaves, white flowers with a yellow spot; mainly Wales and north-west England in lakes and canals.

name: Sagittaria graminea
tip: North American pond plant rarely naturalised; very narrow strap-like leaves and white three-petalled flowers lacking arrow-shaped leaves, so unlike native Arrowhead.

name: Sagittaria latifolia
tip: Introduced arrowhead with broad arrow-shaped leaves and white flowers in whorls; larger than native Arrowhead, with bracts and sepals that look different, in canals and ponds.

name: Sagittaria rigida
tip: Introduced aquatic arrowhead with narrow strap-like submerged leaves and sometimes a few broader floating ones, white flowers held low; confirmation by a specialist is advised.

name: Alstroemeria aurea
tip: Escaped garden plant forming clumps of leafy stems topped with heads of orange-yellow lily-like flowers streaked red; leaves twisted at the base, widely naturalised on waste ground.

name: Amaranthus albus
tip: Low sprawling annual with whitish stems and small leaves with wavy edges; green flowers in tight clusters along the stem; casual on tips and waste ground.

name: Amaranthus blitum
tip: Spreading annual with notched, oval, long-stalked leaves and slender green spikes with a blunt tip; the leaves often show a pale mark; mostly southern England.

name: Amaranthus cruentus
tip: Tall annual with dense drooping reddish or green spikes of flowers; grown as a crop and found as a casual on rubbish tips and tracks.

name: Amaranthus deflexus
tip: Sprawling weed with whitish-green stems, small diamond-shaped leaves and short leafy spikes; a casual of pavements and tips, separate from other pigweeds by its spreading habit.

name: Amaranthus hybridus
tip: Upright annual with slender green spikes and smooth, pointed oval leaves; resembles Common Amaranth but less hairy; a casual weed of cultivated ground, hard to separate.

name: Amaranthus retroflexus
tip: Tall hairy annual with dense stout green spikes of flowers bearing spiny bracts, and a hairy stem; the most frequent pigweed of arable fields and waste ground.

name: Atriplex halimus
tip: Silvery evergreen shrub with oval leaves covered in mealy hairs and small flowers in leafy spikes; grown for coastal hedging and naturalised on shores in the south.

name: Atriplex hortensis
tip: Tall annual salad crop with large triangular leaves that are green or red, rarely mealy; the fruiting bracts are large and rounded; occasional escape.

name: Atriplex laciniata
tip: Silvery, mealy plant of sandy shores with diamond-shaped, toothed leaves; the whole plant looks frosted, and it spreads across strandlines and dunes.

name: Atriplex longipes
tip: Coastal annual of saltmarsh edges with narrow leaves and fruiting bracts on long stalks; hard to separate from Babington's and other oraches, so specialist needed.

name: Atriplex pedunculata
tip: Very rare saltmarsh shrubby annual of east England, with thick fleshy grey mealy leaves and fruiting bracts on stalks; keep distinct from Sea-purslane.

name: Atriplex portulacoides
tip: Silvery-grey shrubby plant forming thick low bushes along muddy saltmarsh creeks, with narrow oval smooth leaves and tiny yellow-green flowers in slim spikes.

name: Atriplex praecox
tip: Small coastal annual of strandlines with narrow, slightly mealy leaves and small flowers; flowers earlier than other oraches, mainly northern and western shores; specialist confirmation needed.

name: Atriplex sagittata
tip: Introduced tall orache with shiny, bright green triangular leaves coarsely toothed and without mealiness; spreads along road verges and waste ground, especially in east England.

name: Bassia scoparia
tip: Garden plant with dense, feathery narrow leaves in a neat cone shape turning red in autumn; an occasional casual on waste ground.

name: Chenopodiastrum hybridum
tip: Hairless goosefoot with shiny, maple-like, lobed and coarsely toothed leaves and open branched clusters of green flowers; common arable and waste ground weed.

name: Chenopodiastrum murale
tip: Goosefoot with shiny, sharply toothed, nettle-like leaves, not mealy and a coarser look; common on farmyards and waste ground, with branched, leafy flower spikes.

name: Chenopodium opulifolium
tip: Mealy grey-green low goosefoot with small, three-lobed leaves and rounded dense flower clusters; scattered on arable fields and waste ground, mainly in southern England.

name: Chenopodium suecicum
tip: Variable annual with mealy-free, pale green oval or lobed leaves and flower clusters in open spikes; hard to tell from similar goosefoots, so specialist confirmation is needed.

name: Chenopodium vulvaria
tip: Grey mealy, spreading annual smelling strongly of rotten fish when rubbed; small diamond-shaped untoothed leaves; rare and declining, mainly southern coastal and sandy ground.

name: Dysphania ambrosioides
tip: Aromatic annual or perennial, strongly scented when crushed, with narrow toothed leaves and tiny greenish flowers in leafy spikes; found on waste ground and pavements.

name: Lipandra polysperma
tip: Low sprawling annual with reddish stems and small, untoothed oval leaves; dense clusters of green flowers; not mealy; local on disturbed damp ground and field edges.

name: Oxybasis chenopodioides
tip: Rare mealy-leaved annual of brackish saltmarsh edges in the south and east, with small triangular leaves with two basal teeth and dense clustered flowers.

name: Oxybasis glauca
tip: Low spreading goosefoot with oak-like lobed leaves that are green above and clearly mealy white below; found on disturbed damp ground and farmyards.

name: Oxybasis urbica
tip: Rare goosefoot with diamond-shaped, coarsely toothed leaves and long erect spikes; the plant is slightly mealy; scattered in southern and eastern England on waste ground.

name: Salicornia disarticulata
tip: Fleshy leafless annual of muddy saltmarsh with jointed, green stems and tiny flowers; glasswort species look alike, so a specialist is needed to confirm.

name: Salicornia europaea
tip: Upright jointed fleshy annual of saltmarsh mud, green and turning red in autumn, with tiny flowers sunk in the spike; glasswort species need a specialist to separate.

name: Salicornia obscura
tip: Annual glasswort of upper saltmarsh with greyish, bluish, jointed stems and tiny sunken flowers; a specialist is needed to separate it from other glassworts.

name: Salicornia procumbens
tip: Low spreading annual glasswort with shiny, bright green jointed stems and tiny sunken flowers; found on muddy saltmarsh in south-east England; specialist needed to confirm.

name: Salsola kali
tip: Sprawling grey-green annual of sandy shores with fleshy, spine-tipped narrow leaves and flowers tucked in leaf axils; spiny to touch, unlike Sea-blite.

name: Sarcocornia perennis
tip: Woody-based perennial glasswort with creeping stems and jointed fleshy shoots that stay green and leafless; found on upper saltmarsh in the south and east, unlike annual glassworts.

name: Spinacia oleracea
tip: Familiar vegetable with large, soft, triangular or oval stalked leaves and tiny green flowers in clusters; an occasional escape on tips and verges.

name: Suaeda maritima
tip: Fleshy annual of saltmarsh and shingle with thick, narrow, blunt leaves, often tinged red, with small green flowers in the leaf axils.

name: Suaeda vera
tip: Woody evergreen shrub of shingle and sea walls in the south and east, with fleshy, blue-green narrow leaves that are pointed and small green flowers.

name: Agapanthus praecox
tip: Garden plant with clumps of strap-like leaves and rounded heads of trumpet-shaped blue flowers on tall stems; sometimes escapes into hedgerows and rubbish tips.

name: Allium ampeloprasum
tip: Tall garlic relative with flat leaves and a dense round head of pink-purple flowers; hybridises with cultivated leeks, found on rocky coasts in Wales and the south-west.

name: Allium carinatum
tip: Local garlic relative with a loose head of bulbils mixed with purplish-pink flowers on long stalks; leaves are keeled and the plant is rarely common.

name: Allium cepa
tip: Well-known vegetable with hollow round leaves and a swollen stem below a large ball-shaped head of whitish-green flowers; seen as a relic of cultivation.

name: Allium moly
tip: Garlic relative with broad, bluish-green leaves and a flat-topped umbel of bright yellow starry flowers; an established garden escape on banks and hedgerows.

name: Allium neapolitanum
tip: Early garlic with three-angled flowering stem, flat leaves and an open umbel of showy white flowers; naturalised on banks and verges, mostly in the south.

name: Allium nigrum
tip: Garden escape with broad flat leaves and a round head of white to pale pink flowers with green stripes; garden-origin, naturalised locally.

name: Allium oleraceum
tip: Slender garlic of dry grassland and verges with a loose head of bulbils and dull pink-green flowers; leaves are hollow, and flowers a dull pink or greenish colour.

name: Allium paniculatum
tip: Rarely naturalised garlic with a loose, spreading umbel of papery pinkish-cream flowers on unequal stalks, and narrow leaves; very local and probably overlooked.

name: Allium pendulinum
tip: Spring-flowering garlic with a flat-topped head of white flowers with a greenish midstripe, narrow leaves and a three-angled stem; naturalised locally.

name: Allium roseum
tip: Garlic with broad flat leaves and a loose umbel of pale pink bell-shaped flowers, often with bulbils; invasive on road banks in the south-west and Channel Islands.

name: Allium sativum
tip: Cultivated bulb with flat leaves and a bulbil-bearing head in a long beak; rarely flowers, pinkish-white, and usually only found as a garden relic.

name: Allium schoenoprasum
tip: Tufted plant of grassy rocky places with hollow tubular leaves and a tight globular head of pink-purple flowers; native in rare spots, widely cultivated.

name: Allium scorodoprasum
tip: Tall garlic relative with flat leaves and a head of purple-brown bulbils and a few reddish flowers; rare, along river banks in Scotland and northern England.

name: Allium siculum
tip: Tall garden garlic with swaying umbel of drooping bell-shaped flowers in cream, green and maroon, followed by upright seed pods; found on verges near gardens.

name: Allium sphaerocephalon
tip: Rare leek of dry limestone grassland at the Avon Gorge and Jersey, with an egg-shaped head of dark purple flowers and mostly hollow leaves.

name: Galanthus elwesii
tip: Garden snowdrop with wide, greyish-green leaves flat or folded, a larger white flower with a green mark at the base and tip of the inner petals.

name: Galanthus plicatus
tip: Snowdrop with broad leaves that are folded back at the edges, hence pleated, with large white flowers; garden escape, found on woodland edges and churchyards.

name: Galanthus woronowii
tip: Snowdrop with bright green narrow leaves and a single green mark on each inner petal near the base only; garden escape of woodland and verges.

name: Leucojum vernum
tip: Snowdrop-like bulb with bell-shaped white flowers with equal petals, each tipped green; larger than Snowdrop and flowering a little later; scattered garden escape and rare natives.

name: Narcissus bicolor
tip: Garden daffodil with a white spreading perianth and a yellow trumpet; naturalised only locally, and there are many daffodil hybrids; specialist advised to confirm.

name: Gagea lutea
tip: Woodland bulb with a single broad flat basal leaf and a loose cluster of yellow stars, green-striped on the back; other Gagea species are rarer and narrower-leaved.

name: Gagea serotina
tip: Tiny white lily with purple-veined, bell-like petals and thread-like leaves, found only on a few high rock ledges in Snowdonia, North Wales.

name: Lilium martagon
tip: Tall lily with nodding, pinkish-purple spotted flowers whose petals curl right back, and leaves in whorls up the stem; naturalised in a few woods.

name: Lilium pyrenaicum
tip: Garden escape with greenish-yellow, dark-spotted turk's-cap flowers that smell unpleasant, on a leafy stem with many alternate narrow leaves; naturalised locally in the west.

name: Tulipa saxatilis
tip: Small tulip with pale pink to lilac flowers and a yellow centre, with glossy shiny leaves; a rare escape, usually near gardens in Britain.

name: Tulipa sylvestris
tip: Slender tulip with a nodding bud that opens to a yellow star, outer petals greenish; naturalised in old orchards, parks and gardens.

name: Limnanthes douglasii
tip: Garden annual with yellow petals tipped white, and shiny divided leaves with toothed lobes, often escaping on damp disturbed ground.

name: Linum bienne
tip: Slender flax with pale blue flowers, often streaked veins, and narrow single-veined leaves; differs from cultivated flax by being a wiry perennial of grassland near the coast.

name: Linum perenne
tip: Taller, more tufted flax with sky-blue flowers and many narrow leaves; a garden escape, and a scarce native subspecies grows on chalk in East Anglia.

name: Diphasiastrum alpinum
tip: Greyish-green clubmoss with flattened, branching shoots and tiny scale-like leaves pressed along the stems; grows on mountain heaths and grassland in northern and western uplands.

name: Lycopodiella inundata
tip: Small creeping clubmoss with spreading leaves and cones raised on thin upright stalks; grows on bare wet peaty heathland, mostly in the south and west.

name: Lycopodium annotinum
tip: Creeping clubmoss with upright branches clothed in spiky leaves and stalkless cones; leaves sit in distinct bands of yearly growth; upland heaths in the north.

name: Lycopodium lagopus
tip: Clubmoss with creeping stem, with each upright shoot topped by a single cone ending in a white hair; not truly British, so a specialist should confirm.

name: Lythrum hyssopifolia
tip: Slender, branched annual with tiny pink flowers sitting singly in leaf axils and narrow leaves; very rare on seasonally flooded ground in the south and east.

name: Althaea officinalis
tip: Tall plant with soft velvety grey leaves and pale pink five-petalled flowers; grows in coastal marshes and estuaries, mostly in the south.

name: Malva alcea
tip: Mallow with large pink flowers with notched petals, and upper leaves cut into narrow deep lobes; star-shaped hairs on stems.

name: Malva arborea
tip: Tall, woody-based biennial with soft lobed leaves and purple-centred pink flowers; grows on coastal cliffs, rocks and waste ground, mainly western coasts.

name: Malva multiflora
tip: Resembles Tree-mallow but flowers are paler lilac-pink and clustered on shorter stalks; casual or naturalised near the coast in the south-west.

name: Malva setigera
tip: Rare casual with pale pink flowers and lobed hairy leaves, easily mistaken for other mallows; a specialist should confirm identification.

name: Pilularia globulifera
tip: Aquatic fern of muddy pond edges with thin, grass-like, curled leaves and tiny round spore cases at the base; local in shallow water.

name: Paris quadrifolia
tip: Woodland plant with a single whorl of four oval leaves and one green star-like flower with a dark purple central berry-like ovary.

name: Montia parvifolia
tip: Low succulent annual with tiny oval leaves and minute white to pink flowers; a rare naturalised alien so a specialist should confirm.

name: Morus nigra
tip: Spreading tree with rough heart-shaped toothed leaves and dark purple edible fruits like blackberries; planted in gardens, rarely escaping.

name: Myrica pensylvanica
tip: Shrub with aromatic, waxy-fruited, narrow oval leaves with a few teeth near the tip and white fruits; planted, rarely naturalised in bogs.

name: Luma apiculata
tip: Evergreen with peeling orange-cinnamon bark, small oval aromatic leaves and white cup-shaped flowers with many stamens; garden shrub in mild western areas.

name: Ugni molinae
tip: Small evergreen shrub with glossy oval leaves, pink-tinged white nodding bell flowers and later red aromatic berries; grown in mild gardens.

name: Nothofagus alpina
tip: Chilean southern beech with narrow-oval, deeply veined leaves with sharp double teeth, much larger than Roble Beech; planted in parks, woods and forestry.

name: Nothofagus obliqua
tip: Fast-growing Chilean tree with small, wavy-edged oval leaves with uneven bases and tiny flowers; unlike true beech the leaf is toothed; planted in parks and forestry.

name: Nuphar advena
tip: American relative of Yellow Water-lily with similar floating heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers; very rarely planted so a specialist should confirm.

name: Nuphar pumila
tip: Smaller than Yellow Water-lily, with flowers only up to 3 cm across and leaves under 10 cm with a pointed lobe; local in northern lakes.

name: Forsythia suspensa
tip: Shrub with arching branches, bright yellow bell flowers in early spring before leaves appear, and leaves that are often divided into three leaflets.

name: Jasminum beesianum
tip: Scrambling shrub with pinkish-red flowers fading to paler, scented, and oval leaves; occasional garden shrub, rarely persisting.

name: Jasminum nudiflorum
tip: Green-stemmed scrambler with bright yellow flowers appearing in winter on bare stems, and leaves of three leaflets; common garden plant, occasionally naturalised.

name: Jasminum officinale
tip: Vigorous climber with white, sweetly scented flowers and pinnate leaves of five to nine leaflets; a common garden plant, rarely escaping.

name: Circaea alpina
tip: Smaller, weaker than Enchanter's-nightshade, with heart-shaped leaves with shiny blades and tiny white flowers; grows in damp shady rocky places in the uplands of the north.

name: Epilobium alsinifolium
tip: Small mountain willowherb with a creeping base, pale pink flowers with notched petals, and small toothed leaves; grows by springs and streams in the northern uplands.

name: Epilobium anagallidifolium
tip: Tiny creeping willowherb with a nodding top and few, pale pink or reddish flowers; leaves almost smooth-edged; grows by mountain streams and in wet flushes.

name: Epilobium brachycarpum
tip: North American annual willowherb with flowers in a branched panicle, small pink petals and narrow toothed leaves; casual and increasing on waste ground in the south.

name: Epilobium komarovianum
tip: Low creeping willowherb, with small bronze-tinged oval leaves and tiny pale pink to white flowers; a New Zealand alien, so a specialist should confirm.

name: Epilobium lanceolatum
tip: Downy willowherb with leaves narrowing into stalks and pale pink petals; unlike Broad-leaved Willowherb, stigma is club-shaped; in southern England on waste ground.

name: Epilobium pedunculare
tip: New Zealand creeping willowherb with small round leaves and pale pink to white flowers; commonly escapes on paths, walls and rockeries.

name: Ludwigia grandiflora
tip: Invasive aquatic plant with large bright yellow five-petalled flowers and oblong hairy leaves in stands; wide choking in ponds and ditches; mainly in the south.

name: Ludwigia palustris
tip: Creeping plant of wet muddy places with opposite oval leaves and tiny green petalless flowers in leaf axils; rare, mainly in the New Forest.

name: Oenothera stricta
tip: Yellow evening-primrose with narrow leaves and flowers fading orange-red, with a sweet scent; rare, casual in dunes and waste ground.

name: Ophioglossum azoricum
tip: Tiny fern with a single oval leaf blade and a short spore spike; very rare, found in short turf near the coast, mainly in Scilly.

name: Ophioglossum lusitanicum
tip: Very small winter-green fern with a narrow undivided blade and a minute spike; found only in Scilly and the Channel Islands.

name: Anacamptis laxiflora
tip: Tall orchid with loose spikes of deep reddish-purple flowers and narrow keeled leaves; occurs in wet meadows in the Channel Islands.

name: Anacamptis morio
tip: Short orchid with purple flowers whose side petals are marked by green veins, and an unspotted rosette of leaves; grows in old meadows.

name: Cephalanthera damasonium
tip: Woodland orchid with creamy-white flowers that remain mostly closed, and broad ribbed leaves; mainly in southern beechwoods on chalk.

name: Cephalanthera longifolia
tip: Woodland orchid with open white flowers and long narrow leaves held in two ranks; local in woods mostly in the south.

name: Cephalanthera rubra
tip: Very rare orchid with showy rose-pink flowers, and narrow pointed leaves; found only in a few beechwoods in the Chilterns and Gloucestershire.

name: Coeloglossum viride
tip: Small orchid with greenish-brown flowers with hooded top and a narrow, notched lip; grows in short grassland and dunes.

name: Corallorhiza trifida
tip: Leafless orchid with a coral-like underground root and a few pale yellow-green flowers on a thin stem; grows in damp woods and dune slacks in Scotland.

name: Cypripedium calceolus
tip: Spectacular orchid with a large yellow slipper-shaped lip and twisted maroon petals; extremely rare, in one site in northern England.

name: Dactylorhiza kerryensis
tip: Marsh-orchid with pink-purple flowers and narrow, unspotted or lightly marked leaves; western Ireland, but requires a specialist to separate from relatives.

name: Dactylorhiza traunsteinerioides
tip: Slender marsh-orchid of wet places with narrow unspotted leaves and few small purple flowers with a slim lip; a specialist should confirm.

name: Epipactis atrorubens
tip: Orchid with dark wine-red, vanilla-scented flowers and downy stems; grows on limestone in northern England, Wales and the Burren.

name: Epipactis dunensis
tip: Yellowish-green helleborine of dune slacks in northern England and north Wales, with mostly self-pollinated flowers; a specialist should confirm.

name: Epipactis leptochila
tip: Slender helleborine of beechwoods with nodding yellowish-green flowers with a narrow lip, and leaves in two ranks; local in the south.

name: Epipactis palustris
tip: Marsh orchid with showy flowers whose lip is white and frilly, and brownish sepals; grows in fens and dune slacks.

name: Epipactis phyllanthes
tip: Helleborine with drooping, pale green flowers that hardly open and have a blunt lip; found in dunes and beechwoods; a specialist should confirm.

name: Epipactis purpurata
tip: Late-flowering helleborine with whitish-green flowers, leaves flushed violet below and stems in clumps; found in shady southern woodland.

name: Epipogium aphyllum
tip: Leafless, pale, nearly translucent orchid with a few pinkish-yellow flowers; extremely rare in deep shade of old beechwoods in the Chilterns.

name: Goodyera repens
tip: Small orchid with a rosette of net-veined, oval leaves and a one-sided spike of white flowers with downy hairs; grows in pine woods.

name: Gymnadenia borealis
tip: Smaller than other fragrant-orchids with short pink spikes, flowers with a short spur; grows in acid grassland and heaths in the north and west.

name: Gymnadenia conopsea
tip: Orchid with a long slender spike of pink scented flowers with a very long thin spur and narrow leaves; chalk grassland.

name: Gymnadenia densiflora
tip: Stouter, later flowering fragrant-orchid with a dense spike of pink flowers with a short spur, broader leaves; wet meadows and fens.

name: Hammarbya paludosa
tip: Tiny yellow-green orchid growing in sphagnum, with minute flowers and small leaves with bulbils at the tips; rare in wet bogs.

name: Herminium monorchis
tip: Small orchid with tiny honey-scented yellow-green flowers and two leaves at the base; found in short chalk grassland in southern England.

name: Himantoglossum hircinum
tip: Tall robust orchid with grey-green flowers with an extremely long twisted lip, and a goat-like smell; local in southern and eastern England.

name: Liparis loeselii
tip: Small yellow-green orchid with two glossy ribbed leaves and a few flowers with a narrow lip; rare, in dune slacks and fens.

name: Neotinea maculata
tip: Short spike of many small whitish to greenish flowers with pinkish markings on lip; very local on Burren limestone and Isle of Man.

name: Neotinea ustulata
tip: Small orchid with a dense head with dark red-brown buds that look scorched and open to white spotted lips; short chalk grassland.

name: Neottia nidus-avis
tip: Leafless, honey-brown plant with a nest-like root tangle and brown flowers; grows in deep shade of beech and hazel woods.

name: Ophrys fuciflora
tip: Orchid with large pink sepals and a rounded velvety brown lip marked pale; flowers later than Early Spider-orchid; confined to Kent.

name: Ophrys insectifera
tip: Slender orchid with flowers resembling flies, a dark purple velvety lip with a blue patch and thin green sepals; woods on chalk.

name: Ophrys sphegodes
tip: Orchid with a rounded velvety dark brown lip marked with an H-shape, yellow-green sepals; flowers earlier than Late Spider-orchid; chalk grassland in the south.

name: Orchis anthropophora
tip: Spike of small yellow-green flowers whose lips look like dangling little men with arms and legs; grows on chalk and limestone in the south.

name: Orchis militaris
tip: Orchid with a pale pink to white spike with lilac hoods, each lip like a small figure; confined to a few sites in the Chilterns and Suffolk.

name: Orchis purpurea
tip: Stout orchid with large dark brown hoods and a pale pink lip dotted purple, shaped like a lady in a skirt; local in Kent woods.

name: Orchis simia
tip: Orchid with pinkish-white hooded flowers and a narrow-limbed pink lip with dark tips and a dense spike; very rare in Kent and Oxfordshire.

name: Platanthera bifolia
tip: Two broad oval leaves at the base and greenish-white scented flowers whose two pollen masses are parallel, unlike the Greater Butterfly-orchid where they diverge.

name: Pseudorchis albida
tip: Small, dense spike of tiny greenish-white vanilla-scented flowers with a short blunt lip; basal leaves oval-oblong and the upper ones small. Mostly northern and western upland grassland.

name: Serapias lingua
tip: Large dark purplish-red flowers with a long tongue-like lip hanging down from a hood; narrow leaves. Very rare in Britain, mainly the Channel Islands and the south-west.

name: Serapias parviflora
tip: Similar to Tongue Orchid but with smaller, paler orange-brown flowers and a narrower lip; a very rare Mediterranean orchid in the Channel Islands and Cornwall.

name: Spiranthes romanzoffiana
tip: Spike of creamy-white flowers in three spiral rows, with the lip frilled and constricted; leaves are all on the stem, unlike Autumn Lady's-tresses. Western Ireland, Scotland and Devon.

name: Spiranthes spiralis
tip: Slender spiral of small white flowers in one row; the leaf rosette sits beside the flowering stem, not below it. Short turf, flowering late summer.

name: Bartsia alpina
tip: Dark purple tubular flowers among purplish, toothed bracts on a hairy stem with opposite oval leaves; damp mountain ledges and meadows in northern England and Scotland.

name: Euphrasia cambrica
tip: Small eyebright of short upland turf in Wales. Eyebrights are very difficult; a specialist is needed to confirm this species.

name: Euphrasia campbelliae
tip: Rare eyebright restricted to the Outer Hebrides. Specialist examination of hairs, leaves and corolla is needed to separate it from other eyebrights.

name: Euphrasia foulaensis
tip: Small, often branched eyebright of northern Scottish coasts and islands including Shetland. Eyebrights are a difficult group; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Euphrasia frigida
tip: Small eyebright of high Scottish mountain grassland and flushes, with slender stem and small flowers. Identification within the genus needs a specialist.

name: Euphrasia heslop-harrisonii
tip: Rare British eyebright found in few places in the north. A specialist is needed to confirm it among the many similar eyebright species.

name: Euphrasia marshallii
tip: Eyebright of northern Scottish coasts and islands, often short and rather stiff. Within this difficult group a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Euphrasia officinalis
tip: Small semi-parasitic annual with toothed opposite leaves and white flowers marked lilac and yellow. Many similar species exist; a specialist is needed to name the exact species.

name: Euphrasia ostenfeldii
tip: Small eyebright of northern coasts and islands, mainly in Scotland. As with other eyebrights, a specialist is needed to confirm the species.

name: Euphrasia pseudokerneri
tip: Eyebright of dry chalk and limestone grassland in southern and eastern England, usually branched. A specialist is needed to separate it from similar species.

name: Euphrasia rivularis
tip: Upland eyebright of wet places in Wales and northern England, often with a rather leafy stem. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Euphrasia rotundifolia
tip: Small eyebright with rounded leaves, found on north-western Scottish coasts and islands. A specialist is needed to tell it from other eyebrights.

name: Euphrasia salisburgensis
tip: Slender eyebright with narrow, almost hairless leaves and white flowers, on limestone pavement and dunes in western Ireland and north Wales. Check with a specialist.

name: Euphrasia scottica
tip: Eyebright of damp grassland and flushes in northern Britain and Ireland, often unbranched and rather leafy. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Euphrasia tetraquetra
tip: Eyebright of coastal and downland turf with a stiff, branched habit. The genus is difficult, so a specialist is needed to confirm the species.

name: Euphrasia vigursii
tip: Rare eyebright of heaths and cliff turf in Cornwall and south-west England, with relatively large flowers. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Lathraea clandestina
tip: Leafless parasite with violet flowers in one-sided spikes and pale scaly stems; flowers are mauve-purple, unlike the pale pinkish Toothwort. Naturalised by streams under willow or alder.

name: Lathraea squamaria
tip: Pale pinkish-white parasitic plant with no green colour, drooping one-sided spike of flowers and scaly stems, growing on hazel and elm roots in woods.

name: Melampyrum arvense
tip: Annual with showy pink-purple bracts and yellow-and-purple flowers, narrow leaves on a hairy stem. A very rare arable weed mainly in southern England.

name: Melampyrum cristatum
tip: Dense four-sided spike of overlapping purple-pink crested bracts with yellow flowers peeping out; narrow opposite leaves. Rare in woodland rides in eastern England.

name: Melampyrum sylvaticum
tip: Slender annual of woods with small yellow flowers hanging in pairs, with the lower lip bent down; leaves narrow and untoothed. Mainly northern Britain and Ireland.

name: Odontites jaubertianus
