tip: Rare red-bartsia type with pink flowers in a one-sided spike and narrow toothed leaves. Probably a casual in Britain; identification uncertain, so check with a specialist.

name: Orobanche alba
tip: Parasitic purplish-red plant without green leaves, flowers with a red-purple tint, growing on wild thyme. Coastal and upland grassland in Wales, Scotland and Ireland.

name: Orobanche caryophyllacea
tip: Stout yellowish-brown broomrape with purple tinges and a sweet carnation scent, on bedstraws; very rare, now mainly Kent coastal grassland.

name: Orobanche crenata
tip: Large broomrape with creamy-white flowers veined with violet, parasitic on beans and other legumes. A rare casual of crops, mainly in southern England.

name: Orobanche elatior
tip: Tall yellowish broomrape with dull yellow flowers often tinged brown, on knapweed roots in calcareous grassland, mostly southern and eastern England.

name: Orobanche hederae
tip: Slender broomrape with creamy flowers tinged purple, growing at the base of ivy; stigma yellow. Commonest near the coast and in gardens.

name: Orobanche picridis
tip: Yellowish broomrape with purple-tinged, sweet-scented flowers on bristly oxtongue; found on coastal cliffs and clay slopes in south-east England.

name: Orobanche rapum-genistae
tip: Tall, stout, dull yellow-brown broomrape with reddish veins growing on broom and gorse. Locally frequent, mainly in the south and west.

name: Orobanche reticulata
tip: Broomrape with yellowish flowers tinged purple, parasitic on thistles, with a dark purple stigma. Rare, in limestone and calcareous grassland in northern England and the south.

name: Parentucellia viscosa
tip: Sticky hairy annual with pale yellow flowers in a leafy spike and opposite narrow toothed leaves; damp grassland, mainly in the south and west.

name: Phelipanche purpurea
tip: Slender broomrape with violet-blue flowers and bluish stem, parasitic on yarrow. Very rare in England and the Channel Islands.

name: Rhinanthus angustifolius
tip: Taller than Yellow-rattle, with yellow flowers whose upper-lip teeth are longer and often violet; leaves narrow and toothed. Rare in northern Scotland and eastern England.

name: Oxalis debilis
tip: Garden weed with clover-like leaves on long stalks, bright pink flowers with a darker throat; bulbil-bearing roots; common in the south and west.

name: Oxalis decaphylla
tip: Garden escape with many leaflets, up to about ten per leaf, and pale pink flowers; leaves are not clover-like in structure. Very rare casual.

name: Oxalis dillenii
tip: Small hairy yellow-sorrel with clover-like leaves and no runners, flowers in groups of two to three; rare alien in southern England.

name: Oxalis incarnata
tip: Leafy-stemmed pink-sorrel with pale pink to lilac flowers and small bulbils; naturalised in warm sheltered places in the south and west.

name: Oxalis latifolia
tip: Pink-flowered clover-like sorrel with bulb-like roots, forming dense patches in beds and paths, mainly in the south and west.

name: Oxalis megalorrhiza
tip: Garden escape with tuberous roots, fleshy stems and yellow flowers; rare and naturalised in warm gardens, such as in south-west England.

name: Oxalis pes-caprae
tip: Clump of clover-like leaves with bright yellow, larger flowers with a flushed throat in winter and spring; weed of bulb fields in Scilly and Cornwall.

name: Oxalis rosea
tip: Slender pink-flowered sorrel with clover-like leaves, usually in gardens; a rare escape. Check carefully against other pink-sorrels.

name: Oxalis stricta
tip: Yellow-flowered sorrel with an upright stem, clover-like leaves and no bulbils or runners; a common garden weed in many parts of Britain.

name: Oxalis tetraphylla
tip: Pink-sorrel with four leaflets per leaf, each with a dark purple band; flowers pink with a yellow throat. Common in gardens, mainly in warm areas.

name: Oxalis valdiviensis
tip: Rare garden escape with clover-like leaves and yellow flowers, sometimes veined orange; identification uncertain so check with a specialist.

name: Paeonia mascula
tip: Large crimson bowl-shaped flowers and deeply lobed leaves on stout stems; very rare and found only on Steep Holm in the Bristol Channel.

name: Corydalis cava
tip: Early spring woodland plant with a hollow rounded tuber, finely divided blue-green leaves and a spike of dull purple or white flowers. Tuber is hollow, unlike Bird-in-a-bush.

name: Corydalis solida
tip: Spring woodland plant with a solid tuber, lobed pale blue-green leaves and a spike of pinkish-purple spurred flowers; bracts are fingered, unlike Hollowroot.

name: Dicentra eximia
tip: Garden perennial with finely cut greyish leaves and arching heart-shaped pink flowers; a rare escape, not usually long-established.

name: Dicentra formosa
tip: Garden plant with finely cut blue-green leaves and hanging pink heart-shaped flowers; locally naturalised, mainly in northern and western Britain.

name: Fumaria bastardii
tip: Scrambling plant with large pink flowers with dark tips, over 9 mm long, and broad leaf segments; mostly south-west England and Wales. Hard to separate from other fumitories.

name: Fumaria capreolata
tip: Strong climbing fumitory with creamy-white flowers with dark red tips, leaf-stalks that curl like tendrils; locally common in the south-west and Ireland.

name: Fumaria densiflora
tip: Compact fumitory with very small pale pink flowers packed in dense spikes and blue-grey, finely divided leaves; East Anglian arable fields.

name: Fumaria occidentalis
tip: Rare climbing fumitory with white or pale pink flowers, tipped dark red, with a long lower petal; confined to Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.

name: Fumaria parviflora
tip: Spiky fumitory with very narrow channelled leaf segments and small whitish-pink flowers tipped dark red; local arable weed, chiefly southern and eastern England.

name: Fumaria purpurea
tip: Sturdy climbing fumitory with large purplish-pink flowers, 10 to 12 mm, and toothed fruit sepals; found in hedges and cultivated land, mostly in the south and west.

name: Fumaria reuteri
tip: Climbing fumitory with pale pink flowers dark at tips, in dense clusters, and leaves with flat, broad segments; local in southern England.

name: Fumaria vaillantii
tip: Small slender fumitory with few tiny pale pink flowers in a loose spike, and very narrow blue-green leaf segments; arable land in southern and eastern England.

name: Glaucium flavum
tip: Shingle plant with large yellow poppy flowers, blue-grey wavy leaves and long curved horn-like seed pods. Coastal shingle, mostly in southern and eastern Britain.

name: Papaver atlanticum
tip: Garden poppy with orange or yellow, saucer-shaped flowers and bristly hairy stems; leaves lobed. A rare casual, so identification may need checking.

name: Papaver cambricum
tip: Poppy with bright yellow flowers, bright green lobed leaves and yellow sap. Native in south-west England and Wales, widely planted and escaped elsewhere.

name: Papaver lecoqii
tip: Poppy with scarlet flowers like Long-headed Poppy but with yellow latex that darkens when exposed; lobed leaves. A scarce arable weed in southern England.

name: Papaver setiferum
tip: Opium Poppy relative with lilac flowers, glaucous leaves and a few stiff bristles on the stem. Garden escape or casual, not common.

name: Pseudofumaria alba
tip: Wall plant with finely cut greyish leaves and creamy-white tubular flowers with a yellow lip tip; walls and rocks, widely naturalised across Britain.

name: Roemeria argemone
tip: Poppy with small pale scarlet flowers with a dark spot, bristly stems, and long narrow pods with a few bristles; fruits are club-shaped. Arable land, mostly in the south.

name: Roemeria hispida
tip: Poppy with small dark red flowers and bristly globose pods, with stems rough from stiff hairs. Rare arable weed on chalk in southern and eastern England.

name: Paulownia tomentosa
tip: Small tree with huge heart-shaped hairy leaves and upright clusters of pale violet foxglove-like flowers opening before the leaves. Planted, sometimes self-sown in cities.

name: Erythranthe moschata
tip: Sticky, softly hairy monkeyflower with pale yellow flowers and a musky smell, often now scentless. Wet places, widely naturalised.

name: Erythranthe peregrina
tip: Hybrid-derived monkeyflower with yellow flowers heavily blotched with red-brown, found by streams in parts of Scotland. Needs careful checking against other monkeyflowers.

name: Phytolacca polyandra
tip: Tall herb with oval leaves and upright spikes of small white or pale pink flowers turning into purple-black berries. Rare naturalised garden plant.

name: Abies alba
tip: Tall conifer with flat needles bearing two white bands beneath, notched at the tip, and upright cones; needles lack the pungent smell of Grand Fir.

name: Abies cephalonica
tip: Conifer with stiff, spiky needles spreading all round the twig, two white bands beneath, and upright cones with turned-back bracts. Planted, mostly in parks.

name: Pittosporum crassifolium
tip: Evergreen shrub with leathery oval leaves white-felted below and dark red small flowers in clusters; planted, often near the coast in the south and west.

name: Pittosporum tenuifolium
tip: Evergreen shrub with wavy-edged pale green oval leaves on dark twigs and tiny dark purple, honey-scented flowers; planted, naturalising in mild coastal areas.

name: Asarina procumbens
tip: Sticky hairy trailing climber with soft heart-shaped, lobed leaves and cream-yellow snapdragon-like flowers; a rare garden escape on walls.

name: Callitriche hermaphroditica
tip: Submerged aquatic with narrow, notched leaves in whorls without a floating rosette, and tiny flowers; a hard-to-see plant of clear still water.

name: Callitriche obtusangula
tip: Aquatic starwort making floating rosettes of broad leaves with slender submerged ones; tiny green flowers. Ripe fruit is needed to separate it from other water-starworts; check with a specialist.

name: Callitriche palustris
tip: Very rare starwort with small rosettes and notched submerged leaves; fruit small and narrowly keeled. Easily confused with other water-starworts, so confirmation by a specialist is needed.

name: Callitriche truncata
tip: Wholly submerged starwort with narrow, deeply notched leaves and no floating rosette; rare, mainly in southern England. Fruit is needed to be sure of the identification.

name: Chaenorhinum origanifolium
tip: Small tufted sticky-hairy wall plant with violet and whitish snapdragon flowers on long thin stalks. Naturalised on old walls, notably in Kent; much smaller than Ivy-leaved Toadflax.

name: Cymbalaria hepaticifolia
tip: Tiny creeping wall plant with shallowly lobed, rounded leaves and minute pale lilac snapdragon flowers. Much smaller and more delicate than Ivy-leaved Toadflax; a rare garden escape.

name: Cymbalaria pallida
tip: Trailing wall plant like Ivy-leaved Toadflax but with softly hairy, thicker leaves and pale lilac flowers with a yellow patch in the throat. Occasional garden escape.

name: Digitalis lutea
tip: Tall foxglove with slender spikes of small, narrow pale yellow bells and shiny narrow leaves. Smaller flowers than Common Foxglove and wrong colour; a rare garden escape.

name: Erinus alpinus
tip: Small tufted plant on walls and rocks with spoon-shaped toothed leaves and short clusters of five-lobed purple-pink flowers. Established on old walls in a few places.

name: Limosella aquatica
tip: Tiny annual of drying mud with rosettes of long-stalked spoon-shaped leaves and minute whitish flowers on short stalks. Found on pond and reservoir margins, mostly in England and Wales.

name: Limosella australis
tip: Tiny mud plant like Mudwort but with narrow, awl-like leaves and no spoon-shaped blade. Very rare, known from estuary mud in Wales.

name: Linaria arenaria
tip: Small sticky-hairy annual with tiny pale yellow flowers and a short spur, on coastal dunes. Introduced, naturalised in a few places such as south-west England.

name: Linaria dalmatica
tip: Tall blue-grey toadflax with broad, clasping, pointed leaves and big lemon-yellow snapdragon flowers with orange throat. Larger and broader-leaved than Common Toadflax; garden escape.

name: Linaria pelisseriana
tip: Slender, upright toadflax with narrow leaves and violet flowers with a white throat. Native in Jersey; elsewhere in Britain only a rare casual or garden escape.

name: Linaria repens
tip: Greyish toadflax with whorled narrow leaves and white or pale lilac flowers streaked with violet veins. Spreads by suckers on banks and waste ground; mainly southern and eastern England.

name: Linaria supina
tip: Low, spreading toadflax with grey-green narrow leaves and yellow flowers with an orange palate. A rare casual or garden escape on waste ground, not a native.

name: Misopates orontium
tip: Upright annual of arable fields with narrow leaves and pink snapdragon flowers, lacking a spur but with a swollen base. Local, mainly in southern and eastern England.

name: Plantago arenaria
tip: Annual plantain with leafy branching stems and narrow opposite leaves; tiny brownish flower heads. Introduced casual of waste ground, sometimes with bird seed; unlike other plantains it has no rosette.

name: Sibthorpia europaea
tip: Creeping evergreen with hairy kidney-shaped scalloped leaves and minute pink-and-white flowers. Grows in shady damp banks and lanes in south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

name: Veronica alpina
tip: Mountain speedwell with a short terminal cluster of small dark blue flowers and oval leaves on mostly unbranched stems. Rare, on high Scottish mountains.

name: Veronica crista-galli
tip: Mat-forming speedwell from south-east Europe with spikes of blue flowers and toothed leaves; not native. Rare garden relic, uncertain identity so check with a specialist.

name: Veronica fruticans
tip: Small tufted mountain speedwell with a few deep blue flowers with a red eye in short clusters, leaves oval and slightly leathery. Rare, on Scottish mountain rocks.

name: Veronica longifolia
tip: Tall speedwell with long narrow toothed leaves and dense spikes of lilac-blue flowers. A garden plant, escaped on riverbanks and waste ground; much taller than native spiked species.

name: Veronica praecox
tip: Small spring annual with glandular hairs, toothed oval leaves and single deep blue flowers in the leaf axils. Very rare, found on sandy arable ground in Breckland.

name: Veronica salicifolia
tip: Evergreen shrub with narrow smooth leaves and dense spikes of white or lilac-tinged flowers. Planted and naturalised near coasts in the south-west and Ireland; not like any herbaceous speedwell.

name: Veronica spicata
tip: Upright speedwell with long dense spikes of blue flowers and toothed oval leaves. Rare native of dry limestone and chalk turf in East Anglia and Wales; also garden forms.

name: Veronica triphyllos
tip: Small annual with deep blue flowers and leaves cut into finger-like lobes, on sandy arable land. Rare, mainly in East Anglia (Breckland).

name: Veronica verna
tip: Tiny, upright, glandular-hairy annual with lobed leaves and small blue flowers in leafy spikes. Very rare, on dry sandy ground in Breckland and a few other sites.

name: Armeria arenaria
tip: Tufted thrift with broader, flatter grass-like leaves than Thrift and pink globe-shaped flower heads. Rare, mainly sand dune plant of the Channel Islands; seldom seen elsewhere in Britain.

name: Limonium auriculae-ursifolium
tip: Mediterranean sea-lavender with a rosette of broad oval leaves and branched lilac flower sprays. A rare escape; sea-lavenders need a specialist to confirm.

name: Limonium bellidifolium
tip: Small, dense sea-lavender with leaves that wither before flowering and small pale lilac flowers in compact spikes. Very rare, on sandy and shingly saltmarsh edges in East Anglia.

name: Limonium binervosum
tip: Compact sea-lavender of rocky coasts with spoon-shaped leaves with one or three veins and lilac flowers in short spikes. Aggregate of many microspecies; a specialist is needed to name it.

name: Limonium britannicum
tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of southern coastal cliffs with leathery spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in short spikes. A specialist is needed to name it with certainty.

name: Limonium dodartiforme
tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of sea cliffs with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in spreading spikes. A specialist is needed to confirm which microspecies it is.

name: Limonium humile
tip: Sea-lavender of the upper saltmarsh with narrow spoon-shaped, one-veined leaves and loose, sparse spikes of lilac flowers. Compare Common Sea-lavender, which has broader leaves and denser heads.

name: Limonium hyblaeum
tip: Mediterranean sea-lavender with broad oval leaves and branched sprays of lilac flowers. Very rare introduction; sea-lavenders need a specialist to confirm identification.

name: Limonium loganicum
tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of Cornish coastal rocks, with small spoon-shaped leaves and short lilac flower spikes. A specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Limonium normannicum
tip: Low sea-lavender of the Channel Islands, with spoon-shaped leaves and short lilac flower spikes on sea cliffs. A rock sea-lavender microspecies needing a specialist to name it.

name: Limonium paradoxum
tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies restricted to coastal rocks near Oban in western Scotland, with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers on short spikes. Confirm with a specialist.

name: Limonium parvum
tip: Very small rock sea-lavender microspecies with tiny spoon-shaped leaves and short lilac spikes on sea cliffs. Separation from other rock sea-lavenders needs a specialist.

name: Limonium platyphyllum
tip: Robust garden sea-lavender with large oval leaves and big airy branched sprays of lilac flowers. A rare escape well away from the coast, unlike native sea-lavenders.

name: Limonium procerum
tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of western coasts with larger spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in longer spikes. A specialist is needed to confirm identification.

name: Limonium recurvum
tip: Rock sea-lavender found only on limestone cliffs and quarries on Portland, Dorset, with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in curved spikes. A specialist can confirm it.

name: Limonium transwallianum
tip: Rock sea-lavender microspecies of western coasts, with spoon-shaped leaves and lilac flowers in short spikes. Very similar to other microspecies, so a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Limonium vulgare
tip: Saltmarsh perennial with broad leaves with one main vein and dense, branched sprays of lilac flowers. Common on muddy estuary marshes; Lax-flowered Sea-lavender has narrower leaves and sparse spikes.

name: Polemonium caeruleum
tip: Tall plant with ladder-like pinnate leaves and nodding to upright violet-blue bowl-shaped flowers with orange anthers. Rare native of limestone dales in northern England; also a garden escape.

name: Polygala amarella
tip: Small milkwort with the lower leaves larger and broader, forming a rosette, which taste bitter. Rare, on chalk and limestone grassland in Kent and the north.

name: Polygala calcarea
tip: Low milkwort with a basal rosette of larger leaves and bright blue flowers, rarely white. Lives on chalk and limestone grassland in southern England; Common Milkwort lacks the rosette.

name: Bistorta affinis
tip: Clump-forming knotweed with long narrow basal leaves and short dense pink spikes. A garden plant; Red Bistort has clasping heart-based stem leaves and slimmer spikes.

name: Bistorta amplexicaulis
tip: Tall garden knotweed with heart-shaped, clasping stem leaves and long slender spikes of crimson flowers. Naturalised on roadsides and waste ground, flowering until autumn.

name: Fagopyrum cymosum
tip: Robust perennial with arrow-shaped, triangular leaves and white flower clusters in branched heads. A rare garden escape; compare Buckwheat, which is annual and more slender.

name: Fagopyrum esculentum
tip: Annual crop with triangular heart-shaped leaves, red-tinged stems and clusters of white or pink flowers. Occasional casual on tips and field edges, grown for grain or game cover.

name: Fallopia dumetorum
tip: Twining climber with heart-shaped leaves and tiny greenish-white flowers; fruits have three winged ridges. Native in hedgerows and woods, mostly south-east England; compare Black-bindweed, which has unwinged fruits.

name: Koenigia alpina
tip: Tall garden knotweed with narrow pointed leaves and big airy sprays of tiny white flowers. Occasional garden escape on waste ground; less coarse than Japanese Knotweed.

name: Koenigia campanulata
tip: Clump-forming knotweed with white-felted undersides to leaves and nodding pink or white bell-like flowers. Widespread garden escape on damp banks and roadsides, especially in the west.

name: Koenigia islandica
tip: Tiny, weak, mat-forming annual with small oval leaves and minute greenish flowers. Very rare, found only on a few mountain sites in Skye and Mull.

name: Koenigia mollis
tip: Tall garden knotweed with broad softly hairy oval leaves and large branched sprays of tiny white flowers. Rare escape; best checked with a specialist.

name: Koenigia polystachya
tip: Dense patch-forming plant with long narrow pointed leaves and rounded clusters of pink-white flowers. Aggressive garden escape on damp roadsides and streamsides, widely naturalised.

name: Koenigia weyrichii
tip: Tall garden knotweed with long oval leaves white-felted beneath and large sprays of tiny white flowers. Very rare escape; specialist confirmation advised.

name: Muehlenbeckia complexa
tip: Wiry, tangled evergreen climber with tiny round leaves and small greenish flowers followed by white fleshy fruits. Naturalised on walls and hedges in the south-west and Scilly.

name: Oxyria digyna
tip: Mountain plant with fleshy, kidney-shaped leaves, a sour taste and tiny greenish-red flowers turning to flat winged fruits. Common on damp rocks in Scottish and Welsh uplands.

name: Persicaria minor
tip: Slender low annual of damp ground with narrow leaves and thin spikes of tiny pink flowers. Stipule sheaths have long bristles; unlike Water-pepper, leaves are not peppery.

name: Persicaria mitis
tip: Annual of damp places with narrow leaves and slender, often nodding pink spikes; the leaves are not hot to taste. Stipule sheaths have long bristles. Local in southern England.

name: Persicaria nepalensis
tip: Low spreading annual with winged leaf stalks, triangular-oval leaves and round heads of tiny white or pink flowers. Garden escape of damp waste ground.

name: Polygonum boreale
tip: Sprawling knotgrass of the north with oval to narrow leaves and pinkish-white flowers in leaf axils. Scarcely separable from Knotgrass without fruit, so specialist advice is useful.

name: Polygonum cognatum
tip: Mat-forming knotgrass with small thick, grey-green leaves and clustered pink-green flowers. Rare casual from the east; confirm with a specialist.

name: Polygonum depressum
tip: Low mat-forming knotgrass with small oval leaves and tiny pinkish-green flowers in the leaf axils. Close to Equal-leaved Knotgrass, so a specialist is needed.

name: Polygonum maritimum
tip: Rare coastal knotgrass with thick leathery grey-green leaves with rolled margins and silvery stipules; flowers small and white or pink. Found on sand and shingle beaches on southern coasts.

name: Polygonum oxyspermum
tip: Coastal knotgrass of strandlines with fleshy leaves and small greenish-white or pink flowers. Ripe fruits protrude beyond the perianth. Scarce on sand and shingle, mostly on northern and western coasts.

name: Polygonum rurivagum
tip: Slender, wiry knotgrass with very narrow leaves and pinkish flowers in the leaf axils. Scarce plant of arable fields, mostly in southern and eastern England.

name: Reynoutria sachalinensis
tip: Huge knotweed with large leaves, heart-shaped at the base and hairy beneath, and drooping cream flower sprays. Larger than Japanese Knotweed; invasive on roadsides and riverbanks.

name: Rumex alpinus
tip: Large dock with big rounded, heart-based leaves with wavy edges and dense green flower spikes. Naturalised near old farms and villages, mostly in northern England and Scotland.

name: Rumex aquaticus
tip: Tall water dock with big triangular heart-based leaves and dense whorled flower spikes. Very rare, around Loch Lomond in Scotland. Compare Water Dock, which is more widespread.

name: Rumex confertus
tip: Tall dock with hairy veins under heart-based leaves and dense, narrow flower spikes. Naturalised on waste ground and roadsides, mainly in eastern England.

name: Rumex cristatus
tip: Large dock with big wavy heart-based leaves and dense spikes with big fruiting valves. Naturalised on waste ground, mainly in south-east England.

name: Rumex cuneifolius
tip: Dock with wedge-shaped, spoon-like leaf bases and red-tinged fruit spikes. Introduced; established in a few places in southern England and sandy ground.

name: Rumex maritimus
tip: Annual dock of muddy pond margins, with narrow leaves and whorls of golden-yellow fruits with spiny valves. Local in lowland England; slimmer than Marsh Dock.

name: Rumex palustris
tip: Annual or biennial dock with narrow leaves and golden-brown whorled fruits with bristle-like teeth. Rare, on muddy pond and ditch margins, mainly south-east England.

name: Rumex patientia
tip: Tall, robust dock with broad, long-stalked leaves rounded or slightly wedge-shaped at the base. Fruits heart-shaped, one with a swollen grain. Naturalised on waste ground, mainly in the south.

name: Rumex pulcher
tip: Dock with leaves narrowed in the middle like a fiddle, and widely spreading branches with fruits that have spiny teeth. Common on dry grassy ground in southern and eastern England.

name: Rumex rupestris
tip: Rare dock of coastal shingle and rocks, with blue-green, pointed, shortly toothed leaves and wavy margins. Declined, now confined to south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

name: Rumex salicifolius
tip: Dock with narrow willow-like leaves and slender flowering spikes. Rare introduction from North America; identity best confirmed with a specialist.

name: Rumex scutatus
tip: Greyish, waxy, arrow-shaped leaves with spreading basal lobes, unlike the greener common sorrels. Escape on walls, railways and rubble, mainly in England.

name: Cyrtomium falcatum
tip: Glossy, leathery, undivided pinnae with pointed tips, like holly leaves. Occasional escape on shaded walls and in urban cracks, especially in the south and west.

name: Cyrtomium fortunei
tip: Duller than House Holly-fern, with pinnae distinctly toothed towards the tip and less glossy. Rare garden escape on walls and in shaded urban places.

name: Dryopteris aemula
tip: Fronds triangular, finely divided, yellowish-green with curled-up pinna edges; smells of new hay when crushed. Western woods and shaded banks, mostly in Wales, Ireland and the west.

name: Dryopteris cristata
tip: Narrow, upright, ladder-like fronds with pinnae held in a flat plane, unlike other buckler-ferns. Rare, in fens and wet woods of East Anglia and Ireland.

name: Dryopteris expansa
tip: Triangular, pale yellowish-green fronds, thrice divided, with small pale-centred scales on the stalk. Damp upland woods and rocky slopes, mainly northern Britain.

name: Dryopteris oreades
tip: Golden-green fronds with a strong sweet smell when crushed, tightly tufted and tapering to the base. Mountain rocks and scree, common in the north and west.

name: Dryopteris submontana
tip: Stiff, greyish-green, leathery fronds with glandular undersides; lime-loving. Limestone pavement and rocks in northern England, north Wales and western Ireland.

name: Phymatosorus diversifolius
tip: Leathery, glossy, undivided to deeply lobed fronds arising from a creeping rhizome. Naturalised mainly in mild western spots such as Ireland; confirm locally.

name: Polypodium cambricum
tip: Large, pale green fronds with long, tapering, finely toothed pinnae, unlike the blunter common polypody. Wet western rocks, walls and banks; fronds appear in winter.

name: Polystichum lonchitis
tip: Stiff, dark, glossy, spiny-toothed pinnae, narrow frond once divided. Rare, on mountain rock ledges and base-rich crags in Scotland and northern England.

name: Polystichum munitum
tip: Large evergreen sword-shaped fronds, undivided pinnae with a small ear at base and fine teeth. Planted and self-sown in damp woods, mostly in the west.

name: Pontederia cordata
tip: Upright spikes of blue-violet flowers with a yellow spot, above glossy heart-shaped leaves in shallow water. Garden pond plant, rarely naturalised in the south.

name: Portulaca oleracea
tip: Fleshy, reddish, sprawling stems with paddle-shaped leaves and tiny yellow flowers opening only in sun. Garden weed and bare ground, mainly southern England.

name: Groenlandia densa
tip: Submerged stems with opposite, clasping, pointed leaves in pairs, looking unlike other pondweeds. Clear, calcareous ponds, ditches and streams, mostly south and east.

name: Potamogeton acutifolius
tip: All-submerged, flattened, bristle-tipped narrow leaves with many veins and a pointed tip. Scarce, in clean lowland ponds and ditches of England and Ireland.

name: Potamogeton alpinus
tip: Reddish-tinged floating and translucent submerged leaves, both stalkless-ish and narrow oval. Peaty or acid waters, mainly in northern and western Britain and Ireland.

name: Potamogeton coloratus
tip: Thin, translucent, net-veined leaves, submerged and floating, in base-rich fen pools and ditches. Local in England, Wales and Ireland; leaves are almost see-through.

name: Potamogeton compressus
tip: Flattened stems with long, ribbon-like leaves ending in a tiny point; all submerged. Rare, in lowland lakes and canals of eastern England and Ireland.

name: Potamogeton epihydrus
tip: Ribbon-like submerged leaves with floating oval ones, resembling Bog Pondweed plants in structure. Very rare, in Outer Hebrides lochs only; specialist should confirm.

name: Potamogeton friesii
tip: Narrow, stalkless, many-veined leaves with a notched or blunt tip and flattened stems. Local in lowland, nutrient-rich waters across England and Ireland.

name: Potamogeton gramineus
tip: Both submerged narrow stalkless leaves and floating oval ones, with a thickened stalk under the flower spike. Upland lakes and rivers, mostly north and west.

name: Potamogeton lucens
tip: Large, translucent, wavy, glossy submerged leaves with a short stalk and a point. Clear, deeper water of lakes, canals and rivers, mostly lowland.

name: Potamogeton nodosus
tip: Long-stalked, leathery floating and large submerged leaves with a rounded base. Slow rivers of southern and central England and Ireland; found along the Loddon.

name: Potamogeton obtusifolius
tip: Narrow, blunt, translucent, stalkless leaves with three main veins, all submerged. Still fertile ponds and canals, widespread but local throughout lowland Britain.

name: Potamogeton praelongus
tip: Large, clasping submerged leaves with a hooded tip, plus a very long flower stalk. Deep, clear lakes and rivers, mostly north and west.

name: Potamogeton rutilus
tip: Fine, narrow, pointed submerged leaves with a thin stem, similar to Hairlike Pondweed. Very rare, in Scottish islands lochs and a few in western Ireland; specialist needed.

name: Potamogeton trichoides
tip: Hair-thin, dark, pointed leaves with three veins, like thin threads in dull ponds. Scarce, in lowland ditches and ponds of southern and eastern England.

name: Zannichellia obtusifolia
tip: Slender submerged plant with thread-like opposite leaves and tiny stalkless flowers, resembling Horned Pondweed. Brackish, rarely recorded; a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Cyclamen coum
tip: Small rounded leaves, silver-patterned or plain, and compact flowers with a dark mark at base. Naturalised in gardens and woods; flowers in late winter, not autumn.

name: Cyclamen graecum
tip: Larger, leathery leaves patterned silver, appearing after the autumn flowers. Rarely found outside gardens; scented pink flowers in autumn.

name: Cyclamen repandum
tip: Glossy, dark, ivy-like toothed leaves, with deeply lobed edges, and sweet-scented carmine flowers in spring. Occasional garden escape in southern shady places.

name: Hottonia palustris
tip: Floating or submerged feathery leaves, with whorls of pale lilac flowers above water on leafless stalks. Clean ditches and ponds, mostly lowland England and Ireland.

name: Lysimachia ciliata
tip: Yellow flowers nodding on long stalks, with opposite leaves with fringed stalks. Garden escape in damp places, scattered through England and Ireland.

name: Lysimachia foemina
tip: Low, annual, with small, blue flowers on thin stalks and opposite oval leaves. Very rare weed of arable land in southern England; scarlet Pimpernel is redder.

name: Lysimachia terrestris
tip: Spreading, stoloniferous marsh plant with spikes of yellow flowers. Alien, naturalised by lakes and ponds, but absent from many counties; rare outside the Sphagnum.

name: Lysimachia thyrsiflora
tip: Dense, stalked, rounded clusters of small yellow flowers rising from the leaf bases midway up the stem. Rare, in fens and lake margins in northern Britain.

name: Primula denticulata
tip: Dense, ball-shaped heads of lilac flowers on a stout stalk, above rosettes of toothed leaves. Garden plant that occasionally escapes onto damp banks.

name: Primula elatior
tip: Pale yellow flowers, one-sided cluster on a single stalk, with hairy leaves. Rare, in ancient East Anglian woods; the False Oxlip is a hybrid.

name: Primula farinosa
tip: Rosettes with mealy undersides to leaves, and pink flowers with yellow centre in heads. Rare, in limestone grasslands of northern England and Scotland.

name: Primula florindae
tip: Tall, with fragrant yellow bells in a drooping umbel, above large heart-based leaves. Garden escape by streams and wet banks, mostly Scotland and the north.

name: Primula japonica
tip: Tiered whorls of white, pink or crimson flowers on tall stalks, above large rosettes of leaves. Garden escape in damp streamsides, scattered.

name: Primula juliae
tip: Low, mat-forming primrose with purple-magenta flowers and rounded wrinkled leaves. Garden plant, occasionally found as an escape; confirm by hybrid parentage.

name: Primula prolifera
tip: Tiered whorls of golden-yellow flowers on mealy stalks, above large toothed rosettes. Garden escape on wet banks and streams, scattered.

name: Primula pulverulenta
tip: Tiers of crimson flowers on stalks dusted with white meal, above leafy rosettes. Garden escape on damp stream banks, scattered in Britain and Ireland.

name: Primula scotica
tip: Tiny, dark, purple flowers with a yellow eye on a short stalk, above a mealy rosette. Rare, in coastal turf of north Scotland and Orkney.

name: Adiantum capillus-veneris
tip: Delicate fronds with fan-shaped, lobed, bright green pinnules on black glossy stalks. Rare native on dripping coastal rocks in the west; also escapes on walls.

name: Anogramma leptophylla
tip: Tiny, delicate, pale green triangular annual fern with fine, divided fronds. Very rare, in shaded banks in Channel Islands, south-west England and Wales.

name: Cryptogramma crispa
tip: Bright green, crinkled fronds like parsley, with separate narrow fertile fronds. In screes and rocky mountain places and walls, mostly north and west.

name: Pteris cretica
tip: Pinnate fronds with narrow, ribbon-like, finely toothed pinnae, often paler centre. Garden or greenhouse escape on walls and drains in mild urban places.

name: Reseda alba
tip: Tall, with dense spikes of small white flowers and pinnately cut wavy leaves. Casual on waste ground and roadsides, mostly in southern England.

name: Reseda phyteuma
tip: Short, spiky pale yellow-green flowers on a spike, and divided linear leaves. Rare casual on arable land and waste ground, mostly south.

name: Rhamnus alaternus
tip: Evergreen shrub with glossy, toothed oval leaves and small greenish flowers, unlike the thorny buckthorns. Planted, occasionally self-sown in the south.

name: Asperula cynanchica
tip: Slender, low, wiry plant with tiny whorled leaves, and pinkish-white four-lobed flowers in small clusters. Chalk and limestone grassland, mostly in southern England.

name: Asperula taurina
tip: Whorled leaves and clusters of pinkish-white, long-tubed flowers in spring. Garden escape in woods and banks, occasionally naturalised.

name: Galium boreale
tip: Stiff upright stems with whorls of four three-veined leaves, and bright white flower clusters. Rocky northern Britain and Ireland, damp or rocky meadows.

name: Galium constrictum
tip: Thin, weak, sprawling stems with whorls of narrow, blunt leaves and small white or pink flowers. Marshes in the south-west, Midlands and Ireland.

name: Galium murale
tip: Tiny annual, small whorled leaves, clustered tiny yellowish flowers; prickly fruits. Rare on walls and sandy ground, a few Channel Islands and south coast places.

name: Galium parisiense
tip: Slender annual, with whorls of narrow, backward-prickly leaves and tiny greenish flowers. Rare on old walls and shingle in southern and eastern England.

name: Galium pumilum
tip: Slender, with narrow leaves in whorls of six to eight and white flowers in loose, open sprays. Dry chalk grassland in southern England.

name: Galium spurium
tip: Cleavers-like, but with smooth, small green fruits and greenish flowers. Rare arable weed, mostly southern England; the fruits are not hooked.

name: Galium sterneri
tip: Mat-forming relative of Heath Bedstraw, with leaves in sixes that bear forward-pointing prickles on edges. Limestone grassland in northern England, Wales and Scotland; specialist may confirm.

name: Galium tricornutum
tip: Climbing annual with whorled leaves and tiny white flowers, but large, smooth, curved fruit stalks, unlike Cleavers. Rare arable weed, mostly in southern England.

name: Rubia peregrina
tip: Evergreen scrambler with glossy, leathery leaves in whorls with prickly edges and keel, with tiny greenish-yellow flowers. Hedges and cliffs in southern and western coastal areas.

name: Rubia tinctorum
tip: Scrambling, prickly stems with whorls of leaves, and greenish-yellow flowers, like Wild Madder but less glossy. Occasional relic of cultivation, rare in the south.

name: Ruppia maritima
tip: Submerged, thread-like leaves and tiny flower pair on spike with long stalks; in brackish pools. Coastal brackish lagoons and ditches, scattered around the coast.

name: Ruppia spiralis
tip: Submerged thread-like leaves; fruit stalks coiled spirally after flowering, unlike Beaked Tasselweed. Brackish lagoons and ditches, scattered, mostly east and south coasts.

name: Choisya ternata
tip: Glossy evergreen shrub with leaves of three leaflets, and scented white flowers. Widely planted, rarely self-sown near gardens.

name: Correa backhouseana
tip: Evergreen, with oval leaves white-felted underneath and drooping greenish-yellow tubular bells. Very rare garden plant in mild areas, not often naturalised.

name: Ruta graveolens
tip: Blue-green, strongly smelling, much-divided leaves and clusters of yellow-green flowers with four petals. Old garden herb, sometimes persisting on walls and waste ground.

name: Populus trichocarpa
tip: Tall poplar with sticky, strongly balsam-scented buds and large, heart-based leaves that are white beneath. Widely planted; occasionally self-sown by rivers.

name: Salix arbuscula
tip: Low shrub with shiny, small oval leaves that are hairy beneath at first. Rare, on damp mountain rocks in the Scottish Highlands; hybridises.

name: Salix eriocephala
tip: Hairy twigs and heart-based oval leaves; a rare introduced American willow. Specialist needed to confirm; naturalised only locally.

name: Salix herbacea
tip: Tiny creeping plant with rounded, shiny leaves, only a few centimetres high. Mountain tops and rocks in Scotland, Wales, northern England and Ireland.

name: Salix lanata
tip: Low, rounded shrub with silvery woolly leaves and thick, yellowish catkins. Rare, on high Scottish rocky ledges; the leaves are broad and rounded.

name: Salix lapponum
tip: Shrub with narrow, grey, woolly-white leaves beneath and large silvery catkins. Rare, on upland Scottish and northern English crags.

name: Salix myrsinifolia
tip: Dark green leaves that blacken when dried, hairless or slightly hairy, and finely toothed. Scottish and northern English streamsides; hybrids common, so specialist may confirm.

name: Salix myrsinites
tip: Low, spreading, with small, glossy, finely toothed leaves and purple twigs. Rare, on mountain rocks in the Scottish Highlands, on base-rich rocks.

name: Salix phylicifolia
tip: Shrub with shiny dark leaves, silvery beneath, and smooth twigs. Streamsides and rocks in northern England and Scotland; hybridises.

name: Salix reticulata
tip: Creeping mat plant with rounded, net-veined, leathery leaves. Rare, on damp, base-rich mountain ledges in the Scottish Highlands.

name: Salix triandra
tip: Tall shrub with narrow, glossy, finely toothed leaves and a flaking bark. Osier beds and riverbanks, mostly in southern England.

name: Thesium humifusum
tip: Small creeping semi-parasite of chalk turf with narrow one-veined leaves and tiny greenish-white five-lobed flowers; much smaller than flax. Local in southern and eastern England.

name: Acer cappadocicum
tip: Planted maple with five to seven pointed lobes, hairless leaves and milky sap; yellow-green flower clusters open with the leaves, and young leaves are often reddish.

name: Koelreuteria paniculata
tip: Planted small tree with large pinnate leaves of coarsely lobed leaflets, big airy yellow flower sprays in summer, then papery lantern-like three-sided fruits.

name: Sarracenia flava
tip: Tall green-yellow trumpet-shaped insect-trapping leaves with a lid, and a nodding yellow flower on a long stem. Naturalised in a few bogs.

name: Sarracenia purpurea
tip: Low rosette of red-veined pitchers that hold rainwater, open-mouthed with no upright lid, and a single nodding maroon flower. Naturalised in bogs in Ireland and Britain.

name: Houttuynia cordata
tip: Spreading garden escape with heart-shaped, bluish-green leaves that smell of orange peel when crushed, and a small cone of tiny flowers cupped by four white bracts.

name: Astilbe chinensis
tip: Garden perennial with twice-pinnate toothed leaves and dense feathery spires of tiny pink or whitish flowers; occasionally escapes. Shorter and stiffer than Japanese Astilbe.

name: Astilbe japonica
tip: Garden perennial with much-divided toothed leaves and arching feathery plumes of tiny white flowers; sometimes persists on waste ground near gardens.

name: Darmera peltata
tip: Large garden plant with big round peltate leaves on long stalks, and pink flowers in a rounded head borne on bare stems before the leaves appear in spring.

name: Micranthes nivalis
tip: Tiny mountain plant with a flat rosette of rounded, blunt-toothed leaves and a compact head of small whitish-purple flowers on a hairy stem. Rare in the Scottish and Lake District hills.

name: Mitella ovalis
tip: Low woodland garden plant with heart-shaped toothed basal leaves and slender spikes of tiny fringed greenish-white flowers. A rare garden escape; specialist check advised.

name: Rodgersia podophylla
tip: Large garden perennial with big hand-shaped leaves of five coarsely toothed leaflets, bronze when young, and tall plumes of small creamy flowers. Occasional escape near water.

name: Saxifraga aizoides
tip: Mat-forming plant of wet mountain flushes with fleshy narrow pointed leaves and starry yellow to orange flowers, often spotted. Distinct from yellow stonecrops by its leaf shape and five petals.

name: Saxifraga cernua
tip: Tiny arctic-alpine with lobed kidney-shaped leaves, a single white flower on a hairy stem and red bulbils in the leaf axils. Very rare, on a few Scottish summits.

name: Saxifraga cespitosa
tip: Dense cushions of hairy, three-lobed leaves with a few creamy-white flowers on short glandular stems. Mountain rocks in Wales and Scotland; compare Mossy Saxifrage with its long runners.

name: Saxifraga cuneifolia
tip: Neat rosettes of rounded, long-stalked, toothed leaves and airy sprays of tiny white flowers with yellow and red spots. Garden plant that sometimes escapes onto walls.

name: Saxifraga cymbalaria
tip: Small, leafy, branched annual or biennial with kidney-shaped lobed leaves and small yellow flowers on slender stems. Naturalised in a few places, mostly on walls and rocks.

name: Saxifraga hirculus
tip: Rare bog plant with narrow leaves and large yellow flowers marked with orange dots; stem has rusty hairs. Few northern English and Scottish sites; looks like no other wetland saxifrage.

name: Saxifraga hirsuta
tip: Hairy rosette plant with round-kidney leaves on long hairy stalks and loose sprays of white flowers with small yellow and pink spots. Damp shady rocks in southwest Ireland, naturalised elsewhere.

name: Saxifraga hypnoides
tip: Cushion-forming plant with trailing leafy runners, narrow three-lobed leaves and loose clusters of white flowers on slender stems. Common on limestone and mountain rocks in the north.

name: Saxifraga oppositifolia
tip: Mat of tiny opposite scale-like leaves, with big purple-pink stemless flowers early in spring. Mountain rocks, Wales, northern England, Scotland and Ireland.

name: Saxifraga rivularis
tip: Very small arctic-alpine of wet snow patches with lobed, long-stalked leaves and one to three small white flowers. Rare and confined to high Scottish mountains.

name: Saxifraga rosacea
tip: Tufted plant with glossy three- to five-lobed leaves and white flowers with widely spaced petals. Mountain rocks and stream gravel in Ireland, plus a few Welsh and Scottish sites.

name: Saxifraga rotundifolia
tip: Hairy plant with rounded, coarsely toothed basal leaves and a many-flowered spray of white flowers spotted with red and yellow. Garden escape on banks and walls.

name: Saxifraga spathularis
tip: Tough rosette plant of western Irish mountains with leathery spoon-shaped, toothed leaves and white yellow-spotted flowers. Differs from London Pride by its longer, narrower leaf blades.

name: Saxifraga stolonifera
tip: House-plant escape with rounded hairy marbled leaves, long red runners with plantlets, and white flowers with one long lower petal. Naturalised on a few walls.

name: Saxifraga umbrosa
tip: Garden plant with rosettes of leathery oval toothed leaves and airy sprays of small pink-spotted white flowers. A parent of London Pride; occasionally escapes. Specialist confirmation helps.

name: Tolmiea menziesii
tip: Garden escape with softly hairy heart-shaped lobed leaves that grow plantlets at the leaf base, and slender spikes of small greenish-brown flowers. Shady damp banks and walls.

name: Scheuchzeria palustris
tip: Rare bog plant with narrow channelled grass-like leaves each ending in a tiny pore and a loose spike of few greenish flowers. Peaty pools in Scotland, Ireland and mid Wales.

name: Phygelius capensis
tip: Garden shrub with opposite oval leaves and tall spikes of drooping tubular red-orange flowers with yellow throats. Occasional escape on waste ground.

name: Scrophularia peregrina
tip: Hairless, branched annual figwort with heart-shaped toothed leaves and dark purple small flowers. Rare casual from southern Europe, seen in the south of England.

name: Scrophularia scopolii
tip: Softly hairy figwort with oval toothed leaves and dull brownish-green small flowers in spreading clusters. Very rare casual; identification needs a specialist.

name: Scrophularia scorodonia
tip: Tall softly hairy figwort with wrinkled, heart-shaped leaves and dull purple-red flowers in broad clusters. Very rare in Cornwall, Devon and the Channel Islands.

name: Scrophularia umbrosa
tip: Tall winged-stemmed figwort of damp ground with hairless oval leaves and olive-green flowers with a yellowish flap on the upper lip. Rare introduction, scattered in the north.

name: Scrophularia vernalis
tip: Softly hairy plant with heart-shaped leaves and unmistakable small greenish-yellow flowers in tight clusters. Naturalised in shady spots, mainly in southern England.

name: Verbascum chaixii
tip: Branched, hairy mullein with nettle-like leaves, and yellow flowers with purple-haired stamens in slim spikes. Rare escape or introduction mostly in southern England.

name: Verbascum lychnitis
tip: Tall branched mullein with loosely felted grey leaves and flowers in pale yellow or white, with stamens bearing whitish hairs. Native on chalky, disturbed ground, mostly in the south and east.

name: Verbascum pulverulentum
tip: Branched mullein covered in dense white felt that rubs off, with yellow flowers in single clusters, unlike the unbranched Great Mullein. Eastern England and some southern sites.

name: Verbascum speciosum
tip: Tall candelabra mullein, with branched whitish woolly spikes and clusters of yellow flowers; leaves are broad and covered with star-shaped hairs. Garden plant that seldom escapes.

name: Verbascum virgatum
tip: Sticky-glandular mullein with slender usually unbranched spikes, yellow flowers in small clusters of one to five, and cut-toothed upper leaves. Rare in southwest England.

name: Selaginella kraussiana
tip: Mossy creeping plant with tiny pale green scale-like leaves in flat, two-ranked branches. Escapes from gardens and greenhouses, widespread in mild areas.

name: Ailanthus altissima
tip: Tall suckering tree with very long pinnate leaves with a basal tooth on each leaflet, which smell unpleasant when crushed; bears large winged fruit clusters. Frequent in towns.

name: Alkekengi officinarum
tip: Garden perennial with oval leaves and creamy-white flowers, followed by a red papery inflated calyx like a lantern around the berry. Occasional garden escape.

name: Atropa belladonna
tip: Large bushy plant with dull purple-green bell flowers and single glossy black berries in a green star. Poisonous; on chalk and limestone, mostly south England.

name: Hyoscyamus niger
tip: Sticky, foul-smelling hairy annual with lobed leaves and cream funnel-shaped flowers netted with purple veins, then urn-shaped fruits. Sandy coasts and disturbed ground; poisonous.

name: Lycium chinense
tip: Spiny or thorny shrub with arching stems, narrow leaves and small purple funnel flowers, then orange-red berries. Hard to separate from Duke of Argyll Teaplant, so a specialist helps.

name: Salpichroa origanifolia
tip: Scrambling, trailing plant with small oval leaves and creamy-white bell-shaped flowers, then egg-shaped pale berries. Naturalised on walls and hedgebanks in southern England.

name: Solanum chenopodioides
tip: Branched, nearly hairless annual with small white flowers having reflexed petals and green berries that stay green, wrapped by an enlarged calyx. Rare casual in the south.

name: Solanum laciniatum
tip: Large shrubby nightshade with deeply cut leaves and violet flowers bigger than those of Black Nightshade, then orange egg-shaped berries. Rare escape in mild southern places.

name: Solanum nitidibaccatum
tip: Hairy low annual with small white flowers and berries that remain green; difficult to separate from relatives. Rare casual on waste ground, requires specialist confirmation.

name: Solanum sarrachoides
tip: Sticky-hairy annual with small white flowers and green berries almost enclosed by a long, enlarged calyx. Rare casual on waste ground; a specialist should confirm it.

name: Solanum triflorum
tip: Low, spreading, hairy annual with deeply lobed leaves and small white flowers in clusters of two or three. Rare casual from North America on waste ground.

name: Daphne mezereum
tip: Deciduous shrub flowering on bare twigs in late winter with clusters of scented pink-purple flowers; leaves appear after, with red poisonous berries. Rare in southern limestone woods.

name: Tofieldia pusilla
tip: Tiny tufted plant of wet upland flushes with grass-like, flat leaves and a short compact head of small whitish-green flowers. Northern England and Scotland only.

name: Tropaeolum speciosum
tip: Climbing garden plant with leaves of six long lobes and vivid scarlet flowers, followed by blue berries. Scrambles through hedges and shrubs, mainly in the north and Scotland.

name: Sparganium natans
tip: Slender aquatic with floating or submerged narrow leaves and small round white-green flower heads, usually only one male head at top. Lakes and pools, mostly in the north and west.

name: Typha minima
tip: Small bulrush with thin grass-like leaves and a short rounded brown female spike, separated from the male spike above. Rare naturalised plant of a few riversides.

name: Ulmus laevis
tip: Tree with asymmetric toothed leaves and flowers and fruits dangling on long stalks, with fringed winged fruit. Rare planted tree, differing from English Elm by those long stalks.

name: Parietaria officinalis
tip: Sprawling hairy perennial with alternate pointed oval leaves and tiny green flowers in leaf-axil clusters; leaves lack stinging hairs. Walls, hedge banks and rocky ground in south England.

name: Urtica membranacea
tip: Nettle relative with oval toothed leaves and tiny green flowers, lacking the strong stings of Common Nettle. Rare casual of Mediterranean origin; needs specialist confirmation.

name: Sambucus canadensis
tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves and large flat heads of white flowers, similar to Elder but with more leaflets and larger flower heads. Rare garden escape.

name: Sambucus ebulus
tip: Herb-like patch-forming elder with pinnate leaves with leaf-like stipules, white pink-tinged flowers with purple anthers and black berries. Foul smell when crushed; scattered across England and Wales.

name: Sambucus racemosa
tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves and compact egg-shaped heads of cream-green flowers in spring, followed by bright red berries. Naturalised across the north and in woodland.

name: Viburnum tinus
tip: Evergreen shrub with oval dark glossy leaves and flat heads of pink buds opening white from winter into spring, then dark blue berries. Common in gardens, sometimes escapes.

name: Viola cornuta
tip: Garden perennial with long-spurred, violet-blue flowers on a creeping rootstock, with a spur longer than the petals. Occasionally naturalised on banks and walls.

name: Viola kitaibeliana
tip: Tiny annual with narrow pale cream flowers often tinged with violet, shorter than the leafy sepals. Rare on dunes in Scilly and the Channel Islands.

name: Viola lactea
tip: Violet with pale bluish-white flowers with a curved greenish spur, and narrow, triangular leaves. Rare on heaths, mostly in the south-west of England and Ireland.

name: Viola lutea
tip: Upland grassland pansy with yellow, violet or bicoloured flowers larger than Wild Pansy, with leaves held on slender stems from creeping stolons. Hills of northern England, Wales and Scotland.

name: Viola rupestris
tip: Small, downy violet with rounded heart-shaped leaves and blue-violet flowers with a short spur, close to Common Dog-violet. Only on limestone turf in upper Teesdale.

name: Viola stagnina
tip: Pale blue-white violet with a violet-tinged spur and long narrow heart-based leaves, hairless. Wet fens and lake shores in East Anglia and Ireland; very rare.

name: Parthenocissus tricuspidata
tip: Self-clinging wall climber with three-lobed or compound leaves that colour brilliantly red in autumn; inconspicuous greenish flowers and blue berries. Differs from Virginia-creeper in having sucker discs.

name: Vitis vinifera
tip: Tendril-bearing climber with large lobed leaves and dense clusters of small green flowers, then grapes. Escapes locally, mostly in the south of England.

name: Zostera marina
tip: Marine plant with long ribbon-like leaves with three to seven veins, rooted in sand or mud below low tide, and spikes hidden in the sheath. Larger than Dwarf Eelgrass.

name: Zostera noltei
tip: Small marine plant of muddy shores with narrow thread-like leaves with a notched tip and one vein, and rooted in intertidal mud. Much slimmer than Eelgrass.

name: Narcissus bulbocodium
tip: Tiny daffodil with a wide flaring trumpet and very narrow petals, almost rush-like leaves; naturalised in a few grassy places, unlike the larger wild daffodil.

name: Narcissus cyclamineus
tip: Small daffodil whose petals sweep sharply backwards from a narrow trumpet, giving a windswept look; a garden escape in damp grass, mainly in western Britain.

name: Narcissus hispanicus
tip: Robust, large daffodil with a deep golden trumpet that has a frilled, rolled rim and petals of similar colour; a garden escape in grassy places.

name: Narcissus minor
tip: Smaller than wild daffodil, with a trumpet that is all yellow and petals that are the same shade; a garden escape of grassy banks.

name: Narcissus moschatus
tip: Nodding daffodil with white or very pale cream, drooping flowers and twisted petals; a rare garden escape in western grassland, easily told by its colour.

name: Narcissus nobilis
tip: Big, upright wild-type daffodil with a deep yellow trumpet and paler or equal petals; a naturalised garden plant needing comparison with other trumpet daffodils.

name: Narcissus obvallaris
tip: Sturdy daffodil with an all-golden flower, short stout stem and blue-green leaves; famed around Tenby in Pembrokeshire and found in scattered naturalised sites elsewhere.

name: Narcissus radiiflorus
tip: Poet-type narcissus with pure white spreading petals and a tiny yellow cup edged in red; usually one flower per stem; naturalised in meadows.

name: Narcissus triandrus
tip: Delicate narcissus with two to three nodding, creamy white flowers per stem and backswept petals around a bell-shaped cup; rare escape, often in western grassland.

name: Nothoscordum borbonicum
tip: Garlic-like bulbous plant with an umbel of white flowers striped greenish or pink beneath, with no oniony smell; established in a few warm coastal spots in the south-west.

name: Pancratium maritimum
tip: Large, fragrant white trumpet flowers with a toothed cup, sprouting from dune sand with blue-grey strap leaves; rare, on southern dunes, mainly Channel Islands and the Scillies.

name: Sternbergia lutea
tip: Crocus-like yellow goblets appearing in autumn alongside glossy green strap leaves; a garden escape in dry, sunny banks, flowering well after any spring bulb.

name: Tristagma uniflorum
tip: Low tuft of grey-green, onion-scented, grass-like leaves with solitary six-pointed pale blue stars; a common garden outcast on verges and tips.

name: Rhus copallina
tip: Small shrubby sumach with pinnate leaves whose stalk is winged between the leaflets, turning red in autumn; rarely grown and very rarely self-sown. Needs specialist confirmation.

name: Rhus coriaria
tip: Shrub with pinnate, coarsely toothed leaves, hairy shoots and dense greenish flower spikes, reddish fruit; a rare escape or relic near gardens.

name: Anethum graveolens
tip: Feathery, thread-like blue-green leaves with a smooth stem and flat yellow umbels, smelling strongly of dill; a casual on tips and waste ground.

name: Angelica archangelica
tip: Tall, stout plant with a hollow ribbed stem and big globe-like umbels of greenish-white flowers; naturalised on riverbanks and damp waste ground, with a sweet scent.

name: Angelica pachycarpa
tip: Large angelica with glossy, shiny, much-divided leaves and umbels of white flowers; a rare garden escape, best checked against other angelicas by a specialist.

name: Anthriscus cerefolium
tip: Small, delicate annual with finely cut, parsley-like leaves that smell of aniseed and small umbels of white flowers with no bracts; a casual on waste ground.

name: Apium graveolens
tip: Glossy, strongly celery-scented plant of damp coastal grassland and saltmarsh, with a grooved stem and small greenish-white umbels; the toothed shiny leaflets are lobed.

name: Astrantia major
tip: Clump-forming garden plant with pincushion heads of tiny whitish-pink flowers circled by papery bracts, and palmately lobed leaves; escapes into grassland and verges.

name: Bunium bulbocastanum
tip: Slender umbellifer of chalk fields with finely divided, thread-like leaves and white umbels, growing from a dark rounded tuber; very rare, mainly in the Chilterns.

name: Bupleurum baldense
tip: Tiny, wiry annual with grass-like leaves and tiny clusters of yellow flowers wrapped in small pointed bracts; very rare, on sunny coastal rocks and short turf in southern Britain.

name: Bupleurum falcatum
tip: Tall, slender perennial with sickle-shaped upper leaves and small yellow-green umbels, lacking the encircling bracts of Thorow-wax; rare, in the south-east.

name: Bupleurum fruticosum
tip: Evergreen shrub with blue-green, leathery, oval leaves and yellow umbels in late summer; planted and sometimes self-sown on coastal slopes, as the only woody hare's-ear.

name: Bupleurum rotundifolium
tip: Hairless, blue-green annual with oval leaves that fully clasp the stem, and yellow-green umbels; a rare arable weed or casual, now mostly a bird-seed alien.

name: Bupleurum tenuissimum
tip: Thin, wiry, branched annual with narrow leaves and tiny, almost stalkless greenish-yellow umbels in the leaf forks; rare, on dry brackish ground, in the south-east.

name: Carum carvi
tip: Biennial with feathery leaves, a grooved stem and white umbels that lack bracts; leaves have small leaflet-like lobes at the stalk base; a casual on waste ground and field margins.

name: Chaerophyllum aureum
tip: Stout, hairy chervil with feathery leaves that are yellowish when young and umbels of white flowers; rare, established in northern Britain, and best confirmed by specialist.

name: Chaerophyllum hirsutum
tip: Roughly hairy chervil with deeply divided leaves and white or pinkish umbels; a rare garden plant not established widely, best confirmed by a specialist.

name: Cicuta virosa
tip: Very poisonous water plant with hollow, chambered rootstock and a stout hairless stem; leaves are twice-pinnate with long narrow toothed leaflets; rare, in ditches, fens and lake margins.

name: Coriandrum sativum
tip: Annual with two kinds of leaf: lobed lower leaves and feathery thread-like upper leaves, pungent smell and white to pinkish umbels; an occasional casual on tips and waste ground.

name: Crithmum maritimum
tip: Fleshy, aromatic plant with thick, narrow, grey-green leaflets, in tufts on sea cliffs and shingle; small greenish-yellow umbels are distinct from other cliff umbellifers.

name: Cuminum cyminum
tip: Slender annual with very fine thread-like leaflets and small white or pinkish umbels; a rare casual from spice or bird-seed, best confirmed by a specialist.

name: Eryngium amethystinum
tip: Spiny sea-holly relative with steel-blue stems and flower heads and stiff lobed leaves; a rare garden plant, only an occasional escape, needing specialist confirmation.

name: Eryngium campestre
tip: Spiny whitish-green thistle-like umbellifer with ribbed leaves and small rounded heads; very rare in a handful of southern sites, and a smaller plant than Sea-holly.

name: Eryngium giganteum
tip: Biennial garden plant with silvery-green spiny bracts around a steel-blue egg-shaped flower head, and heart-shaped basal leaves; seeds into gravel and waste ground.

name: Eryngium maritimum
tip: Steely blue-grey, spiny, leathery plant of sand and shingle, with round blue-violet flower heads wrapped in spiny bracts; a distinctive dune and beach plant.

name: Eryngium planum
tip: Branched garden plant with many small blue thistly heads and spiny-edged, flat leaves; has more heads than Sea-holly, which has a few larger ones. Occasional outcast.

name: Eryngium variifolium
tip: Grass-like leaved eryngo with spine-tipped narrow leaves and blue-white heads; an uncommon garden plant and a very rare escape, needing confirmation by a specialist.

name: Falcaria vulgaris
tip: Blue-green, hairless umbellifer with long, narrow, saw-edged leaf segments in threes and many small white umbels; a rare, local plant of field edges and verges, mainly in the east.

name: Ferula communis
tip: Huge fennel-like plant with a thick hollow stem, glossy thread-like leaves and big yellow umbels; grown in gardens and sometimes naturalised in sunny places.

name: Helosciadium repens
tip: Low, creeping, hairless celery relative rooting at nodes, with small white umbels almost stalkless opposite leaves; very rare, in wet grassland in a few counties.

name: Imperatoria ostruthium
tip: Stout plant with three-lobed leaves with broad, toothed segments and large flat umbels of pinkish-white flowers; naturalised in damp ground and old cottage gardens in northern Britain.

name: Levisticum officinale
tip: Tall, glossy celery-scented plant with greenish-yellow umbels and shiny, toothed leaflets; an old herb persisting near gardens and on waste ground.

name: Ligusticum scoticum
tip: Seashore plant with shiny dark-green, thrice-divided, celery-scented leaves and small white umbels; grows on rocky shores and sea cliffs in Scotland, northern England and Ireland.

name: Melanoselinum decipiens
tip: Large, tropical-looking parsley with stout stems and big coarse leaves, dark leaf stalks and big white umbels; very rare garden outcast, needing specialist confirmation.

name: Meum athamanticum
tip: Upland plant with aromatic, very finely feathered leaves in tufts and white or purple-tinged umbels; grows in meadows and mountain pastures in northern England and Scotland.

name: Oenanthe aquatica
tip: Water plant with finely cut submerged leaves and small, stalked white umbels opposite the leaves; found in still water, and differs from other water-dropworts by its hollow, hairless stem.

name: Oenanthe fistulosa
tip: Water-dropwort with hollow, tubular stems and leaf stalks, creeping runners, and dense, spherical umbels with few rays; common in ponds, ditches and reedbeds.

name: Oenanthe fluviatilis
tip: Tall plant of rivers and streams with hollow stem, large round-lobed leaflets and large umbels opposite the leaves; much taller than Fine-leaved Water-dropwort. Mostly southern England.

name: Oenanthe lachenalii
tip: Stout plant of damp grassland and saltmarsh, with parsley-like leaves and spherical umbels of white flowers; the stem is solid, unlike hollow-stemmed relatives, and the fruit is clearly angled.

name: Oenanthe pimpinelloides
tip: Water-dropwort with root tubers and finely divided leaves; stem is solid and spreading; has only one dense, domed umbel; local, in damp grassland in the south and west.

name: Oenanthe silaifolia
tip: Tall water-dropwort of damp meadows with narrow, long, pointed leaflets and a hollow, ridged stem; local, in the Midlands and southern England.

name: Petroselinum crispum
tip: Bright green, shiny, curly or flat leaved herb with tiny yellow-green umbels; found as a casual on tips, walls and waste ground.

name: Peucedanum officinale
tip: Tall, sulphur-yellow umbellifer with long, thread-like leaf segments forming big drooping masses; very rare, on coastal marshes and grassland in Kent and Essex.

name: Physospermum cornubiense
tip: Large plant with lobed, three-parted leaves and white umbels; the fruits are bladder-like, and notched; very rare, in woods and hedges in Devon and Cornwall.

name: Pimpinella peregrina
tip: Slender, hairy-stemmed annual or biennial with simple basal leaves and divided stem leaves and tiny white umbels; a rare casual, specialist confirmation needed.

name: Scandix pecten-veneris
tip: Annual of arable fields, with finely cut leaves, small white umbels, and long beaked fruits like needles; once frequent but now very rare.

name: Selinum carvifolia
tip: Rare plant with hollow, ridged stems and finely cut leaves like carrot; white umbels have smaller bracts than Milk-parsley; fens and wet grassland in a few places.

name: Seseli libanotis
tip: Chalk and limestone plant with grey-green, feathery leaves, grooved stems and white, slightly pinkish umbels with many bracts; rare, in the Cambridge region and Sussex.

name: Sison segetum
tip: Slender hairless annual with narrow leaflets and tiny white umbels; a rare casual of arable or waste ground, specialist confirmation needed.

name: Sium latifolium
tip: Tall, stout, hollow-stemmed plant of ditches and ponds, with once-pinnate toothed leaves, big white umbels and leafy bracts below; fairly local, in lowland England.

name: Smyrnium perfoliatum
tip: Yellow-green flowering plant with rounded, toothed upper leaves that clasp the stem completely, unlike Alexanders; a naturalised plant of verges and old gardens.

name: Thysselinum palustre
tip: Tall, slender plant of fens with finely cut leaves, a hollow-ridged stem, white umbels and milky sap when cut; rare, in East Anglia, and scattered elsewhere.

name: Tordylium maximum
tip: Hairy umbellifer with large outer petals on the white to pinkish flowers and wide, coarsely toothed leaflets; very rare, with a few sites near the Thames estuary.

name: Torilis arvensis
tip: Stiff, hairy, annual with long-stalked umbels, small white to pink flowers and spiny, hooked fruit; rare arable weed in southern and eastern England.

name: Trinia glauca
tip: Small, blue-green, hairless, dioecious plant with very finely cut leaves and tiny white umbels; very rare, on limestone in Devon, nowadays near Torquay and Plymouth.

name: Trocdaris verticillata
tip: Slender plant with leaf segments cut into whorled, thread-like lobes giving a bottlebrush look, and white umbels; local in damp pastures in western Britain and Ireland.

name: Vinca difformis
tip: Evergreen trailing plant with pale blue flowers having wide, overlapping petals, and shiny, hairless oval leaves; a garden escape in hedgerows in south-west Britain.

name: Arisarum proboscideum
tip: Low woodland garden plant with heart-shaped leaves and curious hooded flowers like a mouse, with a long tail; occasionally naturalised under shady garden hedges.

name: Calla palustris
tip: Creeping, marsh plant with shiny heart-shaped leaves, and a white open spathe around a short spike; red berries in autumn; in wet places, including one or two naturalised sites.

name: Dracunculus vulgaris
tip: Large garden arum with deeply cut, fan-like leaves, a mottled stem and a huge dark purple spathe that smells foul; rarely naturalised in the south.

name: Lemna turionifera
tip: Tiny floating duckweed with plants often reddish below, oval and without a ridge or tooth; flowers are almost never seen; specialist confirmation needed.

name: Lysichiton camtschatcensis
tip: Huge, glossy, paddle-shaped leaves and a white spathe around a thick greenish spike; invasive-looking pond-edge plant, introduced to some wet habitats, and foul smelling.

name: Orontium aquaticum
tip: Floating, water-repellent oval blue-green leaves and a thick white stalk tipped with a golden spike of tiny yellow flowers; an introduced plant in ponds and bog pools.

name: Spirodela polyrhiza
tip: Floating plant with flat round fronds up to 1 cm, each having several roots hanging beneath, and purplish below; much larger than other duckweeds with fewer roots.

name: Wolffia arrhiza
tip: Microscopic floating green fronds like grains of meal, and no roots at all; a rare, introduced plant of ponds and canals, mostly in the south-east.

name: Zantedeschia aethiopica
tip: Large garden lily with glossy arrow-shaped leaves and a white funnel-like spathe around a yellow spike; naturalised in ditches and damp ground in the south-west.

name: Aralia chinensis
tip: Spiny, little-branched small tree with huge twice-pinnate leaves and big sprays of small cream flowers; very rare garden plant, hard to separate from Japanese Angelica-tree.

name: Aralia elata
tip: Prickly, little-branched suckering tree with giant twice-pinnate leaves and huge sprays of small cream flowers in late summer; occasionally self-sown or suckering from gardens.

name: Aralia racemosa
tip: Rare garden escape with large leaves divided into toothed leaflets and branched sprays of tiny greenish-white flowers followed by dark red berries. Not a native; occasional near gardens.

name: Hedera algeriensis
tip: Ivy with large, shallowly lobed, bright green leaves that are scarcely toothed, carrying star-shaped scale hairs. Occasional garden escape; larger and paler than common ivy. Specialist check advised.

name: Hedera colchica
tip: Ivy with very large, glossy, unlobed heart-shaped leaves, often over 15 cm, and a faint celery smell when crushed. Common in parks and gardens, sometimes escaping.

name: Hydrocotyle moschata
tip: Small creeping New Zealand pennywort with rounded, shallowly scalloped leaves covered in hairs, forming mats on damp ground. Rare introduction, mainly in western Scotland and Ireland.

name: Hydrocotyle novae-zeelandiae
tip: Mat-forming creeper with small round, scalloped, nearly hairless leaves on slender stalks. Introduced, naturalised on damp lawns and banks, mainly in western Britain and Ireland.

name: Hydrocotyle ranunculoides
tip: Invasive aquatic with bright glossy, rounded, shallowly lobed leaves floating or standing above water, forming dense rafts. Tiny whitish flowers hide among the leaves. Spreading in southern England.

name: Aristolochia clematitis
tip: Upright plant with heart-shaped leaves and clusters of pale yellow tubular flowers swollen at the base, held in the leaf axils. Scarce relic of old cultivation on waste ground.

name: Aristolochia hirta
tip: Hairy Mediterranean birthwort with heart-shaped leaves and dull brownish-purple tubular flowers with a curved tube. A rare garden curiosity, not truly established in Britain.

name: Aristolochia rotunda
tip: Birthwort with heart-shaped leaves and solitary brownish-yellow tubular flowers with a flared lip, arising from a rounded tuber. Rare garden casual, not native here.

name: Asarum europaeum
tip: Low evergreen carpeter with glossy, kidney-shaped leaves and a single dull brownish bell flower hidden at ground level. Rare naturalised plant of old woods and estate grounds.

name: Asparagus officinalis
tip: Feathery bright green plant with threadlike branchlets, small greenish-yellow bells and red berries. The coastal form is prostrate; garden form is tall and escapes onto verges.

name: Asparagus prostratus
tip: Sprawling coastal form of wild asparagus with short, stiff, grey-green branchlets and small greenish bells. Found on sea cliffs and dunes in south-west Britain and Ireland.

name: Furcraea parmentieri
tip: Giant agave-like rosette with stiff sword leaves and a huge branched flower spike of greenish-white blooms. Only a rare tender garden plant in the mildest places.

name: Hyacinthoides italica
tip: Spring bulb with a conical spike of starry pale blue flowers and narrow strap leaves, upright rather than nodding. Naturalised rarely on grassy ground; smaller than bluebell.

name: Maianthemum bifolium
tip: Low woodland plant with only two glossy heart-shaped stem leaves and a small spike of tiny white four-petalled flowers. Very rare, in a few northern English woods.

name: Maianthemum kamtschaticum
tip: Spreading woodland plant like May lily but with several broad oval, pointed leaves up the stem and a spike of small white flowers. Rare garden escape.

name: Muscari botryoides
tip: Small bulb with upright narrow leaves and a short dense spike of globular blue flowers with white teeth. Naturalised on grassy ground.

name: Muscari comosum
tip: Distinct spike with dull brownish fertile flowers below and a bright violet-blue tuft of sterile flowers on top. Rare introduction on arable ground in the south-east.

name: Muscari neglectum
tip: Dense spike of small dark blue urn flowers with pale teeth; leaves narrow and floppy. Native in sandy Breckland grassland of East Anglia, widely naturalised elsewhere.

name: Ornithogalum arabicum
tip: Large white starry flowers with a conspicuous glossy black centre in a flat-topped cluster, with strap leaves. Only a tender garden or casual plant here.

name: Ornithogalum nutans
tip: Nodding white flowers in a one-sided raceme, with a broad green stripe on the outside of each petal; leaves narrow with a pale midstripe. Naturalised in grass, churchyards and orchards.

name: Ornithogalum pyrenaicum
tip: Tall spike of many greenish-white flowers, the lower ones opening first, and narrow leaves that wither before flowering. Local in woods and hedges around Bath and the south-west.

name: Polygonatum multiflorum
tip: Arching, rounded stem with oval leaves in two ranks and clusters of two to five hanging green-tipped white bells from each leaf joint. Woods; common in gardens.

name: Polygonatum odoratum
tip: Stem sharply angled, with bells usually one or two together, white with green tips and scented. A rare plant of limestone woods and rocky slopes.

name: Polygonatum verticillatum
tip: Narrow leaves in whorls of four to eight around the stem, with small greenish-white bells hanging in the axils. Very rare, in a few Scottish and northern English woods.

name: Ruscus hypoglossum
tip: Evergreen with flattened leaf-like green stems lacking a spine tip, bearing tiny greenish flowers on the surface. Rare garden escape in woods; prickly butchers-broom has sharp points.

name: Scilla autumnalis
tip: Small bulb flowering in late summer with a short head of starry lilac-blue flowers before the very narrow leaves appear. Local on dry coastal turf in southern England.

name: Scilla bifolia
tip: Early spring bulb with two narrow leaves and a loose spike of one to few starry, bright blue flowers. Rare garden escape on grass and in parks.

name: Scilla bithynica
tip: Spring bulb with broad, shiny leaves and a loose spike of up to twelve small pale blue starry flowers. Occasional escape in parks and churchyards.

name: Scilla forbesii
tip: Early spring bulb with bright blue starry flowers having a white centre, upward facing, several on one stem, with narrow leaves. Naturalised in grass near gardens.

name: Scilla liliohyacinthus
tip: Robust bulb with broad strap leaves and a tall spike of many pale blue bells with darker veins. Rare garden escape in woodland, mostly southern England.

name: Scilla luciliae
tip: Early spring bulb with large, bright blue starry flowers with white centres, one to three per stem, held upward. Naturalised on lawns and verges; larger flowers than Forbes form.

name: Scilla messeniaca
tip: Spring bulb with a loose spike of small pale blue bells and narrow leaves. A rare garden escape, hard to separate from other squills without specialist help.

name: Scilla peruviana
tip: Large domed head of many violet-blue starry flowers on stout stem above broad leaves fringed with fine hairs. Rare garden escape on south-western coasts and banks.

name: Scilla sardensis
tip: Early spring bulb with small nodding-to-erect rich blue flowers lacking a distinct white centre, borne in a loose cluster above narrow leaves. Rare garden relic.

name: Scilla siberica
tip: Intense deep blue nodding bell flowers, one to three per stem, with broad glossy leaves. Widely naturalised in grass, churchyards and parkland in early spring.

name: Scilla verna
tip: Low tuft with narrow curled leaves and a short head of bright blue starry flowers. Local on short coastal turf of west and north Britain and Ireland.

name: Triteleia laxa
tip: Wiry stem topped by a loose umbel of violet-blue funnel flowers, with grassy leaves. Rare Californian bulb occasionally escaping from gardens.

name: Aristaloe aristata
tip: Small stemless rosette of narrow fleshy leaves with soft white teeth and bristle tips, and orange-red tubular flowers. Tender houseplant, not naturalised outdoors.

name: Asphodelus albus
tip: Tall unbranched spike of white starry flowers each marked with a brown central vein, above a tuft of long narrow leaves. Rare garden plant.

name: Hemerocallis fulva
