tip: Clump of long arching strap leaves with tall stems of large tawny-orange trumpet flowers, each lasting one day. Common garden escape on roadsides and waste ground.

name: Hemerocallis lilioasphodelus
tip: Clumps of strap leaves with scented clear yellow lily-like trumpet flowers on tall stems. Rare garden escape; the common orange day-lily has tawny flowers.

name: Kniphofia uvaria
tip: Tough tufted plant with keeled grassy leaves rough on the edges and a dense torch-like spike of orange-red tubular flowers. Garden escape on coastal cliffs and dunes.

name: Phormium cookianum
tip: Tall fountain of stiff, arching sword-like leaves with a flower spike of dull yellowish-green tubular flowers and twisted pods. Less stiff than New Zealand flax; planted in mild places.

name: Phormium tenax
tip: Large clump of tall stiff sword leaves, sometimes with coloured stripes, and tall spikes of dull red tubular flowers. Planted widely in coastal gardens, seldom established.

name: Simethis mattiazzii
tip: Tufted plant with grassy leaves and loose starry white flowers tinged purple outside, with yellow stamens. Extremely rare in Ireland, on Kerry heathy slopes, and in the south of England.

name: Asplenium marinum
tip: Leathery evergreen fern with glossy, once-divided fronds bearing rounded, blunt-toothed leaflets, growing in sea caves and cliff crevices. Always close to the coast of western Britain and Ireland.

name: Asplenium obovatum
tip: Small evergreen fern of rock crevices with lance-shaped, glossy, once-divided fronds with small toothed leaflets. Western coasts and mild, wet districts; similar to forked and sea spleenworts.

name: Asplenium onopteris
tip: Evergreen fern with twice-divided, triangular, glossy dark fronds with narrow leaflets, found on shady banks and walls. Very rare, in southern Ireland.

name: Asplenium septentrionale
tip: Tiny tufted fern with narrow, grass-like fronds that fork into two or three slender tips, growing in acid rock crevices and walls. Local in uplands.

name: Asplenium viride
tip: Small tufted fern with a bright green stalk and once-divided frond of rounded, scalloped leaflets, found in cool limestone crevices in uplands of northern Britain.

name: Athyrium distentifolium
tip: Tall deciduous fern with a shuttlecock of twice-divided fronds with rounded dots of spores, found in damp mountain corries. Difficult to tell from lady-fern; fronds widest in the middle.

name: Blechnum cordatum
tip: Evergreen fern with a large tuft of leathery once-divided fronds with long untoothed leaflets, with new fronds often coppery red. Garden plant, occasionally escaping in mild areas.

name: Blechnum penna-marina
tip: Small creeping fern with narrow, once-divided, glossy dark fronds with fine untoothed leaflets, the fertile ones taller. Local on damp upland slopes in the north and west.

name: Cystopteris diaphana
tip: Delicate bladder-fern with thin, pale green, twice-divided fronds and tiny toothed lobes, growing on shaded rocks. Not clearly native in Britain; specialist confirmation required.

name: Cystopteris dickieana
tip: Delicate fern with pale, twice-divided short fronds with blunt toothed lobes, growing in shady damp coastal rock crevices and caves, mostly in north-east Scotland. Needs specialist checking.

name: Cystopteris montana
tip: Delicate fern with broad, triangular, finely divided fronds, found on damp rocky ledges in high Scottish mountains. Larger and more finely cut than brittle bladder-fern.

name: Gymnocarpium robertianum
tip: Triangular, matt, grey-green fronds with sticky glandular hairs that smell faintly of resin, growing on limestone screes. Distinct from oak fern by hairs and dull colour.

name: Matteuccia struthiopteris
tip: Tall shuttlecock of large pale green fronds, with separate dark brown fertile fronds in the centre. Garden escape, naturalised beside streams in a few places.

name: Onoclea sensibilis
tip: Broad, deeply wavy-lobed, pale green sterile fronds in a spreading patch, with separate beaded brown fertile fronds. Rare garden escape in damp places.

name: Thelypteris palustris
tip: Slender creeping fern with thin, pale green, twice-divided fronds with untoothed lobes, growing in fen and wet carr. Local, mainly in lowland East Anglia and Ireland.

name: Woodsia alpina
tip: Very small tufted fern of mountain rock crevices with narrow, hairy, divided fronds that curl at the edges. Extremely rare, in a few Scottish and Welsh upland sites.

name: Woodsia ilvensis
tip: Small tufted fern with narrow, once-divided fronds with oblong, rusty-hairy leaflets, growing in cliff crevices. Extremely rare in a few Scottish and Welsh upland sites.

name: Woodwardia radicans
tip: Large evergreen fern with leathery, arching, twice-divided fronds producing small buds near the tips. Garden plant, naturalised on a few wooded banks in the south-west.

name: Impatiens capensis
tip: Tall, succulent plant with oval toothed leaves and hanging orange trumpet flowers spotted with brown, having a curved spur. Naturalised along rivers and canals in southern England.

name: Impatiens noli-tangere
tip: Succulent plant with swollen stem joints, oval toothed leaves and yellow trumpet flowers with a hooked spur. Native only in a few streamside woods in north-west England and Wales.

name: Impatiens parviflora
tip: Slender balsam with pointed toothed leaves and small pale yellow flowers with a short straight spur. Common weed of shady waste ground and woodland edges.

name: Berberis buxifolia
tip: Evergreen shrub with small, oval, leathery, spine-tipped leaves and clusters of small yellow flowers. Occasional bird-sown escape; leaves untoothed, unlike many other barberries.

name: Berberis glaucocarpa
tip: Large evergreen barberry with spiny, toothed leathery leaves in clusters and yellow flowers followed by dark blue-black berries. Common planted shrub that occasionally self-sows. Specialist confirmation advised.

name: Alnus rubra
tip: Tree with catkins in late winter and leaves with rolled edges, hairy beneath. Rare in plantations; common alder has a blunt notched leaf tip.

name: Betula nana
tip: Low shrub under a metre with tiny, rounded, blunt-toothed leaves and small catkins. Very local on boggy moorland in the Scottish Highlands and northern England.

name: Corylus maxima
tip: Large shrub like hazel but with nut husks fully enclosing the nuts, longer than the nut. Planted in hedges and gardens; yellow catkins appear in late winter.

name: Aegonychon purpureocaeruleum
tip: Creeping plant with narrow, dark, pointed leaves and clusters of flowers opening reddish-purple and turning bright blue. Very rare, on wooded scrub banks in the south-west.

name: Amsinckia lycopsoides
tip: Rough annual with narrow bristly leaves and curled one-sided spikes of small orange-yellow flowers. Uncommon casual of arable fields and waste ground. Specialist needed to separate fiddlenecks.

name: Anchusa ochroleuca
tip: Bristly plant with narrow wavy leaves and clusters of small pale yellow flowers on branched stems. Rare casual of waste ground and garden margins.

name: Anchusa officinalis
tip: Bristly, tall plant with narrow wavy leaves and dense branched clusters of purple-blue flowers whose throats are closed by white scales. Casual on waste ground and rough verges.

name: Borago pygmaea
tip: Annual with bristly oval leaves and pale blue star-shaped flowers hanging on slender stalks. Rare casual or garden escape of waste ground; smaller than common borage.

name: Brunnera macrophylla
tip: Clump-forming plant with large heart-shaped, rough leaves and sprays of small bright blue forget-me-not flowers with white centres. Common garden plant, escaping onto shady verges.

name: Buglossoides arvensis
tip: Hairy annual of arable fields with narrow leaves and small white funnel flowers. Scarce, in chalky and limy cornfields in southern England; flowers smaller than corn gromwell.

name: Cynoglossum germanicum
tip: Hairy plant with leaves shiny green above and tongue-shaped, and dull reddish-purple small flowers; nutlets have barbs. Rare in dry woods; leaves greener and less grey than hounds-tongue.

name: Cynoglossum officinale
tip: Grey-green softly hairy plant with tongue-shaped leaves and dull maroon funnel flowers, smelling of mice. Fruits are flat nutlets covered in sticky barbs. Dry grassland and dunes.

name: Echium pininana
tip: Very tall bristly biennial forming a huge spire of pale blue flowers in its second summer. Naturalised mainly in Cornwall, Scilly and south-west coasts. Far taller than other viper's-buglosses.

name: Echium plantagineum
tip: Bristly plant with funnel flowers that are pink in bud, opening bright violet-blue, with five stamens sticking out. Mostly Cornwall, Scilly and Channel Islands; wider flowers than Viper's-bugloss.

name: Echium rosulatum
tip: Close to Purple Viper's-bugloss but with a looser, less leafy flower spike and smaller blue flowers. Very local, mainly the Lizard in Cornwall; needs expert confirmation.

name: Lithospermum officinale
tip: Upright rough plant of scrub and chalk edges with small dull cream flowers and remarkably hard, shiny white nutlets like tiny porcelain beads.

name: Lycopsis arvensis
tip: Bristly annual of sandy arable land with small bright blue flowers whose throat is closed by white scales. Leaves are wavy-edged and very rough to the touch.

name: Mertensia maritima
tip: Fleshy blue-grey creeping plant of northern shingle beaches, with bell flowers opening pink then turning blue. Leaves taste faintly of oysters. Mainly Scotland, northern England and Ireland.

name: Myosotis alpestris
tip: Rare mountain forget-me-not with large, deep sky-blue flowers in a dense, short head. Found on a few high rocky ledges in Scotland and Teesdale.

name: Myosotis sicula
tip: Tiny annual forget-me-not with minute pale blue flowers on short stems in dry sandy turf. Confined to Jersey, in the Channel Islands.

name: Myosotis stolonifera
tip: Creeping forget-me-not of upland springs and stream sides, with pale blue flowers and sprawling leafy runners. Mostly northern England and Scotland; flowers smaller and paler than Water Forget-me-not.

name: Omphalodes verna
tip: Low spring garden escape that spreads in shady places, with sky-blue flowers having a white eye and heart-shaped leaves. Not the same as the similar Common Forget-me-not.

name: Plagiobothrys scouleri
tip: Very rare small annual with tiny white flowers on coiled spikes and narrow leaves. A casual introduction, mostly in damp disturbed ground; needs checking by a specialist.

name: Pulmonaria longifolia
tip: Lungwort with long, narrow, evenly pale-spotted leaves tapering to a point, and flowers pink turning blue. Rare, in Hampshire, the Isle of Wight and Dorset woods.

name: Pulmonaria obscura
tip: Lungwort with plain dark green leaves lacking pale spots, and flowers that turn from pink to blue. Native to a few woods in Suffolk and Essex.

name: Pulmonaria rubra
tip: Early spring garden escape with unspotted soft leaves and salmon or brick-red flowers that never turn blue, unlike other lungworts.

name: Symphytum asperum
tip: Tall comfrey whose stems and leaves are covered in sharp prickles. Flowers open pink and turn blue-violet. Naturalised in hedgerows and waste ground.

name: Symphytum bulbosum
tip: Low comfrey spreading by small tubers, bearing pale creamy-yellow flowers in spring. Leaves are not running down the stem. Uncommon naturalised garden escape.

name: Symphytum caucasicum
tip: Low comfrey with grey-downy leaves and flowers that open pink and turn sky blue. An infrequent garden escape in rough grass and verges.

name: Trachystemon orientalis
tip: Early spring plant with violet-blue flowers whose petals curl right back, with stamens protruding. Huge heart-shaped hairy leaves appear after flowering. Shady garden escape.

name: Alyssum alyssoides
tip: Small, grey, starry-haired annual with tiny pale yellow flowers whose petals are notched. Seed pods are round and flat. A rare casual of dry sandy ground.

name: Arabidopsis petraea
tip: Rare mountain cress with small white or lilac-tinged flowers and lobed leaves in a rosette, found on damp rock ledges in Scotland, Wales and Ireland.

name: Arabis alpina
tip: Tufted rock-cress with grey-hairy, toothed leaves and white flowers. Extremely rare, growing only on mountain rock in Skye and nearby Scottish areas.

name: Arabis caucasica
tip: Spreading, mat-forming grey-hairy cress with showy white flowers in early spring. A common garden plant often found on walls and banks nearby.

name: Arabis collina
tip: Biennial or perennial rock-cress escape with white to pinkish flowers and hairy toothed leaves clasping the stem. Rare, naturalised on walls and banks; needs expert checking.

name: Arabis procurrens
tip: Mat-forming garden escape that spreads by creeping runners, with glossy dark leaves and white flowers. Rare on walls and rough ground.

name: Arabis scabra
tip: Rare rock-cress with a hairy basal rosette and hairless clasping stem leaves, with white flowers in early spring. Restricted to Avon Gorge and a few limestone sites.

name: Aurinia saxatilis
tip: Grey-leaved garden plant with dense heads of bright golden-yellow flowers. Spills from walls and rockeries, unlike native yellow crucifers with green leaves.

name: Barbarea stricta
tip: Yellow winter-cress with tiny flowers and long, upright, narrow pods pressed against the stem. Upper leaves are deeply lobed. Local on damp river banks and waste ground.

name: Barbarea verna
tip: Yellow winter-cress usually grown as salad. It has very long narrow pods and its lower leaves have many lobe pairs. Local escape on field edges and waste ground.

name: Brassica oleracea
tip: Robust waxy blue-green perennial on sea cliffs, with fleshy wavy leaves and tall spikes of pale yellow flowers. Cliff plant of south and west coasts.

name: Bunias orientalis
tip: Tall rough bristly plant with bright yellow flowers and lumpy, warty seed pods. Lower leaves are deeply lobed. Increasingly found on road verges and waste ground.

name: Camelina sativa
tip: Slender yellow-flowered annual with clasping arrow-shaped stem leaves and pear-shaped pods. Occasional casual on arable land and waste ground.

name: Cardamine bulbifera
tip: Woodland plant with pink-lilac flowers and small dark bulbils at the leaf bases. Leaves are pinnate. Local in southern woodland, especially the Chilterns and the Weald.

name: Cardamine corymbosa
tip: Small white-flowered cress with simple oval leaves at the base and creeping stems. A garden weed and nursery escape common around towns.

name: Cardamine heptaphylla
tip: Woodland cress with white flowers and leaves that have several pairs of toothed leaflets. Flowers are large. Rare naturalised plant of shady places.

name: Cardamine impatiens
tip: Tall biennial of shady limestone and woodland, with tiny white flowers, pinnate leaves with narrow leaflets and ear-like clasping bases. Pods open explosively.

name: Cardamine quinquefolia
tip: Rare garden escape with whorled leaves of five leaflets and pink-lilac flowers in spring. Easily confused with other woodland Cardamine; needs expert confirmation.

name: Cardamine raphanifolia
tip: Large, robust relative of Cuckooflower with pale lilac-pink flowers, bigger leaflets and thicker stem. Naturalised on stream banks and damp woodland.

name: Cardamine trifolia
tip: Evergreen woodland-edge plant with glossy three-part leaves and clusters of white flowers that are sometimes tinged pink. A garden escape in damp shady spots.

name: Cochlearia anglica
tip: Fleshy scurvygrass of estuarine mud, with white flowers and clasping stem leaves. Seed pods are large and inflated, unlike other coastal scurvygrasses.

name: Cochlearia megalosperma
tip: Scurvygrass of the Cochlearia officinalis group with larger seeds, white flowers and fleshy leaves. Occurs near coasts. Specialist needed to confirm the identification.

name: Cochlearia micacea
tip: Small tufted scurvygrass of Scottish mountain springs and flushes, with long leaf stalks, white flowers and rounded pods. Grows only in uplands.

name: Cochlearia pyrenaica
tip: Upland scurvygrass of metal-rich streamsides in northern Britain, with kidney-shaped basal leaves, white flowers and small round pods. Not coastal.

name: Coincya monensis
tip: Bright yellow, crucifer with lobed bristly leaves and large veined flowers. Coastal on cliffs and shingle in Wales, Lancashire and Isle of Man, and scattered inland.

name: Coincya wrightii
tip: Endemic to Lundy, in the Bristol Channel, with yellow veined flowers on bristly stalks and large lobed leaves. Very rare, only on Lundy cliffs.

name: Crambe maritima
tip: Big waxy blue-green plant of shingle beaches, with wavy, crinkled leaves and domed masses of white honey-scented flowers. Hard to mistake for other seaside crucifers.

name: Descurainia sophia
tip: Slender grey-green annual with very finely divided leaves and tiny pale yellow flowers. Seed pods are long, narrow and held angled upward on spreading stalks.

name: Diplotaxis tenuifolia
tip: Yellow crucifer of walls and waste ground, with strong smell when crushed and deeply cut leaves. Taller and bushier than Annual Wall-rocket.

name: Draba aizoides
tip: Tiny mountain cushion plant with bright yellow flowers and stiff fringed narrow leaves in a rosette. Rare, on rock in Wales, plus Gower coast.

name: Draba incana
tip: Whitlow-grass with small white flowers, a leafy stem and star-shaped hairs that make the plant look grey. Local on mountain rocks and dunes.

name: Draba norvegica
tip: Very small tufted mountain whitlow-grass with white flowers and hairy toothed leaves, usually without stem leaves. Very rare, on high Scottish rock ledges.

name: Drabella muralis
tip: Slender annual with white flowers, oval clasping leaves on the stem and a rosette. Rare, found on limestone walls and rocks, mainly Wales and west England.

name: Erophila glabrescens
tip: Tiny spring annual of dry bare ground with deeply notched white petals; one of a critical group of microspecies. Specialist needed to confirm.

name: Erophila majuscula
tip: Tiny annual whitlow-grass with deeply notched white petals; one of a critical microspecies group distinguished by fine detail. Specialist needed to confirm.

name: Eruca vesicaria
tip: Salad plant with cream flowers veined purple and a peppery smell. Leaves have a large end lobe. Occasional escape on waste ground and verges.

name: Hornungia petraea
tip: Tiny, delicate annual of limestone rocks and bare soil with minute white flowers and neat, finely divided leaves. Local, found mostly on southern limestone.

name: Iberis amara
tip: Flat-topped heads of white or lilac-tinged flowers, with two petals larger than the others. Rare, found on chalk in the Chilterns and a few other southern sites.

name: Isatis tinctoria
tip: Tall blue-green plant with big branching sprays of small yellow flowers and hanging dark pods like flattened black spoons. Grown formerly for dye, naturalised on cliffs and banks.

name: Lepidium latifolium
tip: Tall, hairless perennial with broad leaves and dense heads of tiny white flowers. Mostly found on coastal salt marshes and sea walls, with a few inland.

name: Lepidium ruderale
tip: Foul-smelling annual with tiny greenish flowers lacking petals. The lower leaves are lobed and the upper leaves entire. Found on waste ground and by roads.

name: Lepidium sativum
tip: Grown as a salad; fine, divided bright green leaves and tiny white flowers. Casual escape on waste ground, with small round flat pods.

name: Malcolmia maritima
tip: Low annual garden flower with pink, red, lilac or white fragrant flowers and long thin pods. Established on coastal sand and shingle in places.

name: Matthiola incana
tip: Grey, densely downy shrubby plant with sweetly scented pink to purple flowers and leaves not lobed. Grows on sea cliffs, notably Isle of Wight, Dorset and Sussex.

name: Matthiola sinuata
tip: Biennial grey plant of sandy coasts with lilac-purple flowers and wavy-lobed woolly leaves; stickily hairy pods. Very rare, found in south-west Britain and Wales.

name: Microthlaspi perfoliatum
tip: Small annual with tiny white flowers and pale green stem leaves clasping the stem. Rare on arable land and walls, especially in the Cotswolds.

name: Noccaea caerulescens
tip: Small tufted plant with a rosette and small white flowers with violet anthers. Native on lead-rich soil, such as old mine spoil in the Pennines and Wales.

name: Pachyphragma macrophyllum
tip: Spring woodland garden plant with big heart-shaped leaves and clusters of white flowers with an unpleasant garlic smell. Naturalised in a few damp shady places.

name: Peltaria alliacea
tip: Very rare garden-escape perennial with blue-grey clasping leaves and heads of white flowers. Smells of garlic when crushed. Needs a specialist to confirm.

name: Pseudoturritis turrita
tip: Tall greyish biennial with creamy flowers and clasping leaves, similar to Tower Mustard but with leaves having hairs. Rare casual; needs checking by a specialist.

name: Raphanus sativus
tip: Familiar salad plant with white or lilac veined flowers and beaded pods. Casual on waste ground; wild forms are bristly, with lobed leaves.

name: Rapistrum perenne
tip: Tall, bristly yellow-flowered perennial with pods that narrow in joints. Rare casual of waste ground and verges, mainly eastern and southern England.

name: Rapistrum rugosum
tip: Hairy annual with pale yellow veined flowers and knobbly pods. Lower leaves are lobed. Casual on waste ground, mainly in the south.

name: Rorippa amphibia
tip: Tall stout waterside plant with narrow, toothed or lobed leaves and many small yellow flowers; pods are short and oval. Common by rivers and ponds in England.

name: Rorippa austriaca
tip: Rhizomatous yellow-cress with undivided toothed, clasping stem leaves and small yellow flowers. Rare introduction, on river banks and waste ground in places.

name: Rorippa islandica
tip: Small, mainly upland yellow-cress of wet stony places with pinnately lobed leaves and short pods. Very rare, in the Scottish Highlands; needs careful checking.

name: Sisymbrium altissimum
tip: Tall annual with pale yellow flowers and very long thin pods, held erect. The upper leaves are narrow and thread-like. Casual of waste ground.

name: Sisymbrium loeselii
tip: Annual with small yellow flowers, pods short and pressed to the stem, and arrow-shaped terminal lobe. Occasional casual on waste ground.

name: Sisymbrium strictissimum
tip: Tall perennial with pale yellow flowers, toothed oval undivided leaves and long thin pods. A rare naturalised plant on waste ground and verges.

name: Sisymbrium volgense
tip: Rare creeping-rooted perennial with pale yellow flowers and deeply lobed leaves, found in waste places. Specialist needed to confirm.

name: Subularia aquatica
tip: Tiny submerged aquatic with a rosette of awl-shaped leaves and small white flowers held above the water. Found in clear, acidic lakes in uplands.

name: Teesdalia nudicaulis
tip: Small annual of sandy, acid soils, with a rosette of lobed leaves and tiny white flowers whose outer petals are larger. Local on heaths and dunes.

name: Thlaspi alliaceum
tip: Smells of garlic when crushed. Bushy annual with small white flowers and leaves clasping the stem. Rare, casual on waste ground and field edges.

name: Turritis glabra
tip: Tall greyish biennial with a basal rosette and upright spike; stem leaves clasp the stem with arrow-shaped bases and pale cream flowers give way to long, upright, flattened pods.

name: Cabomba caroliniana
tip: Aquatic plant with finely fan-divided underwater leaves and a few small floating oval leaves; white, yellow-centred flowers sit at the surface. Aquarium escape in canals and ponds.

name: Calceolaria chelidonioides
tip: Small annual with pinnately lobed, hairy leaves resembling greater celandine and tiny yellow pouched flowers. Rare casual of waste ground, from gardens, mostly in southern England.

name: Campanula alliariifolia
tip: Tall garden bellflower with creamy white nodding bells and heart-shaped, long-stalked basal leaves; rough-hairy. Occasional escape on banks and verges, unlike the blue native bellflowers.

name: Campanula cochleariifolia
tip: Small tufted bellflower with round toothed basal leaves and slender stalks of nodding, pale blue bells; spreads on walls and rocky ground. Smaller and more delicate than harebell.

name: Campanula fragilis
tip: Sprawling garden bellflower with rounded, scalloped, glossy leaves and flat, starry, pale violet-blue flowers on trailing stems. Rare wall and rock garden escape.

name: Campanula garganica
tip: Low, mat-forming rock-garden bellflower with hairy heart-shaped toothed leaves and flat, five-pointed, violet-blue stars. Escapes onto walls and pavements, mainly near gardens.

name: Campanula glomerata
tip: Stiff upright bellflower with tight terminal clusters of violet funnel-shaped flowers and unstalked upper leaves clasping the stem. Native on chalk and limestone grassland; also in gardens.

name: Campanula lactiflora
tip: Tall garden bellflower with big branched heads of pale milky blue or lilac bells and many leafy stalkless stem leaves. Occasional garden escape on banks and rough ground.

name: Campanula medium
tip: Tall biennial with large inflated bells in blue, pink or white and rough, hairy, toothed leaves. Garden plant occasionally found on waste ground and verges.

name: Campanula patula
tip: Slender branched bellflower with widely open lilac funnels on thin spreading stalks and narrow, rough-edged leaves. Rare native of hedgebanks and verges in southern and western England and Wales.

name: Campanula pyramidalis
tip: Very tall garden bellflower with long pyramid-shaped spikes of many blue stars and glossy heart-shaped lower leaves. Rare escape from cultivation, often on walls.

name: Campanula rapunculoides
tip: Spreading, invasive patches of tall stems with one-sided spikes of nodding purple bells; heart-shaped lower leaves. Spreads by underground runners, a persistent garden and roadside weed.

name: Campanula rapunculus
tip: Biennial with a fleshy white root, wavy-edged basal leaves and a narrow spike-like panicle of pale blue small bells. Rare, now mostly casual on banks and waste ground.

name: Campanula rhomboidalis
tip: Upright perennial with broad oval toothed stem leaves and nodding blue bells in a one-sided cluster. Garden plant occasionally recorded as a rare escape on grassy banks.

name: Legousia hybrida
tip: Low arable annual with small violet star-shaped flowers whose petals are shorter than the sepals, and wavy-edged clasping leaves. Local on chalky cornfield margins in southern England.

name: Legousia speculum-veneris
tip: Annual with bright violet-purple flat flowers, petals longer than the sepals, in loose branched clusters; larger-flowered than Venuss-looking-glass. Rare casual of arable land and gardens.

name: Lobelia dortmanna
tip: Submerged rosettes of stiff, hollow, quill-like leaves in clear acid lakes; a bare flower stem rising above water bearing a few pale lilac nodding flowers. Upland Britain and Ireland.

name: Lobelia urens
tip: Slender upright plant of damp acid grassland with small blue-violet two-lipped flowers in a spike and toothed oblong leaves. Very local in southern England, especially Devon and Sussex.

name: Phyteuma orbiculare
tip: Chalk-grassland plant with tight globe-shaped heads of deep blue-violet flowers with curved, claw-like buds and narrow toothed stem leaves. Local on the South Downs and Wiltshire chalk.

name: Phyteuma scheuchzeri
tip: Mountain rampion with rounded heads of violet-blue flowers on leafy stems; lower leaves heart-shaped on long stalks. Rare garden escape, not native in Britain or Ireland.

name: Phyteuma spicatum
tip: Woodland plant with dense oblong spikes of cream-white flowers tipped green and heart-shaped stalked basal leaves. Rare native of woods and hedgebanks, restricted to East Sussex.

name: Pratia angulata
tip: Mat-forming creeper with tiny rounded toothed leaves rooting along stems and small white flowers, flushed purple, on slender stalks. Rare garden escape of lawns and damp paths.

name: Pratia pedunculata
tip: Dense mat of tiny oval leaves rooting along creeping stems, with small pale blue flowers on very short stalks. Garden escape found on paths and damp grass.

name: Trachelium caeruleum
tip: Tall plant with large dense flat-topped heads of tiny violet tubular flowers and toothed oval leaves. Naturalised on old walls and cliffs, mainly in southern and western Britain.

name: Wahlenbergia hederacea
tip: Delicate creeping plant of damp acid ground with ivy-shaped, pointed-lobed leaves and single pale blue bells on hair-thin stalks. Native of western and southern Britain and Ireland.

name: Cannabis sativa
tip: Tall annual with palmate leaves of five to seven narrow toothed leaflets and a strong smell; flowers are tiny green clusters. Occasional casual on waste ground and from bird seed.

name: Centranthus calcitrapae
tip: Small annual with pink flowers in lax clusters and a short spur, pinnately lobed lower leaves. Rare casual or naturalised in southern England and the Channel Islands.

name: Dipsacus laciniatus
tip: Tall teasel with deeply cut, divided stem leaves and spiny stems, white to pale pink heads. Rare casual or escape, differing from common teasel in its deeply lobed leaves.

name: Dipsacus pilosus
tip: Branched teasel with small rounded heads of pale lilac or white flowers, stalked leaves and recurved spines. Local in damp woods and hedgerows in southern England.

name: Dipsacus sativus
tip: Spiny teasel with prickly seed heads bearing stiff hooked bracts, once used for raising cloth. Lilac flowers; rare outside cultivation, found on verges and waste ground.

name: Dipsacus strigosus
tip: Tall teasel with pale yellow-white flowers in oval heads, bristly stems and long prickly leaves. Rare casual or escape, most likely misidentified as wild teasel.

name: Linnaea borealis
tip: Evergreen creeping subshrub with paired nodding pink bells on slender forked stalks and small rounded leaves. Rare plant of Scottish pine woods and mossy ground.

name: Lonicera caprifolium
tip: Climber whose upper pairs of leaves are fused around the stem, forming a disc; creamy-yellow fragrant flowers in clusters. Rare woodland and hedge escape, flowering earlier than common honeysuckle.

name: Lonicera henryi
tip: Evergreen climber with narrow dark glossy leaves and clusters of small dull purplish-red and yellowish flowers followed by black berries. Rare garden escape.

name: Lonicera xylosteum
tip: Upright shrub with paired, hairy oval leaves and pairs of cream-yellow flowers held on short stalks, followed by joined red berries. Rare native of woods and scrub on chalk.

name: Scabiosa atropurpurea
tip: Annual garden plant with domed heads of dark crimson to purple flowers on tall stems, with lobed leaves. Rare casual on waste ground and tips.

name: Symphoricarpos orbiculatus
tip: Small suckering shrub with tiny pink-white flowers in leaf axils and clusters of purplish-pink berries on arching twigs. Naturalised rarely in hedges and shrubberies.

name: Valeriana phu
tip: Tall perennial with creamy-white flower heads; lower leaves are plain, upper ones divided into leaflets. Often grown for gold foliage; rare garden outcast.

name: Valeriana pyrenaica
tip: Tall plant of shady damp places with heart-shaped, toothed leaves and rounded clusters of small pale pink flowers. Naturalised in woods and stream banks, mainly in western Britain and Ireland.

name: Valerianella dentata
tip: Small forked annual cornfield weed with tiny pale lilac flowers and fruits that are narrow with an obvious tooth. Rare, mainly on calcareous arable land in southern England.

name: Valerianella eriocarpa
tip: Annual cornsalad with tiny pale lilac or white flowers and fruits covered with hairs, with a prominent calyx tooth. Rare arable weed on chalky soil in southern England.

name: Valerianella rimosa
tip: Cornfield annual with tiny pale pink flowers and fruits inflated, broadly egg-shaped and hollow. Rare arable weed on chalky soil, southern England.

name: Arenaria balearica
tip: Dense, moss-like mat of tiny glossy rounded leaves with solitary white flowers on short stalks. Garden escape on walls and paths; spreads rapidly on damp shaded surfaces.

name: Arenaria ciliata
tip: Low tufted perennial with white flowers, petals longer than sepals, and small narrow leaves with fringed bases. Rare plant of limestone rocks and grassland, western Ireland.

name: Arenaria montana
tip: Trailing perennial with big white flowers and narrow grey-green leaves, usually in loose clumps. Rare garden escape from gardens and rockeries.

name: Arenaria norvegica
tip: Small cushion plant with white flowers, shorter leaves than other sandworts and pointed, firm leaf shapes. Rare plant of limestone rocks in Scotland, Ireland and Skye.

name: Cerastium alpinum
tip: Mountain mouse-ear with white flowers, grey-hairy woolly leaves and sepals that are densely woolly. Rare, in high rocky ground in the Scottish Highlands, Wales and northern England.

name: Cerastium arvense
tip: Sprawling mat-forming mouse-ear with large white flowers with deeply notched petals, longer than the sepals, and narrow, hairy leaves. Common on grassy banks and dry roadsides.

name: Cerastium brachypetalum
tip: Small, grey-green annual with flowers in tight dense clusters, tiny white flowers, and fruit stalks bent down. Very rare, on calcareous soils in East Anglia.

name: Cerastium cerastoides
tip: Mountain mouse-ear with creeping mats and white flowers with deeply notched petals, longer than the sepals, and tough hairless leaves. Rare, high ground in Scotland.

name: Cerastium nigrescens
tip: Tiny tufted mouse-ear, endemic to Shetland, with grey-green leaves, white flowers, and strongly hairy leaves. Grows only on serpentine on the island of Unst.

name: Cerastium pumilum
tip: Small annual mouse-ear with tiny white flowers, blunt sepals with a papery margin, and sticky, glandular upper parts. Rare, on dry calcareous banks and short grass.

name: Cherleria sedoides
tip: Dense cushion-forming plant of mountain rocks, with narrow leaves, and tiny green-yellow flowers lacking petals. Local in Scottish Highlands, northern England and Ireland.

name: Corrigiola litoralis
tip: Prostrate annual with narrow, blue-green leaves and tiny white flowers in tight clusters. Very rare, found on shingle beaches near Slapton, Devon.

name: Dianthus armeria
tip: Upright pink with bright pink flowers in tight clusters, with white spots, with narrow leaves and sepals with long points. Rare, on dry open grass, southern England.

name: Dianthus barbatus
tip: Biennial with dense flat-topped clusters of flowers in pink, red or white with toothed petals, and broad flat leaves. Garden plant, escapes onto verges and waste ground.

name: Dianthus caryophyllus
tip: Grey-green perennial with large clove-scented flowers in pink, with toothed petals, and long narrow leaves. Naturalised on old walls and castle ruins.

name: Dianthus deltoides
tip: Low, mat-forming pink with small, pink flowers with a ring of darker spots, with toothed petals. Local on dry, sandy, grassy ground, in Britain.

name: Dianthus gallicus
tip: Pink with deeply cut, fringed flowers in pink, and blue-green leaves, growing in tufts. Native on sandy dunes on Jersey, and naturalised in Cornwall.

name: Dianthus gratianopolitanus
tip: Small blue-green tufted plant with solitary pink flowers with toothed petals and a clove scent. Very rare, restricted to limestone cliffs in Cheddar Gorge.

name: Dianthus plumarius
tip: Garden pink with deeply fringed, fragrant pink or white flowers and grey narrow leaves growing in a loose clump. Escapes onto old walls and rockeries.

name: Gypsophila paniculata
tip: Tall, much-branched plant with a cloud of tiny white flowers and narrow, grey-green leaves. Garden plant, occasionally found on waste ground and sandy banks.

name: Herniaria ciliolata
tip: Prostrate plant with tiny oval leaves, green flowers in clusters, and leaves with short fringed hairs. Very rare, on coastal gravel in the Lizard, Cornwall.

name: Herniaria glabra
tip: Mat-forming plant with tiny green flower clusters along the stem and shiny, hairless, small leaves. Rare, found on sandy and gravelly ground, and paths.

name: Illecebrum verticillatum
tip: Prostrate plant with whitish papery stems like a string of beads and tiny white flowers in clusters. Very rare, on damp sandy ground in southern England.

name: Minuartia recurva
tip: Tufted perennial with white flowers on short stalks, and narrow, curved, spiky leaves. Rare plant of serpentine and rocky ground; may be misidentified.

name: Moenchia erecta
tip: Small grey-green annual with white flowers held upright, with petals shorter than the sepals, on short erect stems. Local on dry open grass and heaths in southern England.

name: Petrorhagia dubia
tip: Slender hairy annual with small pink flowers in tight heads, and narrow leaves. Rare introduction on waste ground and sandy ground, in southern England.

name: Petrorhagia nanteuilii
tip: Slender annual with small pink flowers, one at a time, with notched petals and papery bracts. Very rare, on the south coast of England and the Isle of Wight.

name: Petrorhagia prolifera
tip: Slender annual with small pink flowers in a head wrapped with brown papery bracts, and narrow leaves. Rare on sandy and gravelly ground.

name: Petrorhagia saxifraga
tip: Wiry, tufted perennial with small flowers in loose clusters, pale pink or white with notched petals. Rare garden escape, on walls and dry banks.

name: Polycarpon tetraphyllum
tip: Small annual with whorls of four small oval leaves and tiny white flowers in clusters. Rare in dry open places, mostly on the south coast and in the Channel Islands.

name: Sabulina rubella
tip: Small tufted mountain plant with white flowers on short stalks, and narrow, pointed leaves with sticky glandular hairs. Very rare, on base-rich rocks in Scotland.

name: Sabulina stricta
tip: Dwarf tufted plant with white flowers with petals shorter than sepals, and thread-like leaves. Rare, restricted to Upper Teesdale, on sugar limestone.

name: Sabulina tenuifolia
tip: Slender annual with white flowers in loose branched clusters, petals shorter than the sepals, and thread-like leaves. Rare, on dry calcareous ground in southern England.

name: Sagina nivalis
tip: Tiny tufted pearlwort of mountain rocks with flowers on short stalks, with petals longer than sepals, with very short stems. Very rare, in the Scottish Highlands.

name: Sagina saginoides
tip: Small pearlwort with flowers on stalks, with five petals, and narrow leaves in tufts. Local on mountain rocks and wet ground in Scotland.

name: Sagina subulata
tip: Mat-forming pearlwort with small white flowers on glandular-hairy stalks, with five petals, and bristle-like leaves. Local on dry sandy heaths and coastal rocks.

name: Saponaria ocymoides
tip: Trailing perennial with masses of small pink flowers and small oval hairy leaves. Garden plant, occasionally escaped onto rocks, walls and banks.

name: Scleranthus annuus
tip: Small spreading annual with tiny green flowers in clusters and narrow, spiny, bristle-like leaves. Local on dry, sandy, arable and waste ground.

name: Scleranthus perennis
tip: Tiny greenish flowers in tight clusters on a tufted, wiry perennial with needle-like paired leaves. Very rare, on dry rocky ground in Radnorshire and Worcestershire.

name: Silene acaulis
tip: Forms a dense, bright green cushion on mountain rocks, studded with stemless pink flowers. Compare cushion saxifrages, which lack the notched pink petals.

name: Silene alpestris
tip: Garden escape with white fringed petals and sticky stems beneath the flowers. Told from bladder campion by its fringed petal tips and small, narrow leaves.

name: Silene baccifera
tip: Straggling plant with small greenish-white flowers followed by shiny black berries instead of dry capsules. A rare casual, mostly of waste ground.

name: Silene catholica
tip: Rare casual of waste ground with small pinkish flowers on a stickily hairy, branched stem. A specialist may be needed to separate it from other annual catchflies.

name: Silene chalcedonica
tip: Garden plant with dense flat heads of bright scarlet flowers, each with four deeply notched petals. Occasionally escapes onto banks and verges.

name: Silene conica
tip: Small annual of coastal sands with an inflated, ribbed, hairy calyx and tiny pink flowers. Rare, found mainly on dunes and sandy ground in eastern and southern Britain.

name: Silene gallica
tip: Sticky, hairy annual with small white or pink flowers held in one-sided spikes. Lacks the inflated calyx of bladder campion and the sand catchfly.

name: Silene italica
tip: Sticky biennial with creamy flowers whose petals roll inwards by day and open at dusk. Local on dry, sandy and rocky ground in southern and eastern England.

name: Silene multifida
tip: Rare casual with narrow, divided lower leaves and small whitish flowers in loose clusters. Easily overlooked among other white catchflies, so confirm with a specialist.

name: Silene noctiflora
tip: Sticky annual of arable fields whose white or pinkish flowers open in the evening. Has three styles and a hairy calyx, unlike white campion.

name: Silene nutans
tip: Nodding flowers with white petals curled inwards by day and opening at dusk; stems are sticky above. Local on dry grassland, cliffs and shingle.

name: Silene otites
tip: Tall slender plant with whorls of tiny yellowish-green flowers on a long spike. Rare, confined mostly to sandy Breckland heaths in East Anglia.

name: Silene schafta
tip: Low garden plant forming mats with bright magenta flowers late in the year. A rare escape with notched petals and narrow leaves.

name: Silene suecica
tip: Small tufted plant with sticky bands on the stem and bright pink flowers with notched petals. Very rare, on mountain rocks in Cumbria and Angus.

name: Silene viscaria
tip: Tall plant with a sticky band beneath each node and spikes of magenta flowers. Local on dry rocky outcrops in Wales and Scotland, and sandy places.

name: Spergula morisonii
tip: Tiny slender annual with thread-like leaves and little white flowers. Very rare, on sandy arable and heathy ground, mainly in East Anglia. Needs careful checking against pearlworts.

name: Spergularia bocconei
tip: Small pink-flowered annual of coastal sand and grass, with short fleshy leaves and a brown papery stipule. Rare, mostly on south-west coasts.

name: Spergularia rupicola
tip: Clump-forming, sticky perennial of sea cliffs with fleshy leaves and pink flowers with white centres. Told from other sea-spurreys by its woody base and stickiness.

name: Stellaria nemorum
tip: Broad, stalked, heart-based leaves and loose clusters of white flowers with deeply cleft petals. Grows in damp shady woods, mostly in northern and western Britain.

name: Stellaria palustris
tip: Waxy, bluish-green plant with narrow leaves and white flowers whose petals are cut almost to the base. Rare, in base-rich fens and marshes.

name: Euonymus japonicus
tip: Glossy evergreen shrub with thick, toothed, dark green leaves and small greenish flowers. Widely planted by the sea and sometimes self-sown in hedges.

name: Ceratophyllum submersum
tip: Submerged plant with soft, thrice-forked leaves in whorls, less stiff and spiny than rigid hornwort. Rare in ponds and ditches of southern and eastern England.

name: Helianthemum apenninum
tip: Low shrubby plant with white flowers and leaves white-downy beneath. Very rare, on limestone in the Avon Gorge, Brean Down and a few Yorkshire sites.

name: Helianthemum oelandicum
tip: Small mat-forming rock-rose with yellow flowers and greyish downy leaves, lacking stipules. Very rare, on limestone in Durness, Teesdale and the Brecon area.

name: Tuberaria guttata
tip: Yellow annual whose petals each bear a dark red spot at the base. Very rare, found on coastal rocks in Wales, Channel Islands and western Ireland.

name: Tuberaria lignosa
tip: Rosette-forming perennial with yellow flowers on a leafless stem, lacking the dark petal spots of spotted rock-rose. Very rare casual.

name: Colchicum autumnale
tip: Crocus-like pink-lilac flowers appearing in autumn without leaves; large glossy leaves appear in spring. Told from autumn crocuses by six stamens.

name: Calystegia soldanella
tip: Trailing bindweed with fleshy kidney-shaped leaves and large pink funnel flowers striped white. Grows on sandy beaches and dunes.

name: Cuscuta epithymum
tip: Leafless red thread-like parasite twining over gorse and heather, with small clusters of pink flowers. Slender stems and compact heads separate it from greater dodder.

name: Cuscuta europaea
tip: Thicker, reddish-yellow parasitic threads on nettles and hops with pinkish flowers in clusters. Rare, mainly in southern and eastern England.

name: Cornus alba
tip: Shrub with bright red winter stems, creamy flowers in flat heads, and white or bluish-white berries. Widely planted and sometimes naturalised in hedges.

name: Cornus canadensis
tip: Low creeping plant with whorled oval leaves and flowerheads ringed by four white bracts. Naturalised in a few northern Scottish moorlands.

name: Cornus suecica
tip: Small upland plant with whorls of oval leaves and tiny dark purple flowers ringed by white bracts. Found on northern moors and mountains.

name: Aeonium balsamiferum
tip: Succulent with rosettes of sticky green leaves at the ends of branched stems and yellow star flowers. Only a rare garden escape in mild areas.

name: Aeonium cuneatum
tip: Succulent rosette plant with wedge-shaped leaves and yellowish flowers in a pyramidal head. A rare escape in frost-free coastal spots.

name: Chiastophyllum oppositifolium
tip: Fleshy toothed leaves in opposite pairs and arching spikes of small yellow flowers. A garden plant sometimes persisting on walls and rocky banks.

name: Crassula aquatica
tip: Tiny aquatic or mud plant with opposite narrow leaves and minute white flowers in the leaf axils. Very rare and easily overlooked.

name: Crassula decumbens
tip: Tiny succulent annual with small, fleshy opposite leaves and minute white flowers. Naturalised on bare ground and paths in the Isles of Scilly.

name: Crassula pubescens
tip: Tiny, slightly hairy succulent forming small mats, with minute white or pinkish flowers. A rare introduction on damp ground.

name: Crassula tillaea
tip: Minute reddish moss-like annual on sandy or gravelly ground, with tiny white flowers crowded among overlapping fleshy leaves.

name: Petrosedum forsterianum
tip: Yellow stonecrop with flat, bluish-green leaves and flower buds that droop, unlike the reflexed stonecrop. Found on rocks and walls in the west.

name: Petrosedum rupestre
tip: Yellow stonecrop with leaves bent backwards and flowerheads nodding in bud. Grows on walls, rocks and roofs, and often spills from gardens.

name: Petrosedum sediforme
tip: Grey-green stonecrop with pale yellowish-white flowers and thick, flat leaves arranged spirally. Naturalised on walls and rocks in a few places in southern England.

name: Phedimus hybridus
tip: Garden stonecrop with toothed, flat, fleshy leaves and yellow flowers in flat heads. An occasional escape on walls and waste ground.

name: Phedimus kamtschaticus
tip: Robust garden stonecrop with toothed alternate leaves and flat heads of yellow flowers. Escapes onto walls and banks.

name: Phedimus spurius
tip: Mat-forming stonecrop with flat toothed leaves in opposite pairs and pink or purplish flowers. Often escapes from gardens onto walls.

name: Phedimus stellatus
tip: Annual stonecrop with flat, lobed or toothed leaves and starry pinkish flowers in leafy spikes. A rare garden casual.

name: Sedum dasyphyllum
tip: Tiny blue-green stonecrop with plump opposite leaves and small white flowers flushed with pink. Naturalised on old walls.

name: Sedum hispanicum
tip: Greyish tufted stonecrop with narrow leaves and white flowers, often pink-streaked, held in loose branched heads. Occasional on walls and rocks.

name: Sedum kimnachii
tip: Rare garden stonecrop with narrow succulent leaves and yellow flowers. A specialist may be needed to confirm it among other yellow stonecrops.

name: Sedum lydium
tip: Tiny, mat-forming stonecrop with crowded narrow green leaves tinged red and small white or pink flowers. Naturalised on walls and rocks.

name: Sedum praealtum
tip: Robust stonecrop with bright green shiny leaves in dense rosettes and clusters of yellow flowers. Naturalised on walls and banks.

name: Sedum sexangulare
tip: Dense mats of tiny, six-ranked cylindrical leaves and yellow flowers; unlike biting stonecrop, it tastes bland. Naturalised on walls and rocks.

name: Sedum spathulifolium
tip: Rosettes of flat, spoon-shaped, grey-blue leaves with yellow flowers. Naturalised on walls, rocks and banks, especially in the north and west.

name: Sedum villosum
tip: Small biennial with sticky, hairy, alternate leaves and pink flowers. Local in damp, rocky mountain places in northern England and Scotland.

name: Thuja occidentalis
tip: Evergreen conifer with flat sprays of scale-like leaves and small upright cones. Often planted in gardens and sometimes self-sown.

name: Dicksonia antarctica
tip: Tree fern with a thick fibrous trunk and a crown of large arching fronds. Planted in mild gardens, occasionally self-sown in western areas.

name: Hypolepis ambigua
tip: Creeping fern with delicate, finely divided, hairy fronds along a long rhizome. A rare, localised garden escape or introduction.

name: Diapensia lapponica
tip: Extremely rare cushion plant with cream-white five-petalled flowers over tight evergreen leaves. Known only in the Highlands, near Lochaber.

name: Drosera anglica
tip: Sticky-leaved carnivorous bog plant with long narrow leaves held erect and small white flowers. Told from round-leaved sundew by its elongated leaves.

name: Drosera intermedia
tip: Carnivorous plant with oblong leaves that curve upwards in a fan and flower stalks that arise from below the rosette. Grows in wet peat and bog.

name: Elaeagnus commutata
tip: Silvery, scaly shrub with oval leaves and small yellow fragrant flowers. A rare planted shrub that occasionally persists.

name: Elatine hexandra
tip: Tiny creeping annual with opposite oval leaves and minute pinkish or white flowers. Rare in the margins of ponds and lakes.

name: Elatine hydropiper
tip: Tiny annual of muddy margins with rounded leaves and minute flowers, the petals pinkish. Rare, in Britain mainly in northern England.

name: Equisetum hyemale
tip: Evergreen unbranched horsetail with stiff, rough, grey-green stems. Told from other horsetails by its black-banded sheath and very rough stem.

name: Equisetum pratense
tip: Slender horsetail with few whorled, simple branches and a rough texture. Very rare, found in a few Scottish areas.

name: Equisetum ramosissimum
tip: Slender, branching horsetail with grooved stems and small black-tipped teeth. Very rare, in damp places in Britain.

name: Equisetum variegatum
tip: Slender evergreen horsetail with dark sheaths that have pale margins. Local in dunes and damp sand.

name: Andromeda polifolia
tip: Low bog shrub with narrow, blue-green leaves and clusters of pink urn-shaped flowers. Grows on wet peat, mainly in northern areas.

name: Arbutus unedo
tip: Evergreen tree with shiny toothed leaves, white urn-shaped flowers and rough red fruits in autumn. Native in south-west Ireland, planted elsewhere.

name: Arctostaphylos alpinus
tip: Low deciduous shrub with net-veined, toothed leaves and white urn flowers, turning red in autumn, with black fruits. Scottish mountains only.

name: Arctostaphylos uva-ursi
tip: Prostrate evergreen with leathery oval leaves, pinkish-white urn flowers and red berries. Grows on heaths and moors.

name: Daboecia cantabrica
tip: Low heath shrub with long spikes of large purple bells, and white-felted leaf undersides. Native only in western Ireland.

name: Erica ciliaris
tip: Heather with large pink bell flowers on one side of the spike and fringed leaves in threes. Local on southern heaths and in west Ireland.

name: Erica erigena
tip: Tall heath with pinkish-purple bells and protruding brown anthers that flower early in spring. Native in western Ireland, introduced elsewhere.

name: Erica lusitanica
tip: Tall evergreen heath with fine bright green leaves in whorls of three and white bells. Naturalised in Cornwall and Devon, flowering in winter.

name: Erica mackayana
tip: Heather with whorls of three leaves and pink-purple bells; hairy leaves distinguish it from cross-leaved heath. Native in western Ireland.

name: Erica terminalis
tip: Tall evergreen heath with narrow whorled leaves and many pink bells in clusters. Planted in gardens and occasionally naturalised.

name: Erica vagans
tip: Dense heath with pink or white bells with dark anthers visible and dense leaves. Native on the Lizard in Cornwall only.

name: Gaultheria mucronata
tip: Prickly, evergreen shrub with small white flowers and plum, pink or white berries. Often planted and occasionally naturalised.

name: Gaultheria procumbens
tip: Low creeping evergreen with glossy oval leaves smelling of wintergreen when crushed; nodding white bells and bright red berries. Garden escape, naturalised in a few acid woods.

name: Gaultheria shallon
tip: Dense evergreen thicket shrub with leathery oval leaves and sticky-hairy stems; pinkish-white urn flowers in one-sided spikes, dark purple berries. Widely planted and naturalised in woods.

name: Hypopitys monotropa
tip: Leafless, waxy pale yellowish plant with scale leaves and a nodding head of bells, parasitic on fungi in shady beech and pine woods and dunes. No green colour.

name: Kalmia angustifolia
tip: Small evergreen shrub with narrow oval leaves in whorls or pairs and small crimson-pink saucer flowers set below the shoot tips. Rare garden plant, hardly naturalised.

name: Kalmia latifolia
tip: Evergreen shrub with glossy laurel-like leaves; pink buds open to pale pink cup flowers with ten pouches holding the anthers. Planted in gardens, rarely persisting in the wild.

name: Kalmia polifolia
tip: Low evergreen with narrow leaves rolled at the edges and whitish beneath, topped by clusters of rose-pink saucers. Garden plant, occasionally naturalised on peat.

name: Kalmia procumbens
tip: Mat-forming creeping evergreen of Scottish mountain tops, with tiny rolled narrow leaves and tiny pink bells. Looks like a dwarf heather but leaves are opposite.

name: Leucothoe fontanesiana
tip: Arching evergreen shrub with long pointed oval leaves and dangling spikes of small white urn flowers from the leaf axils. Garden shrub, occasionally naturalised.

name: Moneses uniflora
tip: Tiny evergreen with a ring of rounded leaves and a single large nodding white flower with a long green style. Rare, in a few Scottish pine woods.

name: Orthilia secunda
tip: Wintergreen with one-sided spike of nodding greenish-white bells and a long straight style; leaves are pointed and often in a lopsided rosette. Local in damp woods and dunes.

name: Phyllodoce caerulea
tip: Dwarf heath-like evergreen with narrow needle-like leaves and nodding purple-pink urn flowers on sticky stalks. Extremely rare, in the Scottish Highlands (Cairngorms area).

name: Pyrola media
tip: Wintergreen with a straight style projecting beyond the whitish-pink bells, longer than Common Wintergreen. Rare in northern Britain and Ireland, in damp woods and moors.

name: Pyrola minor
tip: Wintergreen with small globular whitish-pink bells whose style is short and does not project. Local in damp woods, dunes and mountain ledges.

name: Pyrola rotundifolia
tip: Wintergreen with rounded glossy leaves and white open flowers with a long down-curved style. Local in fens, dune slacks and damp rocky places.

name: Rhododendron groenlandicum
tip: Low evergreen with narrow leaves rolled at the edges and rusty woolly beneath, topped by white flower clusters. Rare garden escape on peaty ground.

name: Rhododendron luteum
tip: Deciduous shrub with sticky hairy leaves and strongly scented bright yellow funnel flowers in clusters before or with the leaves. Planted, naturalised in some woods.

name: Vaccinium corymbosum
tip: Tall deciduous shrub with oval leaves and small white urn flowers; large blue berries. Garden plant, rarely escaping, bigger than native Bilberry.

name: Vaccinium macrocarpon
tip: Creeping evergreen with oval leaves and pink flowers with back-curved petals; fruit large red berries. Garden plant naturalised on bogs, bigger than native Cranberry.

name: Vaccinium microcarpum
tip: Wiry creeping evergreen of peat bogs with tiny narrow leaves, whitish beneath, and pink flowers with swept-back petals. A specialist may be needed to separate from related cranberries.

name: Vaccinium uliginosum
tip: Low deciduous shrub of moors with blue-grey oval leaves and round stems; small pink-white urns and bluish berries. Local in northern uplands.

name: Eriocaulon aquaticum
tip: Aquatic plant with submerged narrow leaves and stalks bearing small greyish-white buttons. Very rare in Britain, in lochs of Skye, and in western Ireland.

name: Euphorbia corallioides
tip: Tall hairy spurge with oval leaves and yellow-green flower heads with rounded, kidney-shaped glands. Casual or planted occasionally, escaped from gardens.

name: Euphorbia cyparissias
tip: Tufted spurge with many thin narrow leaves on short branches and yellow-green bracts turning reddish. Garden escape on dry banks and in graveyards.

name: Euphorbia dulcis
tip: Spurge with oval blunt leaves that turn purple, softly hairy; flower glands are purplish. Rare, naturalised in shady places, escaped from gardens.

name: Euphorbia esula
tip: Spurge with narrow leaves and yellow-green bracts, spreading by creeping roots. A group needing specialist confirmation; local casual on waste ground.

name: Euphorbia hyberna
tip: Hairy perennial spurge with oval leaves and warty fruits, yellow-green. Rare, in woods of south-west Ireland and a few places in south-west England.

name: Euphorbia oblongata
tip: Upright perennial spurge with narrow oval leaves finely toothed near the tip and yellowish-green flower heads. Garden escape, naturalised locally. Check against similar spurges with a specialist.

name: Euphorbia paralias
tip: Fleshy bluish-green spurge of sand dunes with crowded overlapping oval leaves in rows up the stem. Local on southern and western coasts.

name: Euphorbia platyphyllos
tip: Softly hairy annual spurge with oval toothed leaves and three-lobed flower heads; warty fruits. Rare, in arable fields and bare ground in southern England.

name: Euphorbia portlandica
tip: Hairless blue-green spurge with oval leaves, often with red stems; sandy coast. Local on southern and western coasts of Britain and Ireland.

name: Euphorbia stricta
tip: Slender annual spurge with oval toothed leaves and small, warty-fruited flower heads. Very rare, in the Wye Valley and Gloucestershire woodland edges.

name: Euphorbia waldsteinii
tip: Spurge with narrow leaves and yellowish-green flower heads. Rare garden escape; hard to separate from Leafy Spurge, so a specialist is needed to confirm it.

name: Acacia melanoxylon
tip: Evergreen tree with sickle-shaped leaf-like stalks and balls of pale cream-yellow flowers. Introduced Australian species, planted and self-sowing locally, mainly in the south-west.

name: Astragalus alpinus
tip: Low pea with pinnate leaves and short heads of cream-and-violet flowers; hairy pods. Very rare, on mountain rock ledges in the Scottish Highlands.

name: Astragalus danicus
tip: Low hairy pea with pinnate leaves and round heads of purple flowers. Local on chalk and dune grassland, from eastern England and north Scotland.

name: Astragalus glycyphyllos
tip: Tall sprawling pea with large pinnate leaves and dense short spikes of greenish-cream flowers; curved pods. Local on grassy banks and scrub, mainly in the south.

name: Astragalus odoratus
tip: Garden milk-vetch with pinnate leaves and cream or yellowish flower spikes. Seldom seen as casual outside gardens, so check with a specialist.

name: Cicer arietinum
tip: Hairy annual pea with small toothed pinnate leaflets and white to bluish solitary flowers; inflated short pods. A rare crop relic or casual on waste ground.

name: Colutea arborescens
tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves, yellow pea flowers with red-marked standard, and puffed-up papery pods. Planted and naturalised on railway banks and waste ground.

name: Coronilla valentina
tip: Evergreen shrub with grey-green pinnate leaves and rounded heads of scented yellow pea flowers. Garden shrub, rarely casual.

name: Cytisus nigricans
tip: Upright broom-like shrub with three-parted leaves and spikes of small yellow flowers in summer. Garden shrub, rare casual.

name: Cytisus striatus
tip: Tall broom with silky, hairy pods and green angled twigs, yellow flowers in May. Local in the south and west, on waste ground and heaths.

name: Ervilia sylvatica
tip: Scrambling vetch with many pairs of leaflets and drooping sprays of white flowers veined with purple. Local in woods, cliffs and rocky areas.

name: Ervum gracile
tip: Slender climbing vetch with small pale blue-lilac flowers in few-flowered stalked heads; leaflets narrow. Very local on waste ground and field margins. Check with a specialist.

name: Galega officinalis
tip: Tall hairless pea with pinnate leaves and upright spikes of lilac-blue or white flowers. Garden escape on roadsides and rough ground.

name: Genista aetnensis
tip: Tall nearly leafless broom with arching green stems and many yellow flowers in summer. Rare, planted shrub, occasionally casual.

name: Genista anglica
tip: Low spiny shrub with small narrow hairless leaves and yellow pea flowers; spines distinguish from other greenweeds. Local on heaths and moors.

name: Genista hispanica
tip: Dense, spiny small shrub with narrow leaves and clusters of yellow flowers on short stems. Garden shrub, very rarely escaping.

name: Genista monspessulana
tip: Tall evergreen broom shrub with trifoliate leaves and sweet-scented yellow flowers. Garden plant, rare casual in the south-west.

name: Genista pilosa
tip: Low spineless shrub with small hairy narrow oval leaves and yellow flowers in the axils. Very rare, on southern and western sea cliffs and heaths.

name: Genista tinctoria
tip: Spineless low shrub with narrow, oval leaves and yellow pea flowers in spikes; pods hairless. Local in old grassland and rough pastures.

name: Hippocrepis comosa
tip: Low spreading pea with pinnate leaves and heads of yellow flowers; horseshoe-shaped pods. Local on chalk and limestone grassland.

name: Hippocrepis emerus
tip: Shrub with pinnate leaves, small leaflets and pairs of pale yellow flowers on short stalks; pods are thin and jointed. Planted in gardens, rarely naturalised.

name: Lathyrus aphaca
tip: Hairless, grey-green climbing plant with no leaflets, but with pairs of arrow-shaped stipules and a tendril; solitary yellow flowers. Rare, in southern England on waste ground.

name: Lathyrus grandiflorus
tip: Climbing perennial pea with large purple and pink flowers, usually two per stalk, and winged stems absent. Garden escape on waste ground.

name: Lathyrus heterophyllus
tip: Climbing pea with broad winged stem and pink flowers in few-flowered clusters, leaves of two or three pairs of leaflets. Rare garden escape.

name: Lathyrus hirsutus
tip: Slender annual pea with hairy pods and small blue and pink flowers in pairs. Rare, in southern England in disturbed ground.

name: Lathyrus japonicus
tip: Fleshy, spreading pea of shingle beaches with grey-green pinnate leaves and purple-and-blue flowers. Local on the coasts of Britain and Ireland.

name: Lathyrus niger
tip: Upright pea with blue-green leaflets turning black when dried and purple flowers fading blue. Rare, in woods of Scotland and the north.

name: Lathyrus oleraceus
tip: Familiar crop pea with large leaf-like stipules, tendrils and white or purple flowers. Relic of cultivation on tips and rough ground.

name: Lathyrus palustris
tip: Winged-stemmed climbing pea of fens with narrow leaflets and bluish-purple flower clusters. Rare, in fens in East Anglia and a few other sites.

name: Lathyrus sylvestris
tip: Large winged-stemmed climbing pea with narrow leaflets and pink flowers; branched tendrils. Local in hedges and scrub.

name: Lathyrus tuberosus
tip: Slender unwinged pea with pairs of leaflets and bright magenta-pink flowers; underground tubers. Rare casual in cornfields and waste ground.

name: Lathyrus vernus
tip: Upright pea with no tendrils, pairs of pointed leaflets and nodding flowers opening purple and fading blue-green. Garden plant, rarely escaping.

name: Lotus angustissimus
tip: Small, slender annual with tiny trifoliate leaves and one or two yellow flowers; pods very slender. Rare, in the south on dry open ground.

name: Lotus maritimus
tip: Low, spreading pea with leaves of three leaflets plus stipules, and large pale yellow flowers singly; winged pods. Rare, introduced on grassland.

name: Lotus subbiflorus
tip: Small hairy annual trefoil with one to two yellow flowers per head and narrow stipules; local on coast grassland in the south and west.

name: Lotus tenuis
tip: Slender trefoil with narrow leaflets, and long thin stalks bearing small yellow flower heads. Local in damp grassland, mostly in the south and east.

name: Lupinus arboreus
tip: Evergreen shrub with silvery leaves of palmate leaflets and spikes of pale yellow, sometimes bluish, scented flowers. Naturalised on sand and shingle in the south and west.

name: Lupinus nootkatensis
tip: Perennial lupin with hairy palmate leaves and spikes of blue-purple flowers. Introduced and naturalised on river shingle in Scotland and northern England.

name: Lupinus polyphyllus
tip: Tall lupin with palmate leaves of many leaflets and dense spikes of colourful flowers. Naturalised on roadsides, riverbanks and waste ground.

name: Medicago arborea
tip: Evergreen shrub with grey-green trefoil leaves and clusters of yellow pea flowers followed by coiled pods. Rare, planted and escaped in the south, usually coastal.

name: Medicago littoralis
tip: Small, hairy annual medick with clover-like leaves and a few small yellow flowers. Rare, in a few sandy sites in the south.

name: Medicago minima
tip: Small downy annual medick with spiny burs coiled in several turns; leaves clover-like. Local on sandy soils, such as Breckland and coasts.

name: Medicago polymorpha
tip: Spreading, almost hairless annual with trefoil leaves and clusters of small yellow flowers; flat spiny coiled pods. Local on grassland and waste ground.

name: Medicago truncatula
tip: Rare annual medick with trifoliate leaves, small yellow flowers and barrel-shaped coiled pods. Casual on waste ground and tips.

name: Melilotus indicus
tip: Annual melilot with trifoliate toothed leaves and tiny pale yellow flowers in slender spikes. Casual, on waste ground, tips and roadsides.

name: Ononis reclinata
tip: Small sticky-hairy restharrow with trifoliate leaves, pink flowers shorter than the calyx and no thorns. Very rare, on a few southern coasts.

name: Ononis spinosa
tip: Spiny low shrub with pink pea flowers and trifoliate toothed leaves, forming tangled mats. Local on rough grassland, mostly on lime-rich soils.

name: Ornithopus compressus
tip: Hairy, low annual with pinnate leaves and small pale yellow flowers in clusters of few; pods curved. Rare, in the Channel Islands or casual elsewhere.

name: Ornithopus pinnatus
tip: Slender, feathery annual with pinnate leaves and small orange-yellow flowers veined with red, in small heads. Rare, in the Isles of Scilly, Channel Islands and some sandy heaths.

name: Ornithopus sativus
tip: Sprawling annual with pinnate leaves and small pale pink flowers in tiny heads; the curved, beaded pods resemble a bird's foot. Cultivated, occasionally casual on sandy ground.

name: Oxytropis campestris
tip: Silky tufted plant with pinnate leaves and pale creamy-yellow, often purple-tinged flowers in short heads. Rare, on Scottish mountain rock ledges, notably Clova and Glen Shee.

name: Oxytropis halleri
tip: Tufted silky plant with pinnate leaves and bluish-purple pea flowers in rounded heads. Shorter-stalked than Yellow Oxytropis; grows on dry coastal Scottish grassland and rocks.

name: Securigera varia
tip: Sprawling hairless pea with pinnate leaves and rounded heads of pink and white flowers. Pods break into joints. Escape from cultivation on roadsides and waste ground.

name: Spartium junceum
tip: Tall, rush-like shrub with almost leafless green stems and large fragrant yellow pea flowers. Differs from Broom by round stems, no ridges, and larger flowers. Naturalised locally.

name: Thermopsis montana
tip: Upright perennial with clover-like three-part leaves and a tall spike of bright yellow pea flowers. Garden escape, occasionally naturalised.

name: Trifolium aureum
tip: Yellow clover with golden globular heads that turn brown with age. Larger than Hop Trefoil, with leaflets all attached together. Rare, mainly on northern and western grassland.

name: Trifolium bocconei
tip: Small hairy annual clover with pink flowers in stalkless clustered pairs at stem branches. Very rare, on dry coastal turf in Cornwall, especially the Lizard.

name: Trifolium fragiferum
tip: Low creeping clover; pink heads become inflated and pinkish like small strawberries or balloons when fruiting. Grows on damp grassland, often near the coast.

name: Trifolium glomeratum
tip: Low, hairless annual clover with tight, stalkless balls of small pink flowers at each stem joint. Spiky star-shaped fruiting calyces. Found on sandy ground in south and east England.

name: Trifolium incarnatum
tip: Upright hairy clover with long cylindrical heads of vivid crimson flowers. Wild Cornish plants have paler cream-pink flowers. Frequent as a field crop or casual.

name: Trifolium occidentale
tip: Low clover with small white heads and leaflets often bearing a pale V mark. Rooting stems and early flowering distinguish it from White Clover. Found coastally in south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

name: Trifolium ochroleucon
tip: Upright, hairy clover with big, blunt, creamy-yellow heads. Very rare, on clay grassland and verges in East Anglia and the southern Midlands.

name: Trifolium ornithopodioides
tip: Tiny prostrate plant with few-flowered white or pinkish heads and trefoil leaves. Pods spread like a bird's foot. Found on damp heathy ground in the south and west.

name: Trifolium scabrum
tip: Low, stiff, hairy annual with small white or pinkish heads tucked into leaf axils. Fruiting calyces are rigid and curved. Grows on dry bare banks and coastal turf.

name: Trifolium squamosum
tip: Low annual clover with small pink heads at stem tips, lying on a pair of leaves. Calyces become spiky and star-like in fruit. Found on coastal grassland in the south.

name: Trifolium stellatum
tip: Hairy annual with pinkish-white heads, whose red-tinged spreading calyx teeth form a starry fruiting head. Naturalised since 1900s on shingle at Shoreham, Sussex.

name: Trifolium strictum
tip: Small, slender, hairless clover with small pink heads on long stalks and narrow leaflets. Very rare, restricted to the Lizard peninsula, Cornwall, in short grassland.

name: Trifolium subterraneum
tip: Hairy, prostrate annual with few creamy-white flowers. After flowering, the head buries itself in the soil. Found on dry sandy turf, mainly in southern England.

name: Trifolium suffocatum
tip: Tiny prostrate annual forming tight, stalkless clusters of white flowers pressed to the ground. Rare, on bare sandy or gravelly coastal ground in the south and east.

name: Trigonella foenum-graecum
tip: Upright, hairy annual with clover-like leaves and pale cream-yellow flowers singly or in pairs. Spice-scented; long beaked pods. Casual from birdseed or cultivation.

name: Ulex minor
tip: Low, spiny shrub of heaths, with small deep yellow flowers in late summer. Smaller than Gorse, with weaker spines and tiny bracteoles. Flowers when Western Gorse is also present.

name: Vicia bithynica
tip: Climbing vetch with pinnate leaves, two to three pairs of leaflets, and one to three purple and yellow flowers. Rare, on coastal slopes in south-west England and Wales.

name: Vicia lathyroides
tip: Tiny, short, softly hairy annual with solitary small purple flowers. Pods black and hairy. Found on sandy ground, dunes and heaths.

name: Vicia lens
tip: Slender annual vetch with few small pale bluish-white flowers and short flat pods. Casual crop escape on tips and waste ground.

name: Vicia lutea
tip: Sprawling, hairless or hairy vetch with large pale yellow flowers, singly or in pairs, and large hairy pods. Rare, on coastal shingle and cliffs.

name: Vicia orobus
tip: Upright vetch with no tendrils and many leaflet pairs; flowers cream-white with purple veins. Found on western rocky woods and hill pastures.

name: Vicia pannonica
tip: Annual vetch with dull yellowish or brownish-purple flowers, one to three together, and hairy pods. Rare casual or escape from cultivation.

name: Vicia tenuifolia
tip: Tall, climbing vetch with long spikes of violet-blue flowers on lengthy stalks, and narrow leaflets. Found on grassy banks, mostly in England.

name: Vicia villosa
tip: Tall climbing vetch with dense one-sided spikes of violet and whitish flowers, hairy stems and wide spreading calyx. Often sown, and persisting on field edges.

name: Frankenia laevis
tip: Low, wiry mat-forming plant with tiny rolled grey-green leaves and small pink flowers. Rare, on drying saltmarsh edges in East Anglia and the south coast.

name: Centaurium littorale
tip: Short centaury with narrow leaves, flowers in a compact head, and a yellow-green tone. Grows in dune slacks, mostly in north-west England, Wales and Scotland.

name: Centaurium portense
tip: Small pink-flowered centaury relative with narrow oval leaves. Specialist check needed. Rare, mainly as a casual or near coasts.

name: Centaurium pulchellum
tip: Branched, slender centaury with many small pink flowers on diverging branches and stalkless blooms. Scarce in southern England on grassy ground and dunes.

name: Centaurium tenuiflorum
tip: Slim branched centaury of coastal grassland, with small pink flowers on distinct short stalks and narrow leaves. Mostly south and east England.

name: Cicendia filiformis
tip: Tiny, thread-like annual with small yellow four-petalled flowers. Found on damp sandy heathy ground in the south-west, Wales and Ireland.

name: Exaculum pusillum
tip: Tiny, slender annual with small pink-and-white flowers and thread-like stems. Found only on Guernsey and Jersey, on damp heathy ground.

name: Gentiana acaulis
tip: Tufted alpine with large deep blue trumpet flowers on short stems and green-spotted throats. Garden plant; not native.

name: Gentiana asclepiadea
tip: Arching leafy stems bearing blue trumpets in pairs in the upper leaf axils; leaves willow-like. Garden plant, seldom escaping.

name: Gentiana nivalis
tip: Tiny annual with small bright blue flowers on short stems. Extremely rare, restricted to Scottish mountain turf in Perthshire and Argyll.

name: Gentiana pneumonanthe
tip: Slender plant with deep blue trumpets striped green outside, on wet heaths. Late flowering and scarce, mainly in the south and north-west.

name: Gentiana verna
tip: Tiny tufted plant with intense bright blue star flowers, at ground level. Very rare, in Upper Teesdale and Burren, Ireland.

name: Gentianella campestris
tip: Biennial with four-lobed purple-blue flowers; outer calyx lobes are broad and overlap the inner pair. Found on acid grassland in the north and west.

name: Gentianella germanica
tip: Short biennial with five-lobed lilac-blue flowers in clusters. Rare, on chalk grassland in southern England, mainly the Chilterns.

name: Gentianopsis ciliata
tip: Slender plant with single blue flowers with fringed petal edges. Grown in gardens; not native in Britain or Ireland.

name: Erodium aethiopicum
tip: Low perennial rosette with feathery hairy leaves and pink flowers. Specialist check advised; sporadic as a garden escape or casual.

name: Erodium manescavii
tip: Tufted perennial with pinnate leaves and bright magenta flowers having dark veins. Garden plant that rarely becomes naturalised.

name: Erodium maritimum
tip: Low plant with tiny pale pink or no petals and unlobed or slightly lobed leaves. Found on coastal turf in south-west England, Wales and Ireland.

name: Erodium moschatum
tip: Sticky, musk-scented plant with pinnate leaves having toothed leaflets and flowers with purple petals. Found on coastal banks and waste ground, mainly in the south and west.

name: Geranium dalmaticum
tip: Low, mat-forming perennial with rounded, deeply cut glossy leaves and pale pink flowers. Occasional garden escape.

name: Geranium herrerae
tip: Garden crane's-bill with deeply cut leaves and pink flowers. Specialist check needed; rare casual.

name: Geranium himalayense
tip: Clump-forming garden plant with big violet-blue flowers with reddish veins, and deeply lobed leaves. Occasional escape.

name: Geranium ibericum
tip: Garden perennial with large violet-blue flowers on branched stems and deeply cut hairy leaves. Occasional escape on verges.

name: Geranium maderense
tip: Tall, fleshy-stemmed garden geranium with big divided leaves and magenta flowers. Tender; naturalised only in mild south-west areas.

name: Geranium nodosum
tip: Woodland garden geranium with glossy three-lobed leaves and lilac flowers having darker veins. Occasionally naturalised.

name: Geranium phaeum
tip: Clump-forming perennial with nodding, almost black-purple, reflexed-petalled flowers. Naturalised on shady roadsides and hedge banks.

name: Geranium platypetalum
tip: Garden geranium with large violet-blue, purple-veined flowers and rounded, lobed hairy leaves. Rare escape.

name: Geranium psilostemon
tip: Tall garden crane's-bill with big magenta flowers with a black central eye. Occasionally escapes.

name: Geranium purpureum
tip: Small, strong-smelling annual like Herb-Robert with a reddish stem, ridged nutlets and small pink flowers. Found on shingle and walls in south-west England and Ireland.

name: Geranium reuteri
tip: Herb-Robert-like plant from Atlantic islands with pink flowers; specialist check needed. Naturalised in Cornwall and southern coasts.

name: Geranium versicolor
tip: Garden geranium with whitish flowers lined with fine violet veins. Naturalised on banks and verges in places.

name: Geranium yeoi
tip: Garden-origin crane's-bill with pink flowers and lobed leaves. Specialist check needed; sporadic escape.

name: Pelargonium inodorum
tip: Sprawling, rare pelargonium relative with lobed leaves and whitish or pinkish flowers. Garden or casual, southern and coastal.

name: Pelargonium tomentosum
tip: Soft, velvety, strongly mint-scented garden pelargonium with big heart-shaped lobed leaves and small white flowers. Tender and rarely seen outside gardens.

name: Ribes alpinum
tip: Small, upright shrub with three-lobed leaves and small greenish flowers in separate male and female spikes. Found in limestone woods in northern England and Wales.

name: Ribes spicatum
tip: Rare northern currant with lobed leaves and hairy undersides; greenish flowers in hairy racemes. Found in limestone woods in northern England and Orkney.

name: Gunnera tinctoria
tip: Huge, rhubarb-like plant with prickly stalks and giant lobed leaves. Dense, cone-like reddish flower spikes appear. Invasive on streamsides in western Britain and Ireland.
